shard.title: The Caribbean and the American mainland tropics
shard.author: Caribbean regional historian agent
shard.note: Thirty territories and twenty-six events covering the British Caribbean from St Kitts 1624 to the independences of 1962-83, plus the mainland tropics (British Honduras, British Guiana, the Mosquito Coast, the Bay Islands) and the wartime occupations of French, Spanish, Dutch and Danish colonies that never appear on the pink map. Belize, Guyana, the Mosquito Coast and the Bay Islands carry region "caribbean" rather than "south-america": they are Caribbean-basin colonies, were governed as part of the British West Indies, and belong with the islands in the legend. Geography gaps recorded in the prose rather than invented as unit ids: no separate units exist for Demerara, Essequibo and Berbice, for the Essequibo region Venezuela claims, for the Grenadines split between St Vincent and Grenada, for Redonda, for Balliceaux, or for the Kalinago Territory in Dominica.

namesOverTime.name: Liamuiga

from.note: A rough marker for the pre-contact centuries, not an event; Kalinago settlement is dated by archaeology, not documents.

namesOverTime.note: Usually translated 'fertile land'. The modern independent state put the name back on its highest mountain.

namesOverTime.name: San Cristóbal
namesOverTime.note: Named on Columbus's second voyage. The Spanish never settled it.

namesOverTime.name: St Christopher's Island
namesOverTime.note: 'St Kitts' was sailors' shorthand from the start and is now the official short name.

namesOverTime.name: St Kitts
namesOverTime.note: Saint Christopher is still the island's formal name inside the state's title, Saint Christopher and Nevis; St Kitts is what is on the map, the airport and the passport.

modernSuccessors.name: Saint Christopher and Nevis
modernSuccessors.note: The smallest sovereign state in the Americas by both area and population.

geoCoverage.label: The English middle of a shared island
geoCoverage.change: England and France divided the island between them in 1627: the English took the centre, the French the two ends. For 86 years the map shows one island under two flags.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: The Treaty of Utrecht gave Britain the French quarters. St Kitts became one colony for the first time, and the French planters left or swore allegiance.

date.note: The date English settlers recorded, under the Julian calendar then used in England; contemporaries wrote the year as 1623/24.

acquisitions.how: Thomas Warner landed about fifteen men at Old Road Bay and planted tobacco with the permission of the Kalinago leader Tegremante, whose people fed them through their first year.

counterparties.name: Kalinago of Liamuiga
counterparties.lost: Within two years they lost the island, their leader and most of their lives: the settlers they had fed turned on them in 1626 and killed or expelled the survivors.
counterparties.note: Kalinago is the people's own name. Older British books call them 'Caribs', a Spanish coinage that also gave English the word cannibal, for which there is no good evidence here.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Nothing at first — the two colonies shared the island by treaty from 1627 — but France lost its quarters permanently in 1713.
counterparties.note: Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc arrived shipwrecked in 1625 and the two rivals agreed to split the island rather than fight over it.

instrument.name: Royal commission to Thomas Warner as governor of St Christopher, Nevis, Barbados and Montserrat
instrument.note: Warner sailed first and got the paperwork afterwards. The Earl of Carlisle's proprietary grant over the same islands followed in 1627 and was disputed for a decade.

people.name: Thomas Warner
people.role: captain who founded the colony and governed it until his death in 1649

people.name: Tegremante
people.role: Kalinago leader who allowed the English to settle and was killed in the 1626 attack

people.name: Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc
people.role: founded the French colony alongside the English in 1625 and signed the 1627 partition

acquisitions.resistance: The Kalinago gathered fighters from neighbouring islands in 1626; the English and French struck first at Bloody Point and killed most of them in a night attack.

evidence.author: Richard S. Dunn
evidence.work: Sugar and Slaves: The Rise of the Planter Class in the English West Indies, 1624-1713
evidence.supports: The founding of St Kitts as the first English Caribbean colony and the Anglo-French partition.

acquisitions.how: France signed over its half of the island at Utrecht after losing the War of the Spanish Succession; British troops had already driven the French planters out in 1702.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Half of one of its oldest Caribbean colonies, together with the French planters' estates, which were auctioned to British buyers from 1726.

instrument.name: Treaty of Utrecht
instrument.note: The same treaty gave Britain the Asiento, the contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America — the moment Britain became the Atlantic's biggest slave trader.

from.note: English Julian dating; contemporaries wrote 1623/24.

statusPeriods.label: Private colony under the Caribbee proprietors
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Earl of Carlisle held the island as a personal grant from Charles I, appointed the governor and took rent from every planter; the Crown ruled at one remove and the French ruled both ends.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Old Road Town, under a proprietor in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Protestant male freeholders only. Enslaved Africans, who were the majority by the 1670s, had no legal standing at all.

statusPeriods.label: Chief colony of the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor-general appointed in London sat at Basseterre and ran the whole Leeward group, while an elected planter assembly voted the taxes and wrote the slave laws.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basseterre, under the Council of Trade and Plantations in London
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders. In 1745 that was fewer than 400 men governing about 20,000 enslaved people.
statusPeriods.note: Sir Charles Wheler's commission of 1671 separated the Leeward Islands from Barbados and gave them their own governor-in-chief.

statusPeriods.label: French occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A French army of 8,000 under the Marquis de Bouillé besieged Brimstone Hill for a month and took it; France governed St Kitts for eighteen months and handed it back at the peace.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Britain had no authority here at all: the island was governed by France. Degree 0 rather than the default 5, which describes a British occupation of someone else's territory.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basseterre, under the French governor-general at Martinique
statusPeriods.note: The British garrison of 1,000 held out for 27 days against 8,000 and was allowed to march out with the honours of war. The Treaty of Versailles returned the island in 1783.

statusPeriods.label: Sugar colony with a planter assembly
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The planter assembly returned with the British flag, and went on voting its own taxes until the assemblies of the small islands were abolished after Morant Bay.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basseterre
statusPeriods.franchise: A property franchise that excluded almost everyone; formerly enslaved people were free from 1838 but nearly all too poor to vote.

statusPeriods.label: Presidency in the Leeward Islands Federation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: London ran St Kitts through a federal governor at Antigua and a local administrator, with a legislature the Colonial Office could out-vote; the elected element came back only in the 1930s.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basseterre, under the Governor of the Leeward Islands at St John's, Antigua
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1937, when a limited franchise returned; universal adult suffrage came in 1952.
statusPeriods.note: Anguilla and Nevis were joined to St Kitts as one presidency in 1882 — an administrative convenience that produced two secession movements. The Leeward Islands Federation was dissolved in 1956 and the colony joined the West Indies Federation from 1958 to 1962.

statusPeriods.label: Associated State of St Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: St Kitts ran everything except defence and foreign affairs, and could take independence whenever its parliament voted for it. Anguilla answered by throwing the St Kitts police off the island in May 1967.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basseterre
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

departures.how: After a London conference in December 1982, Britain legislated St Kitts and Nevis into independence; the opposition boycotted the ceremony and Nevis came in only after being promised the right to leave again.

led.name: Kennedy Simmonds
led.role: Premier who negotiated independence and became the first Prime Minister

led.name: Robert Bradshaw
led.role: sugar-worker, trade unionist and Premier from 1966; built the labour movement that made independence possible and died in 1978

led.name: Simeon Daniel
led.role: Nevis leader who signed his island in only after the constitution gave Nevis a right of secession

departures.movement: People's Action Movement and Nevis Reformation Party

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. The violence in this story came sixteen years earlier, when British paratroopers landed on Anguilla to stop it leaving the same state.

departures.borders: Anguilla had already gone. The new country was two islands rather than three, and its constitution gave Nevis a legal route out that Nevis tried to use in 1998.

slavery.note: St Kitts was the laboratory: the first English Caribbean colony, the first to switch from tobacco to sugar, and by 1770 an island of 20,000 enslaved people and fewer than 1,800 free ones.

abolitionDate.note: The Slave Trade Act ended British trafficking. It freed nobody already enslaved.

emancipationDate.note: Legal freedom came on 1 August 1834 but was followed by four years of unpaid 'apprenticeship'. St Kitts's apprentices struck on the first day of it.

toll.money: £329,393 was paid to St Kitts slave-owners in 1836 for 19,780 people. The 19,780 received nothing. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: The range is for Africans landed in St Kitts across the whole period, from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database; many were re-exported to other colonies, so arrivals overstate the number who stayed.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.work: Legacies of British Slavery database
warrant.supports: £329,393 was paid to St Kitts slave-owners in 1836 for 19,780 people.
warrant.check: ucl.ac.uk/lbs — browse by colony. Every award transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission’s registers, T 71, The National Archives, Kew.

warrant.author: David Eltis and David Richardson
warrant.work: Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade
warrant.supports: The number of enslaved Africans landed in St Kitts: 200,000 to 300,000.
warrant.check: Yale University Press, 2010; the voyage-by-voyage data behind it is at slavevoyages.org, Estimates.

populationTransfer.note: Two hundred years of forced African migration, followed after 1838 by Portuguese Madeirans and by workers walking between the islands looking for wages.

violence.note: The 1626 killing at Bloody Point destroyed the island's Kalinago population, and the 1834 'Apprenticeship rebellion' was put down with martial law and floggings.

commonwealth.note: The British monarch is still head of state, represented by a Governor-General.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar ran the island for 350 years. The state-owned sugar industry finally closed on 31 July 2005, and tourism and citizenship-by-investment replaced it.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, an assembly tradition going back to the 1640s, and a constitution that gives Nevis its own legislature and a legal right to secede.

peak.populationNote: 1980 census for St Kitts and Nevis together. In 1774 the islands held about 23,500 people, of whom roughly 90 per cent were enslaved.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: St Kitts’s largest recorded population: 44,404 people, counted in 1980.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Richard S. Dunn
evidence.work: Sugar and Slaves: The Rise of the Planter Class in the English West Indies, 1624-1713
evidence.supports: Foundation, the Anglo-French partition and the sugar revolution.

evidence.author: B. W. Higman
evidence.work: A Concise History of the Caribbean
evidence.supports: Long-run demography, the Leeward Islands federations and the road to independence.

evidence.author: Andrew Jackson O'Shaughnessy
evidence.work: An Empire Divided: The American Revolution and the British Caribbean
evidence.supports: The 1782 French capture and why the sugar islands did not join the American rebellion.

pedagogy.hook: The British Empire in the Caribbean began with fifteen men planting tobacco on land a Kalinago leader lent them. Two years later they killed him.

misconception.belief: Britain took Caribbean islands from Spain, which had already wiped out the local people.
misconception.correction: St Kitts was taken from the Kalinago, who were living there, farming it, and strong enough that England and France cooperated to attack them at Bloody Point in 1626. Spain never settled the island. The people who lost St Kitts were its inhabitants, not another empire.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Everything the British Caribbean became was tried here first: the shared island, the proprietary grant, the switch from tobacco to sugar, the slave code, and the planter assembly that outlasted slavery by a century.

date.note: Julian date as recorded in England.

keyDates.what: Thomas Warner founds the first English colony in the Caribbean
English and French settlers kill the Kalinago at Bloody Point
Utrecht gives Britain the whole island
Brimstone Hill falls to the French after a 27-day siege
Full emancipation, after four years of apprenticeship
Independence as Saint Christopher and Nevis

namesOverTime.name: Oualie

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact centuries, dated by archaeology rather than documents.

namesOverTime.note: Usually translated 'land of beautiful waters'.

namesOverTime.name: Nuestra Señora de las Nieves
namesOverTime.note: 'Our Lady of the Snows', for the cloud that sits permanently on the peak. English sailors shortened it to Nevis.

modernSuccessors.name: Saint Christopher and Nevis
modernSuccessors.note: Nevis has its own Island Assembly, its own premier and a constitutional right to secede.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: Nevis is a single volcano in the sea; its extent never changed in 355 years.

date.note: The month is not securely recorded; July 1628 is often given.

acquisitions.how: Anthony Hilton took about eighty settlers across from crowded St Kitts and founded a colony at Jamestown, on land the Kalinago had used seasonally and were in no position to defend after 1626.

counterparties.name: Kalinago of Oualie
counterparties.lost: Their remaining foothold in the northern Leewards. The killings at Bloody Point on St Kitts two years earlier had already broken the Kalinago of this group of islands.

people.name: Anthony Hilton
people.role: led the settlement party from St Kitts and became the first governor

statusPeriods.label: Carlisle proprietary colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nevis was part of the Earl of Carlisle's Caribbee grant, governed by a deputy from St Kitts, with an elected assembly of planters from 1658.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Charlestown, under the proprietor in London
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders only.

statusPeriods.label: Richest of the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A local assembly and council governed under the Leeward Islands governor-general; in the 1670s and 1680s Nevis was the Royal African Company's main Caribbean slave market and the wealthiest island in the group.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Charlestown, under the Governor of the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders. In 1780 that was a few hundred men in a population of about 10,000.
statusPeriods.note: A French raid under Iberville in 1706 burned Charlestown and carried off between 3,000 and 3,400 enslaved people, roughly a third of the island's enslaved population.

statusPeriods.label: French occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: French forces took Nevis without a fight while besieging St Kitts, and administered it until the Treaty of Versailles handed it back.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Britain exercised no authority; France governed. Degree 0 rather than the default 5, which describes British occupation of another power's land.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Charlestown, under the French command at St Kitts

statusPeriods.label: Sugar island in slow decline
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The old assembly resumed, governing a shrinking sugar economy; after emancipation the estates broke up and Nevis became an island of small farmers, the first in the British Caribbean where that happened at scale.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Charlestown
statusPeriods.franchise: Property qualifications that almost no formerly enslaved family could meet.

statusPeriods.label: Joined to St Kitts by order of London
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nevis lost its own legislature and was merged with St Kitts and Anguilla into one presidency of the Leeward Islands. Nevisians did not ask for this and have been arguing about it ever since.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basseterre, St Kitts, under the Governor of the Leeward Islands at Antigua
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1937; universal adult suffrage from 1952.

statusPeriods.label: Part of the Associated State
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Full internal self-government was exercised from Basseterre, which is precisely what Nevisians objected to; the Nevis Reformation Party was founded in 1970 to get the island out.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basseterre
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

departures.how: Nevis agreed to enter the new state only after the 1983 constitution gave it its own Island Assembly and a legal procedure for secession — the only such clause in the Commonwealth Caribbean.

led.name: Simeon Daniel
led.role: founder of the Nevis Reformation Party and first Premier of Nevis; negotiated the secession clause

led.name: Kennedy Simmonds
led.role: Prime Minister of the new state

cost.note: No deaths. The cost was constitutional: a country of 45,000 people built with a break-up clause inside it.

departures.borders: The old three-island presidency ended as two states: Anguilla stayed British, and Nevis joined St Kitts on terms it could revoke.

slavery.note: In the 1670s and 1680s Nevis was the Royal African Company's chief Caribbean depot: captives were landed at Charlestown, sold, and shipped on to the other islands and to the mainland colonies.

abolitionDate.note: End of the British slave trade, not of slavery.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom on paper in 1834, four years of unpaid apprenticeship, full freedom in 1838.

toll.money: £151,006 was paid in 1836 to the owners of 8,815 enslaved Nevisians. The 8,815 got nothing. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: Compensation figures come from the Slave Compensation Commission records, digitised by the Legacies of British Slavery database at University College London.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.work: Legacies of British Slavery database
warrant.supports: £151,006 was paid in 1836 to the owners of 8,815 enslaved Nevisians.
warrant.check: ucl.ac.uk/lbs — browse by colony. Every award transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission’s registers, T 71, The National Archives, Kew.

populationTransfer.note: Africans trafficked in for two centuries, then Nevisians leaving: to Trinidad and the Dominican Republic for cane, to Panama for the canal, and to Britain after 1948.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar failed early here, so Nevis broke up into small freeholds sooner than anywhere else in the British Caribbean, and lived on remittances long before tourism.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law with a federal constitution that treats a 93-square-kilometre island as a partner state, not a parish.

peak.populationNote: 1980 census. In 1707 Nevis held about 3,700 enslaved people and 1,100 free colonists.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Nevis’s largest recorded population: 9,428 people, counted in 1980.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Vincent K. Hubbard
evidence.work: Swords, Ships and Sugar: History of Nevis
evidence.supports: Settlement, the 1706 French raid, the sugar economy and the twentieth-century secession movement.

evidence.author: Richard S. Dunn
evidence.work: Sugar and Slaves: The Rise of the Planter Class in the English West Indies, 1624-1713
evidence.supports: Nevis as the richest Leeward island and as a Royal African Company slave market.

pedagogy.hook: Alexander Hamilton, whose face is on the American ten-dollar bill, was born on Nevis and grew up in a Caribbean town that lived on selling people.

misconception.belief: Small colonies were unimportant sideshows to the big ones.
misconception.correction: In the 1680s Nevis, an island of 93 square kilometres, was the busiest English slave market in the Americas and richer per head than any mainland colony. Size on a map tells you almost nothing about a place's weight in the empire's economy.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Nevis shows what happened after sugar failed: estates broken into smallholdings, an island of peasant farmers by 1900, and a people who spent a century arguing that being governed from the next island along was still being governed by someone else.

namesOverTime.name: Wa'ladli

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact centuries; Arawakan and later Kalinago settlement is dated by archaeology.

namesOverTime.note: Also written Wadadli. It is the name on the island's beer and, increasingly, in its schools.

namesOverTime.name: Santa María la Antigua
namesOverTime.note: Named by Columbus for a church in Seville. Spain never settled it: there was too little fresh water.

geoCoverage.label: Antigua and its small dependencies
geoCoverage.change: Barbuda and Redonda were administered from Antigua from 1860 and 1872 but are recorded here as separate places, because they had separate histories.

date.note: The month is not securely recorded; the party crossed from St Kitts during 1632.

acquisitions.how: Edward Warner led a party of settlers from St Kitts and claimed the island for the Earl of Carlisle; Kalinago raiders burned the settlement twice in the 1630s and carried off colonists before being driven out.

counterparties.name: Kalinago of Wa'ladli
counterparties.lost: The island. They used Antigua for fishing and cultivation from bases on Dominica and Guadeloupe, raided the settlers for a decade, and were gone from it by the 1640s.

people.name: Edward Warner
people.role: led the settlement party from St Kitts; son of Thomas Warner

people.name: Christopher Codrington
people.role: brought sugar and the plantation system from Barbados in 1674 and built Betty's Hope

acquisitions.resistance: Kalinago raids destroyed the settlement in 1640 and killed or captured colonists including the governor's wife; the English answered with punitive expeditions to Dominica.

statusPeriods.label: Carlisle proprietary colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governed as part of the Caribbee proprietorship from St Kitts, with an assembly of settlers from the 1640s and almost no interest from London.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St John's, under the proprietor in London
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders.

statusPeriods.label: Sugar colony and naval base
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An elected assembly of planters made the laws and voted the taxes; from 1690 the Leeward Islands governor-general usually resided at Antigua, and from 1728 the Royal Navy based its Caribbean squadron at English Harbour.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St John's, under the Governor of the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders — in 1774 about 500 men in a population of 37,800, of whom 34,000 were enslaved.
statusPeriods.note: Horatio Nelson commanded the Leeward Islands squadron from English Harbour between 1784 and 1787 and was disliked for enforcing the Navigation Acts against Antiguan merchants trading with the new United States.

statusPeriods.label: Capital of the Leeward Islands Federation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The assembly gave up its powers and Antigua was governed by a British governor and a nominated council from St John's, which was also the capital of the whole Leeward group until 1956.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St John's
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1936; universal adult suffrage from 1951.
statusPeriods.note: The Antigua Trades and Labour Union, founded in 1939 after the Moyne Commission, became the political machine that took the island to independence.

statusPeriods.label: Associated State of Antigua
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Antigua governed itself completely except for defence and foreign affairs, and could declare independence whenever its parliament chose. Barbuda spent the whole period asking not to be included.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St John's
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

departures.how: Vere Bird's government took independence at a London conference in December 1980 over the objections of Barbuda's delegates, who walked out and asked Britain to keep their island separate.

led.name: Vere Cornwall Bird
led.role: union leader from 1943, Chief Minister, and first Prime Minister

led.name: Hilbourne Frank
led.role: Barbudan leader who argued at the London conference that Barbuda should not be handed to St John's

led.name: George Walter
led.role: opposition leader and former Premier who opposed the timing of independence

departures.movement: Antigua Labour Party, built on the Antigua Trades and Labour Union

cost.note: No deaths at independence. The unresolved cost was Barbuda's consent, which was never given and remains a live constitutional argument.

departures.borders: The border that mattered was internal: a 62-square-kilometre island with 1,200 people was locked into a state run from another island 40 kilometres away.

slavery.note: Antigua was worked almost entirely by enslaved Africans: by 1774 they were 34,000 of a population of 37,800, cutting cane on around 160 estates on an island with no rivers.

abolitionDate.note: The Slave Trade Act ended British trafficking; enslavement continued.

emancipationDate.note: Antigua was one of only two British colonies to refuse the four-year apprenticeship and free everyone outright in 1834. Planters calculated that on an island with no spare land, freed people would have to work for them anyway.

toll.money: £425,547 was paid to Antiguan slave-owners in 1836 for 29,121 people. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: The arrivals range is from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database and covers the whole period; the compensation figure is from the Slave Compensation Commission records digitised by University College London.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.supports: £425,547 was paid to Antiguan slave-owners in 1836 for 29,121 people.

warrant.work: Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade
warrant.supports: The number of enslaved Africans landed in Antigua: 150,000 to 200,000.
warrant.check: Yale University Press, 2010; the voyage-by-voyage data behind it is at slavevoyages.org, Estimates.

violence.note: The 1736 conspiracy led by an enslaved man called Court, known as Prince Klaas, ended with 88 executions: five broken on the wheel, six hung in chains to starve, and 77 burned alive.

toll.note: The figure is from the court records of the planters who carried out the executions, analysed by David Barry Gaspar. Whether a plot existed at the scale the court described is disputed; the executions are not.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar closed in 1972; the naval dockyard Nelson used is now a World Heritage site full of yachts, and tourism supplies most of the country's income.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, a Westminster parliament, and an eighteenth-century dockyard that is the island's biggest single employer of history.

peak.populationNote: 1980 census for Antigua and Barbuda together, about 74,000. In 1774 the island held 37,808 people, of whom 34,000 were enslaved.

evidence.author: Richard S. Dunn

evidence.supports: Settlement, the Codringtons and the coming of sugar.

pedagogy.hook: Antigua freed every enslaved person outright in 1834 — not out of kindness, but because its planters worked out that on an island with no spare land, free people would have to come back to work anyway.

misconception.belief: Emancipation in 1834 meant enslaved people in the British Caribbean became free that day.
misconception.correction: Almost everywhere it meant six years as an unpaid 'apprentice' for your former owner, until 1838. Only Antigua and Bermuda skipped it. Antigua's planters chose full freedom because they had already concluded that hunger would discipline their workforce more cheaply than law.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Antigua is the cleanest evidence that emancipation was designed around planters' interests, not enslaved people's welfare — and English Harbour shows how tightly the sugar islands and the Royal Navy were locked together.

Prince Klaas's conspiracy; 88 people executed
Full emancipation with no apprenticeship

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact centuries; the name is recorded in later tradition.
English usage settles on the name in the second quarter of the seventeenth century; earlier Spanish charts use variants of Barbada.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: Barbuda is flat, dry limestone with no rivers: it could never grow sugar, which is why its history went a different way from every island around it.

date.note: Earlier English attempts to settle in 1628 and 1666 were destroyed by Kalinago raids; the Codrington lease of 1685 is the start of continuous occupation.

acquisitions.how: The Crown leased the whole island to Christopher and John Codrington for an annual rent of 'one fat sheep if demanded', and the family held it as a private estate for 185 years.

counterparties.name: Kalinago and Arawak of the northern Leewards
counterparties.lost: A hunting and fishing island they had used for centuries and defended successfully against two earlier English attempts, in 1628 and 1666.

instrument.name: Crown lease of Barbuda to the Codrington family
instrument.note: Renewed in 1705 for 99 years and again afterwards; the rent of one sheep a year was never in fact collected.

people.name: Christopher Codrington
people.role: Antiguan planter and Governor of the Leeward Islands who took the lease

contested.note: Sources differ on whether the operative grant is dated 1685 or 1691, and on whether it was a lease or an outright grant — an ambiguity that mattered enormously in the twentieth-century arguments about who owns Barbudan land.

evidence.author: Douglas Hall
evidence.work: Five of the Leewards, 1834-1870: The Major Problems of the Post-Emancipation Period in Antigua, Barbuda, Montserrat, Nevis and St Kitts
evidence.supports: The Codrington lease, the island's provisioning economy and communal land use.

statusPeriods.label: The Codringtons' private island
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: One family held the whole island on a Crown lease and ran it as a supply farm for their Antiguan sugar estates: livestock, provisions, timber and skilled labour, with an overseer and no government at all.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Codrington village, under the family's Antiguan estates
statusPeriods.franchise: None. There was no court, no assembly and no magistrate on the island.
statusPeriods.note: Because there was no sugar there was no gang labour: Barbudans herded, fished, hunted, wrecked and provisioned, and developed an unusually independent community life inside slavery.

statusPeriods.label: Dependency of Antigua
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Codringtons gave up the lease in 1870 and Barbuda was annexed to Antigua and administered from St John's by a warden, with the land treated as Crown land the Barbudans used in common.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St John's, Antigua
statusPeriods.franchise: None until the twentieth century; a Barbuda Council was created in 1976.

statusPeriods.label: Inside the Associated State, under protest
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Barbuda was governed from St John's within a self-governing state, and spent fourteen years petitioning Britain to be separated from it. Britain refused.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St John's, Antigua
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage, exercised in a state where Barbudans were about 1.5 per cent of the electorate.

departures.how: Barbuda left the empire attached to Antigua against the stated wishes of its council; its delegates walked out of the London conference and Britain, unwilling to create a state of 1,200 people, went ahead anyway.

led.name: Hilbourne Frank
led.role: Barbudan council leader who demanded separation at the 1980 London conference

led.name: Vere Cornwall Bird
led.role: Antiguan Premier who insisted the two islands go forward as one state

led.name: Nicholas Ridley
led.role: Foreign Office minister who chaired the conference and refused Barbuda a separate future

cost.note: No one died. The cost was consent: a community of about 1,200 people was made part of a state it had formally asked not to join.

departures.borders: No line moved. A century-old administrative attachment made in 1860 for the convenience of an Antiguan warden became an international border's inside edge.

instrument.name: Antigua and Barbuda Act 1981
instrument.note: The Act contains no special protection for Barbuda; the Barbuda Local Government Act of 1976 remained the only recognition of its separateness.

slavery.note: Barbudans were enslaved without sugar: they raised cattle, grew provisions, cut timber and salvaged wrecks for the Codringtons, and were shipped to Antigua when the estates needed hands.

emancipationDate.note: Barbuda followed Antigua in freeing everyone outright without apprenticeship. Most Barbudans simply stayed and kept using the island in common, which is the origin of the modern land dispute.

toll.money: £8,232 was paid to the Codringtons in 1836 for 501 enslaved Barbudans. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: The 1834 count of 501 people is from the Slave Compensation Commission return. Barbuda's enslaved population grew by natural increase, almost uniquely in the British Caribbean.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

populationTransfer.note: People were moved between Barbuda and the Antiguan estates at the owners' convenience, and after 1834 most Barbudans refused to leave.

consequences.economicLegacy: Land held in common by all Barbudans, written into the Barbuda Land Act of 2007 and contested by the national government after Hurricane Irma destroyed almost every building in September 2017.
consequences.borderLegacy: An 1860 administrative annexation became a permanent constitutional arrangement, and Barbudan separatism has been a live issue in every election since 1981.

peak.populationNote: About 1,200 people at independence; roughly 1,600 before Hurricane Irma in 2017, after which the island was evacuated entirely for several months.

evidence.author: David Lowenthal and Colin G. Clarke
evidence.work: Slave-Breeding in Barbuda: The Past of a Negro Myth
evidence.publisher: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
evidence.supports: The demography of Barbuda's enslaved population and the demolition of the slave-breeding story.

evidence.author: Douglas Hall
evidence.work: Five of the Leewards, 1834-1870: The Major Problems of the Post-Emancipation Period in Antigua, Barbuda, Montserrat, Nevis and St Kitts
evidence.supports: Communal land use, the provisioning economy and post-emancipation continuity.

contested.note: The date and legal nature of the Codrington grant are uncertain, and the persistent story that Barbuda was a 'slave-breeding island' is rejected by the historians who have examined the estate records, though it is still repeated in guidebooks.

pedagogy.hook: For 185 years Barbuda was rented to one family for 'one fat sheep a year, if demanded'. Nobody ever demanded the sheep.

misconception.belief: Barbuda was a 'slave-breeding island' where the Codringtons bred people to sell to the sugar estates.
misconception.correction: Barbuda's enslaved population did grow by natural increase, almost uniquely in the British Caribbean, and that is what started the story. But Lowenthal and Clarke's study of the estate papers found no breeding programme and very few sales: what grew the population was the absence of cane. Sugar work killed people; herding cattle did not.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Barbuda is the control experiment for the whole Caribbean. Same empire, same owners, same era, no sugar — and the population rose instead of falling. That single contrast tells you what the sugar plantation actually was.

namesOverTime.name: Alliouagana

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact centuries; the name survives in later records and modern usage.

namesOverTime.note: Usually translated 'land of the prickly bush'.

namesOverTime.name: Santa María de Montserrate
namesOverTime.note: Columbus named it for the monastery near Barcelona.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: Since 1997 roughly two thirds of Montserrat has been an exclusion zone: the territory is unchanged, the habitable part is not.

date.note: The exact month is not recorded; the settlers crossed during 1632.

acquisitions.how: Thomas Warner sent Irish Catholic settlers from St Kitts, where Protestant colonists had made life difficult for them, to occupy an island the Kalinago used but had not settled permanently.

counterparties.name: Kalinago of Alliouagana
counterparties.lost: An island they had cultivated and fished from bases nearby; they raided the colony repeatedly into the 1650s and were then gone from it.

people.name: Anthony Briskett
people.role: first governor of the Irish settlement

people.name: Thomas Warner
people.role: governor of St Kitts who organised the settlement of Montserrat and Antigua

statusPeriods.label: The Irish colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governed under the Carlisle proprietorship from St Kitts. By 1678 roughly seven in ten of the free population were Irish, more than on any other English island.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Plymouth, under the proprietor in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Male freeholders. Catholics were barred from office for much of the eighteenth century even here.

statusPeriods.label: Sugar colony in the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An elected assembly of planters governed under the Leeward Islands governor-general at Antigua, and turned an island of Irish smallholders into an island of sugar estates worked by enslaved Africans.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Plymouth, under the Governor of the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders; by 1780 that meant a few hundred men governing about 10,000 enslaved people.

statusPeriods.label: French occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A French force under the Marquis de Bouillé took the island in February 1782 and governed it for two years; the Treaty of Versailles returned it and the handover happened in 1784.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: France governed; Britain had no authority. Degree 0 rather than the default 5, which describes a British occupation of somebody else's territory.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Plymouth, under the French command at Martinique

statusPeriods.label: Sugar and limes
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The planter assembly returned; after emancipation the estates were bought up by the Sturge family of Birmingham, Quaker abolitionists who turned the island over to limes and sold plots to freed people.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Plymouth
statusPeriods.franchise: Property qualifications almost no formerly enslaved family could meet.

statusPeriods.label: Presidency of the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Montserrat gave up its assembly and was run by a commissioner under the Governor of the Leeward Islands, with a nominated council; elections returned in 1952 with universal adult suffrage.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Plymouth, under the Governor of the Leeward Islands at Antigua
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1952, then universal adult suffrage.

statusPeriods.label: Colony, then dependent territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British-appointed administrator, later a governor, kept defence, external affairs and internal security while elected ministers ran the rest; Montserrat joined the West Indies Federation in 1958 and stayed British when it collapsed.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Plymouth, then Brades after the volcano destroyed the capital
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.
statusPeriods.note: Montserratians voted repeatedly against independence. In 1995 the Soufrière Hills volcano began erupting; on 25 June 1997 pyroclastic flows killed 19 people, and Plymouth — a capital city — was buried and abandoned.

statusPeriods.label: British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor appointed in London holds defence, external affairs and the public service; an elected Legislative Assembly runs the rest, on a budget of which most is British aid.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Brades, with the government offices moved north of the exclusion zone
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage; full British citizenship was restored to Montserratians by the British Overseas Territories Act 2002.

stillBritish.note: Montserrat is still British by choice: it never sought independence, and after the volcano destroyed the capital in 1997 about two thirds of the population left, most of them for Britain.

departures.how: Montserrat never left. It voted against joining an independent West Indies state, stayed British when the Federation collapsed in 1962, and remains a British Overseas Territory today.

slavery.note: Irish Catholics who came as indentured servants and transported prisoners became, within two generations, owners of enslaved Africans: by 1729 Montserrat held about 6,000 enslaved people and 1,000 free colonists.

abolitionDate.note: End of the British slave trade.

emancipationDate.note: Legal freedom in 1834, then four years of unpaid apprenticeship.

toll.money: £26,331 was paid in 1836 to the owners of 6,401 enslaved Montserratians. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: From the Slave Compensation Commission returns digitised by the Legacies of British Slavery database at University College London.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

populationTransfer.note: Irish indentured servants and Cromwellian prisoners in the 1650s, trafficked Africans until 1807, and a modern exodus after 1995 that took two thirds of the population to Britain.

violence.note: The St Patrick's Day rising of 1768 was betrayed before it began: nine enslaved men were executed and about thirty more transported off the island.

commonwealth.note: As a British territory Montserrat is not a Commonwealth member in its own right; it takes part in Caribbean bodies including CARICOM and the OECS, which is unusual for a non-sovereign territory.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar, then limes, then offshore banking and a recording studio where the Rolling Stones and Dire Straits worked — all ended by hurricane and volcano within a decade.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, an Irish shamrock on the national seal, and the only country outside Ireland where St Patrick's Day is a public holiday — here it commemorates an enslaved people's rising, not a saint.

peak.populationNote: About 12,000 before the eruptions; 4,386 at the 2018 census, with roughly two thirds of the island still inside an exclusion zone.

pedagogy.hook: Montserrat is the only country outside Ireland where St Patrick's Day is a public holiday — and it marks the day in 1768 when enslaved Africans planned to kill the island's Irish planters.

misconception.belief: The Irish sent to the Caribbean in the 1600s were 'Irish slaves', treated the same as enslaved Africans.
misconception.correction: Irish people arrived as indentured servants and as prisoners transported by Cromwell, and were worked brutally for fixed terms of four to seven years. Then they were free, and many bought land and people. By 1729 Irish Montserratians owned about 6,000 enslaved Africans. The suffering overlapped; the legal categories never did, and the second generation shows why that matters.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Montserrat holds two hard truths in one island: colonised Irish people became colonisers, and a volcano showed in 1997 what a British territory is for — Britain paid, evacuated, and the population halved.

namesOverTime.name: Malliouhana

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact centuries; Arawakan settlement here is dated by archaeology.

namesOverTime.note: The name of the pre-Columbian island; the Fountain Cavern on Anguilla holds one of the most important Taíno ceremonial sites in the Lesser Antilles.

namesOverTime.name: Anguilla
namesOverTime.note: From the Spanish or Italian for 'eel', for the island's long thin shape.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island and its cays

date.note: The month is not recorded; 1650 is the date given in the earliest colonial accounts and is generally accepted.

acquisitions.how: English settlers crossed from St Kitts to a dry, flat island with no rivers and poor soil, which the Arawak had used for centuries and which no European power had bothered to occupy.

counterparties.name: Arawak of Malliouhana
counterparties.lost: An island they had lived on for over a thousand years and whose ceremonial cave they had carved; by 1650 disease and Spanish and Kalinago raiding had emptied it.

people.name: Abraham Howell
people.role: named in early accounts as a leader of the first settlers from St Kitts

acquisitions.resistance: There was no resident population left to resist in 1650; French and Irish raiders sacked the settlement in 1688 and French expeditions attacked in 1745 and 1796 and were beaten off by the islanders themselves.

contested.note: The 1650 date rests on later colonial accounts rather than a surviving document; some historians give a range of 1650 to 1656 for the first settlement.

statusPeriods.label: Unregarded settlement in the Caribbee proprietorship
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nobody governed Anguilla in any serious sense: it was too poor for sugar and too dry for planters, and its settlers ran their own affairs and fought off French raids without help.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St Kitts, in theory
statusPeriods.franchise: None; the island had no formal institutions for its first two centuries.

to.note: The attachment to St Kitts was made by stages in the 1820s; 1825 is the usual date given for Anguilla being placed under St Kitts's legislature.

statusPeriods.label: Nominally part of the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Anguilla elected a small vestry and sent a member to St Kitts, but in practice was governed by its own people, who lived on salt, fishing, boatbuilding and stock rather than sugar.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Valley, nominally under the Governor of the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.franchise: The handful of white male freeholders. Anguilla's enslaved population, about 2,600 in 1834, was among the poorest in the Caribbean because the estates were.

from.note: The attachment was made by stages during the 1820s.

statusPeriods.label: Attached to St Kitts against its will
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: London governed Anguilla as an appendage of St Kitts, 100 kilometres away. Anguillians petitioned to be governed directly from Britain in 1825, 1872, 1958 and 1967, and were refused every time.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basseterre, St Kitts
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1952, then universal adult suffrage in a state where Anguillians were a small minority.
statusPeriods.note: The 1872 petition asked to be 'dissevered from St Kitts and administered directly by the Colonial Office'. The Colonial Office filed it.

statusPeriods.label: Locked into St Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla, and in revolt
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: On paper Anguilla was part of a self-governing state run from Basseterre. In fact Anguillians expelled the St Kitts police on 30 May 1967, voted 1,813 to 5 to break away, and governed themselves.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basseterre in law; The Valley in fact
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

statusPeriods.label: British intervention and direct administration
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain landed 315 paratroopers and 40 London policemen at dawn on 19 March 1969 and installed a British Commissioner. The islanders had asked to be re-colonised, and were, at gunpoint.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Valley, under a British Commissioner
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage for the island council that sat alongside the Commissioner.
statusPeriods.note: The Anguilla Act 1971 gave the arrangement a legal basis. The Anguilla Act 1980 formally separated the island from St Kitts and Nevis on 19 December 1980.

statusPeriods.label: British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor appointed in London keeps defence, external affairs, internal security and the public service; an elected House of Assembly runs everything else.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Valley
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

stillBritish.note: Anguilla is British because Anguillians fought to be: they rebelled in 1967 against being made part of an independent St Kitts, and were formally separated from it in 1980.

departures.how: Anguilla never left the empire; it rebelled in order to stay in it. Britain resisted for three years, then accepted the separation from St Kitts in 1980.

slavery.note: Anguilla's estates were too poor to be profitable: around 2,600 enslaved people worked thin soil, and many owners simply left after emancipation, abandoning the land to the people who had worked it.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom on paper in 1834, four years of apprenticeship, full freedom in 1838.

toll.money: £13,528 was paid in 1836 to the owners of 2,600 enslaved Anguillians. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: From the Slave Compensation Commission records digitised by University College London's Legacies of British Slavery project.

populationTransfer.note: Trafficked Africans until 1807, then a century of Anguillian men leaving to cut cane in the Dominican Republic, dig the Panama Canal and work the oil refineries of Aruba and Curaçao.

commonwealth.note: Anguilla is not a Commonwealth member in its own right; it is represented by the United Kingdom.

consequences.borderLegacy: A nineteenth-century administrative convenience, joining Anguilla to St Kitts, produced the only armed British intervention in the Caribbean aimed at keeping a colony British.

pedagogy.hook: In 1969 Britain invaded one of its own colonies with 315 paratroopers, because the colony had rebelled in order to stay British. The islanders greeted the troops with flowers.

misconception.belief: Every colony wanted independence, and Britain had to be pushed out.
misconception.correction: Anguillians voted 1,813 to 5 against being part of an independent St Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla, threw out the St Kitts police, and demanded that Britain take them back. Small territories often calculated that a distant empire was less threatening than a near neighbour. Independence is a choice about who governs you, not a single direction of travel.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Anguilla proves that decolonisation was not one story. The Foreign Office spent 1967 to 1980 trying to get rid of an island that refused to go, and the British Overseas Territories that exist today are mostly places that made the same choice.

keyDates.what: English settlers arrive from St Kitts

date.note: The attachment was made by stages in the 1820s.

keyDates.what: Anguilla is attached to St Kitts, and starts petitioning to leave
Anguillians expel the St Kitts police
British paratroopers land: Operation Sheepskin
Formal separation from St Kitts and Nevis

namesOverTime.name: Santa Úrsula y las Once Mil Vírgenes
namesOverTime.note: Columbus named the whole archipelago after the legend of St Ursula's eleven thousand virgins; the name survives, shortened, in three modern territories.

namesOverTime.name: The Virgin Islands
namesOverTime.note: Still the territory's legal name. 'British Virgin Islands' is the everyday name, used to distinguish it from the neighbouring United States Virgin Islands.

geoCoverage.label: Tortola, Virgin Gorda, Anegada, Jost Van Dyke and about 50 smaller islands

date.note: The seizure took place during the Third Anglo-Dutch War; the month is variously given.

acquisitions.how: Sir William Stapleton, Governor of the Leeward Islands, sent a force that took Tortola from the small Dutch settlement there and annexed it to the English Leeward Islands.

counterparties.name: Dutch settlers of Tortola
counterparties.lost: A privateering and planting settlement that had held Tortola since about 1648; the settlers were expelled and their property taken.

counterparties.name: Taíno of the Virgin Islands
counterparties.lost: They had already lost everything: Spanish raiding and disease emptied the islands during the sixteenth century, more than a century before any European settled them permanently.

people.name: William Stapleton
people.role: Governor of the Leeward Islands who ordered the seizure

people.name: Joost van Dyk
people.role: Dutch planter and privateer whose settlement gave Jost Van Dyke island its name

contested.note: Accounts differ on whether Tortola was taken in 1666 by buccaneers or in 1672 by Stapleton's official expedition; 1672 is the date of the formal annexation to the Leeward Islands.

to.note: Crown colony government was introduced in stages between 1859 and 1867.

statusPeriods.label: Planter assembly in the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Quaker and Anglican planters ran a small sugar and cotton economy with an elected assembly from 1774, under the Governor of the Leeward Islands at Antigua.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Road Town, Tortola, under the Governor of the Leeward Islands
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders. In 1815 they numbered about 1,300 people, against roughly 6,500 enslaved.
statusPeriods.note: The Quaker community on Tortola in the 1740s and 1750s included planters who freed the people they held; the merchant and reformer John Lettsom, born on Little Jost Van Dyke in 1744, freed all the people he inherited on the island.

from.note: Introduced in stages from 1859; the legislature was abolished outright in 1902.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony, then no legislature at all
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After the 1853 riot Britain took control; in 1902 it abolished the legislature entirely and ruled the islands through a commissioner answering to Antigua. There was no elected body of any kind for 48 years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Road Town, under the Governor of the Leeward Islands at Antigua, and from 1956 the Governor of the Leeward Islands at Antigua then Barbados
statusPeriods.franchise: None between 1902 and 1950.
statusPeriods.note: The 'Great March' of 24 November 1949, when about 1,500 people — roughly a quarter of the population — walked to the commissioner's office behind Theodolph Faulkner, forced Britain to restore a legislature in 1950.

statusPeriods.label: Self-governing British territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The 1967 constitution gave the islands a ministerial system under an elected Chief Minister, later Premier, with a British governor keeping defence, external affairs, internal security and the courts.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Road Town, Tortola
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage since 1950.
statusPeriods.note: In 2022 a British commission of inquiry under Sir Gary Hickinbottom found serious failures in governance and recommended suspending the constitution and imposing direct rule; Britain kept the recommendation in reserve while the elected government carried out reforms.

stillBritish.note: The Virgin Islands are still British, with an elected Premier and a British governor, and no significant movement for independence.

departures.how: The islands never left British control; the constitutional argument here is about how much power the governor should keep, not about independence.

slavery.note: Sugar and cotton on steep hillsides made the Virgin Islands one of the poorer slave societies: about 6,500 enslaved people in 1815, and a white population so small that owners lived in permanent fear of the majority.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom on paper in 1834, then four years of apprenticeship.

toll.money: £72,940 was paid in 1836 to the owners of 5,192 enslaved Virgin Islanders. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: Slave Compensation Commission records, digitised by University College London's Legacies of British Slavery database.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

violence.note: In 1853 a cattle tax provoked a rising in which Road Town was burned; most of the remaining white population fled the islands permanently and never came back.

commonwealth.note: Represented by the United Kingdom; a member of CARICOM as an associate and of the OECS.

consequences.economicLegacy: Since a 1984 companies act the territory has become one of the world's largest offshore corporate registries, with hundreds of thousands of companies registered on islands of 31,000 people.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, a Privy Council appeal, and a company law written in the 1980s that made a British territory central to how money moves round the world.

peak.populationNote: 2023 estimate. The population was about 7,000 in 1815 and roughly the same in 1950.

evidence.author: Isaac Dookhan
evidence.work: A History of the British Virgin Islands, 1672 to 1970
evidence.supports: Annexation, the plantation period, the 1853 riot and the twentieth-century constitutional history.

evidence.author: B. W. Higman
evidence.work: A Concise History of the Caribbean
evidence.supports: The islands' place in the Leeward Islands system and in modern offshore finance.

contested.note: The date of English annexation is given variously as 1666 or 1672 depending on whether one counts the buccaneer seizure or Stapleton's formal expedition; both dates appear in the standard accounts.

pedagogy.hook: Between 1902 and 1950 the British Virgin Islands had no elected body of any kind. It took 1,500 people walking to the commissioner's door in 1949 to get one back.

misconception.belief: British colonies steadily gained more self-government over time, moving towards democracy.
misconception.correction: The Virgin Islands went backwards. They had an elected assembly from 1774 and lost it in 1902, when Britain decided the islands were too poor and too small to bother with. Democracy returned only after Theodolph Faulkner's Great March of 1949. Constitutional progress was not a ratchet; it could be, and was, reversed.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Virgin Islands show the whole arc in one small place: enslaved sugar economy, collapse, decades of unrepresentative rule, a protest that won the vote back, and finally an offshore financial centre that made a British territory matter to the world economy again.

keyDates.what: Britain takes Tortola from Dutch settlers
Full emancipation after apprenticeship
The cattle-tax riot burns Road Town
The Great March wins back a legislature
Ministerial government under a new constitution

from.note: A rough marker for the pre-contact centuries, not an event. The name is preserved in later tradition; its meaning is disputed.

namesOverTime.name: Os Barbados

from.note: Usually credited to the Portuguese navigator Pedro a Campos; the voyage and the year are both uncertain.

namesOverTime.note: 'The bearded ones', from the aerial roots of the island's bearded fig trees.

modernSuccessors.name: Barbados
modernSuccessors.note: A parliamentary republic since 30 November 2021, and still a Commonwealth member.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: Barbados sits alone 160 kilometres east of the island chain, out of the path of every invasion fleet. Its extent never changed in 339 years, and no enemy ever took it.

date.note: The date English settlers recorded under the Julian calendar; contemporaries wrote the year as 1626/27.

acquisitions.how: The William and John landed about 80 English settlers and ten Africans it had seized from a captured ship at the place they called Jamestown, now Holetown, on a coast emptied of its inhabitants a century earlier.

counterparties.name: Kalinago and Arawak of Ichirouganaim
counterparties.lost: The island itself. Spanish and Portuguese slave raiding had carried off or killed its people during the 1500s, so the English arrived to find land cleared of its owners.
counterparties.note: Archaeology shows continuous settlement for well over a thousand years before 1500. 'Uninhabited in 1627' is true; 'never inhabited' is false, and the difference is the whole point.

instrument.name: Letters patent to James Hay, Earl of Carlisle, over the Caribbee Islands
instrument.note: Granted after the settlers had already landed, and contested for a decade by a rival grantee, the Earl of Pembroke.

people.name: Henry Powell
people.role: captain of the William and John who led the first settlement party

people.name: James Hay, Earl of Carlisle
people.role: court favourite who held the island as a private grant from Charles I

acquisitions.resistance: There was nobody left to resist in 1627. The violence that emptied Barbados had been done by Iberian slave raiders a hundred years before the English arrived.

contested.note: An English ship under John Powell claimed the island in 1625 and some accounts date the colony from then. Historians generally date it from the 1627 landing, because that is when people stayed.

evidence.author: Richard S. Dunn
evidence.work: Sugar and Slaves: The Rise of the Planter Class in the English West Indies, 1624-1713
evidence.supports: The date, personnel and proprietary basis of the 1627 settlement.

from.note: English Julian dating; contemporaries wrote 1626/27.

statusPeriods.label: Private colony of the Earl of Carlisle
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The island belonged to a court favourite who named the governor and took rent from every settler; the Crown reached Barbados only through him.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bridgetown, under a proprietor in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Protestant male freeholders with ten acres or more. The House of Assembly first met in 1639 and has met ever since.
statusPeriods.note: In 1651 the planters declared for the exiled Stuarts; Sir George Ayscue's fleet blockaded them into surrender, and the Charter of Barbados signed at Oistins in January 1652 confirmed that only the Assembly could tax Barbadians.

statusPeriods.label: Royal colony with a planter Assembly
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown bought out the proprietor and appointed the governor, but the elected Assembly voted every tax, so London governed Barbados by bargaining with the men who owned the plantations and the people on them.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bridgetown, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: A property franchise that excluded almost everyone: enslaved people entirely until 1834, and most Barbadians afterwards. Universal adult suffrage came only in 1951.
statusPeriods.note: From 1833 to 1885 the governor at Bridgetown was also governor-in-chief of the Windward Islands, which is why old maps show Barbados as a regional capital. Barbados joined the West Indies Federation in 1958 and left when it collapsed in 1962.

statusPeriods.label: Full internal self-government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Barbadians governed themselves under a Premier, Errol Barrow, while Britain kept only defence and foreign affairs for five more years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bridgetown
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage since 1951.

departures.how: After a constitutional conference in London in June 1966, Britain legislated Barbados into independence and the flag changed at midnight in the Garrison Savannah with nobody killed.

led.name: Errol Barrow
led.role: Premier, then first Prime Minister; led the independence negotiations after the Federation failed

led.name: Grantley Adams
led.role: labour leader and Prime Minister of the West Indies Federation, who argued that independence should come through federation rather than alone

led.name: Clement Payne
led.role: Trinidad-born organiser whose deportation set off the 1937 riots that began Barbadian mass politics

departures.movement: Democratic Labour Party, built on the Barbados Workers' Union

cost.note: No one died at independence. The deaths in this story came in 1937, when police killed fourteen people during the riots that followed Clement Payne's deportation.

warrant.author: The commission of inquiry into the Barbados disturbances of 1937
warrant.work: Report of the Commission of Inquiry into the disturbances in Barbados, 1937
warrant.supports: No one died at independence. The deaths in this story came in 1937, when police killed fourteen people during the riots that followed Clement Payne's deportation.

warrant.note: Nobody died at independence. The figure on this step is the fourteen the police killed in 1937, and it exists because those deaths produced an inquiry.

departures.borders: The borders did nothing. An island with no land neighbours became a state with exactly the coastline it had in 1627.

instrument.name: Barbados Independence Act 1966
instrument.note: Royal assent on 17 November; independence took effect on 30 November 1966.

evidence.author: Hilary McD. Beckles
evidence.work: A History of Barbados: From Amerindian Settlement to Caribbean Single Market
evidence.supports: The independence negotiations and the 1966 settlement.

slavery.note: Sugar made Barbados the richest English colony and enslaved Africans made the sugar: they were the majority by 1680 and have been the majority ever since.

abolitionDate.note: The Slave Trade Act 1807 ended British trafficking. It freed nobody already enslaved.

emancipationDate.note: The Abolition Act took effect on 1 August 1834 but imposed four more years of unpaid apprenticeship. Full freedom came on 1 August 1838.

toll.money: About £1.72 million was paid in 1836 to Barbadian slave-owners for 83,150 people. The 83,150 received nothing. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: Totals of Africans landed vary widely because Barbados was also a re-export market that sold captives on to other colonies; the range follows the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.author: David Eltis and David Richardson
warrant.work: Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade
warrant.supports: The number of enslaved Africans landed in Barbados: 350,000 to 600,000.
warrant.check: Yale University Press, 2010; the voyage-by-voyage data behind it is at slavevoyages.org, Estimates.

populationTransfer.note: Two forced migrations built the colony: hundreds of thousands of Africans across the Atlantic, and thousands of Irish and Scottish prisoners shipped out under Cromwell in the 1650s.

violence.note: Bussa's rebellion in April 1816 was crushed in four days; several hundred enslaved people were killed in the fighting, executed afterwards, or transported off the island.

commonwealth.note: Barbados removed the British monarch as head of state on 30 November 2021, exactly 55 years after independence, and stayed in the Commonwealth.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar ran the economy for three centuries and then collapsed; tourism and offshore finance replaced it within a generation.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, a House of Assembly sitting continuously since 1639, and Anglican parish boundaries that still divide the island.

peak.populationNote: 1960 census, the last full count before independence. In 1680 the island held about 70,000 people, roughly two thirds of them enslaved — the densest population in the English-speaking world.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Barbados’s largest recorded population: 232,085 people, counted in 1960.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.supports: The whole narrative from Amerindian settlement to independence.

evidence.author: Richard S. Dunn
evidence.work: Sugar and Slaves: The Rise of the Planter Class in the English West Indies, 1624-1713
evidence.supports: The sugar revolution, planter society and the 1661 slave code.

evidence.author: Hilary McD. Beckles
evidence.work: Bussa: The 1816 Revolution in Barbados
evidence.publisher: University of the West Indies, Department of History
evidence.supports: The 1816 rebellion and its suppression.

contested.note: Historians disagree about how completely Barbados was emptied of Amerindian people before 1627, and about how many Africans were landed there as against re-exported to other colonies. Both uncertainties are shown here rather than smoothed away.

pedagogy.hook: By 1660 this island of 430 square kilometres was worth more to England than all of its North American colonies put together.

misconception.belief: Irish people shipped to Barbados in the 1650s were 'Irish slaves', the same as enslaved Africans.
misconception.correction: Thousands of Irish and Scottish prisoners were transported to Barbados and worked brutally, but as indentured servants for a fixed term, after which they were free and could own land and people. The Barbados slave code of 1661 made African enslavement lifelong, inheritable and enforceable by mutilation. The conditions overlapped; the legal categories did not.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Barbados invented the model the rest of the British Caribbean copied: monoculture sugar, mass enslavement, and a written slave code that Jamaica in 1664 and South Carolina in 1691 adapted almost word for word.

date.note: Julian date as recorded in England.
