namesOverTime.name: Wai'tukubuli

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact centuries; the name is still in use and appears on the national trail.

namesOverTime.note: 'Tall is her body'. Dominica is the most mountainous island in the Lesser Antilles, which is exactly why the Kalinago held it longest.

namesOverTime.name: Dominica
namesOverTime.note: Columbus sighted it on a Sunday — dies Dominica — and sailed on. Spain never settled it.

geoCoverage.label: The coast, not the interior
geoCoverage.change: France ceded a Kalinago island that neither power controlled. Britain held the coastal estates; the Kalinago and the Maroons held the mountains for fifty more years.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: After the Treaty of Paris ended French claims and the last Maroon leader, Jacko, was killed in 1814, British authority finally reached the interior.

acquisitions.how: France signed Dominica over to Britain at the Treaty of Paris, although the island had been declared neutral Kalinago territory by both powers in 1660 and neither had asked the Kalinago about any of it.

counterparties.name: Kalinago of Wai'tukubuli
counterparties.lost: The last substantial Kalinago homeland in the Caribbean. Their land was surveyed and sold to British planters from 1765; they were pushed onto the wet windward coast and finally confined to a reserve in 1903.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: A claim, a few hundred French settlers and the coffee estates they had planted along the leeward coast; French planters stayed, and Dominica speaks a French-based Creole to this day.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris
instrument.note: The same treaty gave Britain Canada, Grenada, St Vincent and Tobago, and returned Guadeloupe, Martinique and Havana.

people.name: Jean-Baptiste Belley
people.role: born in Senegal and enslaved on the French islands; later the first Black deputy in a European parliament — a reminder of how far the revolutionary Caribbean reached

acquisitions.resistance: Kalinago and Maroon communities fought British authority for another fifty years; France invaded twice, in 1778 and 1795, both times finding allies among the island's French-speaking population.

acquisitions.how: After twenty years of French invasions, raids and a ransom paid for Roseau in 1805, the Treaty of Paris confirmed Dominica as British and France abandoned its claim for good.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Its remaining claim to Dominica and to the French-speaking Catholic population it had encouraged there.

statusPeriods.label: New British colony on Kalinago land
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Commissioners surveyed and auctioned the island in lots from 1765, an assembly met from 1768, and British and French planters cleared the coastal valleys for coffee and sugar with enslaved labour.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Roseau
statusPeriods.franchise: Protestant male freeholders; French Catholics and free people of colour were excluded, which is one reason France found the island easy to invade.

statusPeriods.label: French occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Marquis de Bouillé took Dominica in a day with help from the island's French inhabitants, and France governed it for five years before returning it at the Treaty of Versailles.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: France governed and Britain had no authority; degree 0 rather than the default 5, which describes a British occupation of another power's land.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Roseau, under the French governor-general at Martinique

to.note: The single-chamber legislature was introduced in 1863 and the assembly abolished itself in 1865; sources differ over which date marks the change.

statusPeriods.label: Planter assembly under siege
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An elected assembly governed a coast ringed by hostile mountains: Maroon wars in 1785-90 and 1809-14, a French invasion in 1795, and another in 1805 that burned Roseau until the island paid a ransom of £12,000.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Roseau
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-holding men. Free people of colour won the vote in 1832 and by 1838 controlled the assembly — the only 'Brown Privilege' legislature in the British Caribbean.
statusPeriods.note: In 1838 Dominica became the only British Caribbean colony with a legislature controlled by people of African descent. Britain replaced it with crown colony rule within a generation.

from.note: The change was made in stages between 1863 and 1865.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony rule
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: London took the legislature away and governed through a nominated council under the Leeward Islands, then from 1940 under the Windward Islands, with an administrator answering to a governor on another island.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Roseau, under the Governor of the Leeward Islands, and from 1940 the Windward Islands at Grenada
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1924, when a limited elected element returned; universal adult suffrage came in 1951.
statusPeriods.note: The Kalinago reserve of about 3,700 acres was established in 1903. In 1930 police fired on Kalinago at Salybia, killing two people, in what colonial reports called the 'Carib War'; a Royal Navy warship was sent and the chief was deposed.

statusPeriods.label: Associated State of Dominica
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Dominica ran its own affairs completely, with Britain keeping only defence and foreign relations and either side free to end the arrangement.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Roseau
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

departures.how: Dominica took independence as a republic on the 485th anniversary of Columbus sighting it, after a London conference in May 1978 and against protests at home about the powers the new constitution gave the prime minister.

led.name: Patrick John
led.role: Premier who negotiated independence and became the first Prime Minister; removed by a general strike in 1979

led.name: Eugenia Charles
led.role: led the opposition to the independence constitution, then became the Caribbean's first woman prime minister in 1980

led.name: Hilary Frederick
led.role: Kalinago chief in the independence period who pressed for recognition of Kalinago land rights in the new state

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. Within a year a general strike brought the government down, and in 1979 Hurricane David killed 42 people and destroyed three quarters of the island's houses.

departures.borders: No border moved. The only internal line that mattered was the Kalinago Territory, created by the British in 1903 and carried into the new republic intact.

slavery.note: Dominica's mountains made it the hardest island to enslave people on: Maroon communities lived free in the interior for decades, and two Maroon wars were fought to break them.

abolitionDate.note: End of the British slave trade.

emancipationDate.note: Legal freedom in 1834, then four years of unpaid apprenticeship.

toll.money: £275,547 was paid in 1836 to Dominica's slave-owners for 14,175 people. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: Slave Compensation Commission records digitised by the Legacies of British Slavery database at University College London.

violence.note: Two Maroon wars, in 1785-90 and 1809-14, ended with the Maroon leader Jacko shot dead in 1814 after 46 years living free in the interior, and his head displayed at Roseau.

populationTransfer.note: Africans trafficked in until 1807, and after emancipation Dominicans leaving for cane fields in Cuba, the Panama Canal, the oil refineries of Curaçao and, after 1948, Britain.

commonwealth.note: Dominica took independence as a republic from the first day, unlike most of its neighbours.

retainedTerritory.note: The Kalinago Territory of about 3,700 acres, created by the colonial government in 1903, is the only Indigenous territory in the eastern Caribbean and is held communally by roughly 2,000 Kalinago people.

consequences.economicLegacy: Coffee, then sugar, then limes, then bananas under a guaranteed British market that the World Trade Organization struck down in the 1990s, taking the island's main export with it.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English law and English government on an island where most people also speak Kwéyòl, a French-based creole — the clearest surviving trace of the century when France, not Britain, shaped Dominica.

peak.populationNote: 1981 census. About 20,000 people lived on the island in 1805, of whom roughly 22,000 were enslaved at emancipation in 1834.

pedagogy.hook: The Kalinago held Dominica for 270 years after Columbus sighted it, because its mountains were too steep for sugar — and their descendants still live there, on the eastern Caribbean's only Indigenous territory.

misconception.belief: The Indigenous peoples of the Caribbean were all wiped out by the Spanish soon after 1492.
misconception.correction: The Taíno of the large islands were destroyed within fifty years. But the Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles fought Spain, France and Britain for three centuries, forced the two powers to declare Dominica and St Vincent neutral in 1660, and are still there: about 2,000 Kalinago live in the Dominican territory today, with their own elected chief.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Dominica shows what determined the shape of empire in the Caribbean: not flags or treaties, but terrain. Where sugar could be planted, the enslaved population and the plantation followed; where it could not, people stayed free.

keyDates.what: Britain and France declare Dominica neutral Kalinago territory — then ignore it
The Treaty of Paris hands the island to Britain
The Maroon leader Jacko is killed after 46 years free in the mountains

The Kalinago Territory is created
Independence as a republic

territories.name: St Vincent and the Grenadines
territories.formalName: Colony of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines

namesOverTime.name: Hairouna

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact centuries; the name is preserved in Garifuna and Vincentian usage.

namesOverTime.note: Often translated 'land of the blessed'. Yurumein is the Garifuna name and is the one used in the Garifuna diaspora today.

namesOverTime.name: Saint Vincent
namesOverTime.note: Columbus is said to have sighted it on St Vincent's day. Spain never settled it and neither did anyone else for 260 years.

geoCoverage.label: A cession on paper; the Garifuna held the windward half
geoCoverage.change: France ceded an island it did not rule to Britain, which could not rule it either. The Garifuna held the north and windward coasts, and a treaty in 1773 formally partitioned the island between them and the Crown.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island, after the deportation
geoCoverage.change: British forces defeated the Garifuna in June 1796 and deported the survivors in 1797. Only then did Britain control all of St Vincent.

acquisitions.how: France handed St Vincent to Britain at the Treaty of Paris, though the island had been declared neutral Kalinago land by both powers in 1660 and was in fact governed by the Garifuna, who were not consulted and did not accept it.

counterparties.name: Garifuna (Kalinago and African descent, then called Black Caribs)
counterparties.lost: Their country. They fought two wars over it, and in 1797 about 5,000 survivors were deported from the island for ever.
counterparties.note: The Garifuna formed in the seventeenth century from Kalinago communities and Africans who escaped or survived shipwrecks. British officials called them Black Caribs and treated them as intruders on their own island.

counterparties.name: Yellow Caribs (Kalinago of the leeward coast)
counterparties.lost: Their land was surveyed and sold to planters alongside Garifuna land, though a smaller Kalinago community remained and their descendants live at Sandy Bay and Owia today.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: A claim and a few hundred French settlers who had been living among the Garifuna by agreement; France invaded twice more to get the island back.

acquisitions.resistance: The Garifuna fought the First Carib War of 1769-73 when British surveyors began cutting a road across their land, and forced Britain to sign a treaty in 1773 dividing the island with them.

acquisitions.how: After sixteen months of war, General Ralph Abercromby's troops burned the Garifuna's provision grounds and villages until the survivors surrendered; the island's northern half was then declared Crown land and sold.

counterparties.name: Garifuna under Chatoyer and Duvalle
counterparties.lost: Everything: their leader killed in March 1795, their land confiscated, and about 5,000 people deported in 1797 to an island 3,000 kilometres away.

people.name: Joseph Chatoyer
people.role: paramount Garifuna chief who led the rising of 1795 and was killed on Dorsetshire Hill on 14 March 1795; now St Vincent's national hero

people.name: Duvalle
people.role: Garifuna commander who continued the war after Chatoyer's death and surrendered in 1796

people.name: Ralph Abercromby
people.role: British general who ended the war by destroying Garifuna food supplies

people.name: Victor Hugues
people.role: French republican commissioner at Guadeloupe who armed the Garifuna and the French Caribbean's freed people against Britain

cost.note: Roughly half of the 4,300 to 5,000 Garifuna held on the barren islet of Balliceaux over the winter of 1796-97 died there, mostly of typhus and dysentery, before the survivors were shipped to Roatán. The counts come from British transport and commissary returns.

warrant.author: Christopher Taylor
warrant.work: The Black Carib Wars: Freedom, Survival, and the Making of the Garifuna
warrant.supports: The two Carib wars, Chatoyer's rising and the deportation to Balliceaux and Roatán.
warrant.check: University Press of Mississippi

acquisitions.resistance: The Second Carib War of 1795-96 was fought alongside French republican forces and freed people from Guadeloupe; the Garifuna held most of the island for a year.

evidence.author: Christopher Taylor
evidence.work: The Black Carib Wars: Freedom, Survival, and the Making of the Garifuna
evidence.supports: The two Carib wars, Chatoyer's rising and the deportation to Balliceaux and Roatán.

statusPeriods.label: Colony on contested ground
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Land commissioners surveyed and auctioned estates while the Garifuna held the windward half; an assembly met from 1768 and a treaty in 1773 recognised a Garifuna territory the planters immediately began to encroach on.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingstown
statusPeriods.franchise: Protestant male freeholders only.

statusPeriods.label: French occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A small French force took Kingstown with Garifuna support and governed the island for four years; France returned it at the Treaty of Versailles, over Garifuna objections.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: France governed and Britain had none; degree 0 rather than the default 5, which describes British occupation of another power's territory.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingstown, under the French governor at Martinique

statusPeriods.label: Sugar colony after the deportation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: With the Garifuna gone, the confiscated north was sold to planters and St Vincent became a sugar island worked by 25,000 enslaved people; the assembly governed until Britain abolished it after Morant Bay.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingstown
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-owning men only; the great majority of Vincentians could never qualify.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony in the Windward Islands
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The assembly was abolished and St Vincent governed by an administrator under the Governor of the Windward Islands at Grenada, with a nominated council; elected members returned in 1925 and universal suffrage in 1951.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingstown, under the Governor of the Windward Islands at St George's, Grenada
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1925; universal adult suffrage from 1951.
statusPeriods.note: La Soufrière erupted on 7 May 1902, killing about 1,600 people — most of them Garifuna and Kalinago descendants farming the north of the island — a day before Mont Pelée destroyed St-Pierre on Martinique.

statusPeriods.label: Associated State of Saint Vincent
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Full internal self-government under a Premier, with Britain keeping defence and external affairs and either side able to end the arrangement.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingstown
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

departures.how: St Vincent took independence at Kingstown ten years to the day after associated statehood, five months after La Soufrière erupted again and forced 20,000 people from their homes.

led.name: Milton Cato
led.role: Premier, then first Prime Minister; led the St Vincent Labour Party to independence

led.name: Ebenezer Joshua
led.role: trade unionist and Chief Minister in the 1950s and 1960s who built mass politics among estate workers

cost.note: Nobody died at independence, but a rebellion broke out on Union Island in December 1979 over neglect of the Grenadines and was put down with help from Barbadian police; one person was killed.

departures.borders: The Grenadines were split between St Vincent and Grenada by colonial administrators in the 1790s and again in 1877; the line survives, so Carriacou is Grenadian and Union Island Vincentian for no reason a map can explain.

slavery.note: Sugar came to St Vincent only after the Garifuna were removed: the island held about 25,000 enslaved people by 1834, on land confiscated from the people deported in 1797.

abolitionDate.note: End of the British slave trade.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom on paper in 1834, then four years of unpaid apprenticeship.

toll.money: £592,509 was paid in 1836 to St Vincent's slave-owners for 22,997 people. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.

populationTransfer.note: About 5,000 Garifuna were deported in 1797, roughly half dying on Balliceaux; then Africans were trafficked in to replace them, and Portuguese Madeirans and 2,500 Indians were indentured after 1845.

toll.note: British commissary returns count 4,338 Garifuna landed on Roatán in April 1797 out of roughly 5,000 held on Balliceaux; the difference is the death toll of the winter.

warrant.author: The British commissary, in the transport returns
warrant.work: British transport and commissary returns for the Garifuna deportation of 1797
warrant.supports: British commissary returns count 4,338 Garifuna landed on Roatán in April 1797 out of roughly 5,000 held on Balliceaux; the difference is the death toll of the winter.

warrant.note: Roughly 5,000 were held on Balliceaux and 4,338 were landed on Roatán. The difference is the winter, and the returns are how we know it.

violence.note: Two Carib wars, a chief killed on Dorsetshire Hill in 1795, and a deportation that removed an entire people from their homeland.

commonwealth.note: A 2009 referendum on becoming a republic was defeated.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar, then arrowroot — St Vincent supplied most of the world's arrowroot for a century — then bananas, then tourism in the Grenadines.
consequences.borderLegacy: The deportation of 1797 created the Garifuna nation of Central America: today roughly 300,000 Garifuna live in Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua, and their language and dance are on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.

peak.populationNote: 1980 census. About 25,000 enslaved people were freed here in 1834, in a total population of roughly 27,000.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1980 census of St Vincent and the Grenadines
populationWarrant.supports: St Vincent and the Grenadines’s largest recorded population: 97,845 people, counted in 1980.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Christopher Taylor
evidence.work: The Black Carib Wars: Freedom, Survival, and the Making of the Garifuna
evidence.supports: The Carib wars, Chatoyer, and the deportation to Balliceaux and Roatán.

evidence.author: Nancie L. González
evidence.work: Sojourners of the Caribbean: Ethnogenesis and Ethnohistory of the Garifuna
evidence.supports: The formation of the Garifuna people and their dispersal across Central America.

evidence.author: B. W. Higman
evidence.work: A Concise History of the Caribbean
evidence.supports: The plantation period, crown colony rule and decolonisation.

pedagogy.hook: In 1797 Britain put an entire people on ships and dumped them on an island 3,000 kilometres away. Half died on the way. Their descendants — about 300,000 Garifuna in Central America — are still there.

misconception.belief: Colonial powers took land from people who were too weak or disorganised to stop them.
misconception.correction: The Garifuna held St Vincent against Britain for 34 years after Britain was given it by treaty. They fought two wars, forced a formal partition treaty in 1773, allied with revolutionary France, and were beaten only when Abercromby's troops burned their food. Britain then removed them physically, because it could not defeat them politically.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: St Vincent is the clearest case in the empire of a deportation used as a policy instrument, and its consequence is a whole nation living somewhere else — the Garifuna of Honduras, Belize and Guatemala, whose language and drumming UNESCO now protects.

keyDates.what: France cedes an island the Garifuna actually govern
A treaty partitions the island between Britain and the Garifuna
Chatoyer is killed on Dorsetshire Hill

date.note: The date the surviving deportees were landed on Roatán; the fleet sailed from Balliceaux in March.

keyDates.what: 4,338 Garifuna survivors are landed on Roatán
La Soufrière erupts and kills about 1,600 people
Independence

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact centuries; the name is preserved in Grenadian tradition.

modernSuccessors.name: Grenada
modernSuccessors.note: Includes Carriacou and Petite Martinique, the southern Grenadines.

acquisitions.how: France ceded Grenada at the Treaty of Paris after a British expedition took it in 1762; the island came with 12,000 enslaved people, a French-speaking Catholic population and a sugar economy already built.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: A century-old colony with its estates, its Catholic church and its planters, who stayed on as second-class subjects barred from office by the Test Acts until 1768.

counterparties.name: Kalinago of Camerhogne
counterparties.lost: They had already lost the island to the French in 1650-54; the last defenders are said to have jumped from the cliff at Sauteurs rather than surrender.
counterparties.note: The Leapers' Hill story is recorded in French accounts of the 1650s; the number who died, usually given as about 40, is not verifiable.

acquisitions.how: France had taken Grenada by storm in July 1779 and held it for four years; the Treaty of Versailles handed it back to Britain, and the French Catholic planters lost their rights all over again.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: The island it had recaptured, and the standing of the French Catholic community it had briefly restored.

statusPeriods.label: British colony with a French population
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British governor and an elected assembly governed an island whose planters, priests and free people of colour were French and Catholic; London wavered for twenty years over whether to let them vote.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St George's
statusPeriods.franchise: Protestant male freeholders at first; French Catholics were admitted in 1768, excluded again after 1783, and the argument fed straight into Fédon's rebellion.

statusPeriods.label: French occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Comte d'Estaing stormed Hospital Hill and took the island; France governed for four years and restored French Catholic rights before handing it back.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: France governed and Britain had no authority; degree 0 rather than the default 5, which describes a British occupation of someone else's territory.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St George's, under the French command

statusPeriods.label: Sugar, then nutmeg
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The planter assembly governed again and stripped French Catholics of office; after Fédon's rebellion was crushed in 1796 the estates were rebuilt with new capital, and from 1843 nutmeg replaced sugar.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St George's
statusPeriods.franchise: Protestant property-owning men; Catholics were readmitted in 1832, but the property bar kept out nearly everyone else.

statusPeriods.label: Capital of the Windward Islands
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The assembly was abolished and Grenada governed by a nominated council; St George's became the seat of the Governor of the Windward Islands, and after 1951 elected ministers slowly took over.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St George's
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1925; universal adult suffrage from 1951, won after the 1951 general strike known as Sky Red.
statusPeriods.note: In February and March 1951 Eric Gairy's Grenada Manual and Mental Workers' Union shut the island down; estates were burned, the sky glowed red at night, and Britain conceded universal suffrage within months.

statusPeriods.label: Associated State of Grenada
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Gairy's government ran everything but defence and foreign affairs, increasingly through a private force known as the Mongoose Gang; Britain kept the constitutional right to withdraw and did not use it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St George's
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

departures.how: Grenada became independent in the middle of a general strike against the government taking it there: the electricity was off, the port was shut, and the New Jewel Movement was demanding that Britain postpone the date.

led.name: Eric Gairy
led.role: union leader from 1950 and Premier; took the island to independence over mass opposition and became its first Prime Minister

led.name: Maurice Bishop
led.role: lawyer and leader of the New Jewel Movement, which struck against independence under Gairy and overthrew him in 1979

led.name: Rupert Bishop
led.role: Maurice Bishop's father, shot dead by police during the anti-Gairy demonstrations on 21 January 1974

led.name: Theophilus Albert Marryshow
led.role: journalist and federationist, 'the father of West Indian nationalism', who campaigned for self-government from 1915

departures.movement: Grenada United Labour Party, opposed by the New Jewel Movement

cost.note: At least one person, Rupert Bishop, was shot dead by police during the pre-independence protests of January 1974; other deaths in the disturbances are reported but not reliably counted.

departures.borders: Carriacou and Petite Martinique came with Grenada because British administrators divided the Grenadines between two colonies in the 1790s; the line has never made sense to the people living on either side of it.

slavery.note: Britain inherited a French sugar island with about 12,000 enslaved people in 1763 and doubled it: by 1834 nearly 24,000 people were enslaved on Grenada, on estates that also grew coffee and cocoa.

abolitionDate.note: End of the British slave trade.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom on paper in 1834, then four years of apprenticeship.

toll.money: £616,255 was paid in 1836 to Grenada's slave-owners for 23,638 people. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: Slave Compensation Commission records digitised by University College London's Legacies of British Slavery database.

violence.note: Fédon's rebellion of 1795-96 killed the lieutenant-governor and 47 other British hostages, cost thousands of Grenadian lives, and burned most of the island's estates.

toll.note: Contemporary British estimates put the enslaved dead at around 7,000 out of about 28,000; modern historians treat the figure as an order of magnitude rather than a count, since no one counted the dead among the enslaved.

populationTransfer.note: Africans trafficked in until 1807, then about 3,200 Indians indentured between 1857 and 1885, and Madeiran Portuguese and Maltese labourers in the 1840s.

commonwealth.note: Grenada remained a Commonwealth realm through the 1979 revolution, the killing of Maurice Bishop in October 1983 and the United States-led invasion that followed, which Britain was not consulted about even though the Queen was still head of state.

consequences.economicLegacy: Nutmeg and mace from the 1840s made Grenada the world's second-largest producer; Hurricane Ivan destroyed 90 per cent of the trees in 2004 and the industry has never fully recovered.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law over a French Catholic substratum: French place names, a Catholic majority, and a French-based creole that survived into the twentieth century.

peak.populationNote: 1981 census. In 1834 the island held about 24,000 enslaved people in a population of roughly 29,000.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Grenada’s largest recorded population: 89,088 people, counted in 1981.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.

evidence.author: Beverley A. Steele
evidence.work: Grenada: A History of Its People
evidence.supports: The whole narrative from Kalinago Camerhogne to independence.

evidence.author: Edward L. Cox
evidence.work: Free Coloreds in the Slave Societies of St. Kitts and Grenada, 1763-1833
evidence.supports: The position of free people of colour and the political exclusions behind Fédon's rebellion.

evidence.author: Michael Craton
evidence.work: Testing the Chains: Resistance to Slavery in the British West Indies
evidence.supports: Fédon's rebellion in the context of Caribbean slave resistance.

pedagogy.hook: In 1795 a free Black planter called Julien Fédon raised the French tricolour over Grenada, held most of the island for fifteen months, and vanished. His body was never found.

misconception.belief: Enslaved people and free people of colour in the Caribbean had no political ideas of their own; rebellions were desperate outbursts.
misconception.correction: Fédon's rebellion had a programme: the French Republic had abolished slavery in 1794, and Fédon fought under its flag for citizenship and emancipation. Free people of colour stripped of the vote by British Protestant planters led it, and enslaved people joined by the thousand. Britain needed fifteen months and thousands of troops to defeat it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Grenada shows how the French and Haitian revolutions ran through the British Caribbean like a current: for three years in the 1790s, Britain's sugar islands were fighting a war of ideas about who counted as a citizen.

keyDates.what: France cedes Grenada at the Treaty of Paris

namesOverTime.name: Iouanalao

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact centuries; the name is recorded in early European accounts of Kalinago usage.

namesOverTime.note: Also given as Hewanorra, the name now carried by the island's international airport.

geoCoverage.label: Second British occupation
geoCoverage.change: Admiral Barrington's fleet took the island as a base for watching the French at Martinique, 40 kilometres away; Britain gave it back at the peace.

geoCoverage.label: Third British occupation, coast only
geoCoverage.change: Britain took the forts; the interior went to the Armée Française dans les Bois, an army of freed people fighting under the French Republic's abolition decree, which drove the British off the island in June 1795.

geoCoverage.label: Fourth British occupation
geoCoverage.change: Abercromby retook Morne Fortune after a month's fighting, and the British then spent two years hunting the Brigands in the forest before restoring slavery on the island.

geoCoverage.label: British for the last time
geoCoverage.change: Britain retook the island within a year of handing it back at Amiens, and kept it: the Treaty of Paris in 1814 ended 150 years of it changing hands.

acquisitions.how: A British squadron took the island from France during the Seven Years' War, and gave it straight back eleven months later at the Treaty of Paris.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Temporarily, a sugar colony and the deep harbour at Le Carénage, now Castries — the best anchorage in the Windward Islands.

contested.note: Contemporary accounts date the surrender to late February 1762; the exact day is given variously.

acquisitions.how: Admiral Samuel Barrington seized St Lucia in the first weeks of the war with France, and beat off d'Estaing's counter-attack at the Vigie with heavy French losses.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: The island and, more importantly, the anchorage from which the Royal Navy watched the French fleet at Fort-Royal in Martinique for the rest of the war.

people.name: Samuel Barrington
people.role: admiral who seized the island and held the beachhead against a French fleet three times his size

acquisitions.how: Sir Charles Grey and Sir John Jervis took St Lucia as part of the campaign to seize France's sugar colonies and put down the revolution's abolition decree in the Caribbean.

counterparties.name: French Republic
counterparties.lost: The island — briefly. France had freed the enslaved people of its colonies by decree in February 1794, and Britain's occupation was, explicitly, an attempt to reverse that.

counterparties.name: The freed people of St Lucia
counterparties.lost: Their freedom, on paper, the day the British landed; they took to the forest and fought for it as the Armée Française dans les Bois.

acquisitions.how: Ralph Abercromby and John Moore retook Morne Fortune after a month's siege, then spent two years hunting the Brigands through the forest before slavery was restored on the island.

counterparties.name: The Brigands, the Armée Française dans les Bois
counterparties.lost: The free republic they had held for a year. Many surrendered on terms and were shipped to Britain as prisoners; others fought on until 1797.

counterparties.name: French Republic
counterparties.lost: Its last foothold in the Windward Islands.

people.name: Ralph Abercromby
people.role: British commander of the 1796 expedition

people.name: John Moore
people.role: brigadier left as governor to fight the two-year forest campaign, which he described as the hardest service of his career

people.name: Jean-Baptiste Goyrand
people.role: French republican commissioner who abolished slavery on St Lucia in 1794 and organised the resistance

acquisitions.how: Britain retook the island within a year of returning it at Amiens; the Treaty of Paris of 1814 finally made it British in law as well as in occupation.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: St Lucia permanently, along with Tobago, at the 1814 settlement.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris (1814)
instrument.note: The 1803 capture was by force; the 1814 treaty converted eleven years of occupation into sovereignty.

statusPeriods.label: First British occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British garrison held the forts and left the French planters, their law and their enslaved workforce exactly as they were, for eleven months.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Le Carénage, under the British commander

statusPeriods.label: Second British occupation
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned the island to France at the Treaty of Paris in 1763 and held nothing here for fifteen years.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Royal Navy ran St Lucia as a fleet base: Gros Islet Bay was the anchorage from which Rodney watched Martinique, and civil government hardly existed.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Castries, under the naval commander-in-chief

statusPeriods.label: Third occupation, and expulsion
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned St Lucia to France at the Treaty of Versailles in 1783 and did not hold it again for eleven years.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain held the forts and the coast; the interior belonged to an army of freed people fighting under the French Republic's abolition decree, and in June 1795 they drove the British garrison into the sea.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Degree 3 rather than the default 5: British authority reached the forts and the harbour and nothing else. For most of these fifteen months the island was governed from the forest.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Morne Fortune

statusPeriods.label: Fourth occupation; slavery restored
statusPeriods.gapReason: For eleven months from June 1795 the island was held by the Brigands, an army of formerly enslaved people fighting for the French Republic; Britain had no authority on it at all.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Military government under John Moore fought a forest war for two years, then reimposed the slave laws the French Republic had abolished in 1794 — the only occasion in the empire when Britain restored slavery to people who were already legally free.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Castries, under a British military governor

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony under French law
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain handed St Lucia back to France at the Treaty of Amiens in 1802 and retook it fifteen months later.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: St Lucia was never given an elected assembly: a governor ruled with a nominated council, and the island kept the French civil code until 1957, so British judges applied Napoleonic law in English.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Castries, under the Governor of the Windward Islands at Grenada from 1885
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1924, when a few elected seats appeared; universal adult suffrage came in 1951.
statusPeriods.note: Because Britain took St Lucia by conquest rather than settlement, the Crown could legislate for it directly by Order in Council — the crown colony model that London preferred everywhere after 1815 precisely because there was no assembly to argue with.

statusPeriods.label: Associated State of Saint Lucia
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Full internal self-government under a Premier, with Britain retaining defence and external affairs and either side free to end it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Castries
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

pedagogy.hook: St Lucia changed hands fourteen times between Britain and France. In 1796 the British took it back and put people who had been legally free for two years back into slavery.

misconception.belief: Britain was the country that ended slavery in the Caribbean.
misconception.correction: Revolutionary France abolished slavery in its colonies in February 1794, forty years before Britain. On St Lucia, freed people formed an army and drove the British out in 1795 to defend that decree. Britain reconquered the island in 1796 and restored slavery. Abolition was not a straight line, and Britain was not always on the abolishing side of it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: St Lucia is the churn of empire made visible: fourteen changes of flag, a French legal code under British judges, a creole language, and a decade in the 1790s when the Caribbean was fighting about whether freedom was for everyone.

geoCoverage.label: Second British period
geoCoverage.change: France held Tobago from 1781 and kept it at the Treaty of Versailles in 1783; Britain took it back by force in the first months of the revolutionary war.

geoCoverage.label: British for the last time
geoCoverage.change: Britain returned Tobago to France at Amiens in 1802 and retook it a year later; the Treaty of Paris in 1814 made it British in law.

acquisitions.how: France ceded Tobago at the Treaty of Paris, and British commissioners immediately surveyed an almost empty island into plantation lots and sold them at auction in London.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: A claim to an island it had never settled properly; Tobago had been fought over by the Dutch, the Courlanders, the French, the English and the Kalinago for 130 years without any of them holding it for long.

counterparties.name: Kalinago of Tobago
counterparties.lost: The island. Repeated European attempts to settle it had been destroyed by Kalinago attacks, but by 1763 disease and warfare had left too few people to stop the surveyors.

acquisitions.how: A British force from Barbados stormed the island at night within weeks of war being declared, and held it for nine years before handing it back at Amiens.

counterparties.name: French Republic
counterparties.lost: The sugar island France had gained at Versailles ten years earlier, together with its 14,000 enslaved workers.

acquisitions.how: Britain retook Tobago a year after returning it, and the Treaty of Paris in 1814 turned eleven years of occupation into permanent British sovereignty.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Tobago for good; France never held it again.

statusPeriods.label: New sugar colony with an assembly
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An elected assembly of new planters met from 1768 and governed a plantation island built from scratch in twenty years: 10,000 enslaved Africans landed to clear forest and plant cane on land auctioned in London.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Georgetown, then Scarborough
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders — perhaps 300 men governing 14,000 enslaved people by 1780.

statusPeriods.label: British military occupation
statusPeriods.gapReason: France took Tobago by storm in June 1781 and kept it at the Treaty of Versailles in 1783; for twelve years the island was a French colony and Britain had no authority there.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military governor ran the island under French civil law, without an assembly, and handed it back to France when the Peace of Amiens was signed.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Scarborough, under a British military governor

statusPeriods.label: Assembly restored, then sugar collapse
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned Tobago to France under the Treaty of Amiens in 1802 and retook it twelve months later when the war restarted.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The planters got their assembly back and kept it for seventy years, through emancipation and the metayage system that replaced wages with a share of the crop, until the sugar economy collapsed entirely.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Scarborough
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-owning men; in 1874 the register held 138 voters for the whole island.
statusPeriods.note: In 1876 the Belmanna riots at Roxborough — a protest against a policeman's arrest of estate workers that turned into a rising and killed the policeman — frightened the assembly into voting away its own existence.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor and nominated council under the Governor of the Windward Islands ran a bankrupt island whose largest merchant house had failed in 1884, taking the sugar trade with it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Scarborough, under the Governor of the Windward Islands at Grenada
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Annexed to Trinidad, then reduced to a ward
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain joined bankrupt Tobago to prosperous Trinidad to save money. In 1899 Tobago lost its own treasury, courts and laws and became a ward of Trinidad, administered from Port of Spain 30 kilometres of sea away.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port of Spain, Trinidad
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1925, then a property franchise, then universal adult suffrage from 1946 — exercised in a colony where Tobagonians were about 4 per cent of the electorate.
statusPeriods.note: Tobagonians never accepted the 1899 arrangement. A House of Assembly was restored in 1980 and the argument over internal self-government continues.

departures.how: A French expedition under the Marquis de Bouillé landed and burned estates until the governor surrendered; the Treaty of Versailles in 1783 confirmed the island as French.

pedagogy.hook: Tobago was once a colony of Courland — a small Baltic duchy in what is now Latvia — and changed hands more often than any other island in the Caribbean.

misconception.belief: Colonial borders were drawn between Europeans and the people they ruled.
misconception.correction: Some of the most consequential lines were drawn between colonies. In 1889 Britain joined bankrupt Tobago to prosperous Trinidad to save money, and in 1899 abolished Tobago's treasury, courts and laws altogether. That accounting decision is why Tobago is part of Trinidad and Tobago today, and why Tobagonians have been arguing about self-government for 130 years.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Tobago is the cheapest lesson in how empires actually behave: an island passed between five European powers for two centuries, then merged with a neighbour to balance a colonial budget, and the merger outlived the empire.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Its last major Caribbean possession outside Cuba and Puerto Rico, and a colony it had held for 299 years and never developed; Chacón was court-martialled in Spain for surrendering it.

counterparties.name: The Indigenous peoples of Trinidad
counterparties.lost: They had already lost almost everything under Spain: the encomienda system, the mission villages and epidemic disease reduced a population of tens of thousands to about 1,100 by 1797. The Santa Rosa Carib Community of Arima descends from the survivors.

counterparties.name: The French planters of Trinidad
counterparties.lost: Nothing at first — Britain confirmed their land titles and their enslaved workforce — but they lost the French legal and social order within a generation.

instrument.name: Treaty of Amiens
instrument.note: Britain took Trinidad by force in 1797; Spain ceded it formally at Amiens in 1802. It was the only conquest Britain kept at that peace.

statusPeriods.label: The original crown colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Trinidad was never given an elected assembly. A governor legislated by Order in Council with a nominated council — a model invented here because London did not want a planter assembly, and then exported across the whole nineteenth-century empire.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port of Spain, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1925, when seven elected seats appeared on a franchise with property, income, language and residence tests; universal adult suffrage came only in 1946.
statusPeriods.note: British officials were explicit about why: a colony with a French-speaking Catholic planter class, a large free coloured population and a Spanish legal code was not to be trusted with an assembly. The 1903 Water Riots, in which the Red House was burned and police killed 18 people, were a protest against exactly this system.

statusPeriods.label: Ministerial government under Eric Williams
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The People's National Movement won the 1956 election and Eric Williams became Chief Minister, then Premier; the governor kept defence, external affairs and the police until independence.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port of Spain
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage since 1946.
statusPeriods.note: Trinidad hosted the capital of the West Indies Federation at Chaguaramas from 1958. When Jamaica voted to leave in 1961, Williams calculated that 'one from ten leaves nought' and took Trinidad and Tobago out too.

departures.how: After the West Indies Federation collapsed, Eric Williams negotiated independence for Trinidad and Tobago alone at a London conference in May 1962, and the flag changed in Port of Spain with no one killed.

misconception.belief: Slavery ended in 1838 and free labour replaced it.
misconception.correction: In Trinidad the planters replaced enslaved Africans with indentured Indians within seven years. Between 1845 and 1917 about 143,900 people came from India on five-year contracts, could be jailed for leaving the estate, and lived in the same barracks. Indenture was not slavery, but it was designed to solve the same problem for the same owners.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Trinidad is where two great imperial systems meet: the Atlantic slave economy and the Indian labour diaspora. Roughly a third of the country is of Indian descent and a third of African descent, and the reason is a decision taken in London in the 1840s.

keyDates.what: Spain's Cédula de Población fills the island with French Catholic planters
Abercromby takes Trinidad; the governor surrenders without a fight
The Fatel Razack lands the first indentured Indians in Trinidad
The Water Riots: the Red House burns, police kill 18 people
Butler's oilfield rising begins mass politics
Independence under Eric Williams

territories.name: Jamaica
territories.formalName: Colony of Jamaica and its Dependencies

namesOverTime.name: Xaymaca

from.note: A marker for the centuries of Taíno settlement, dated by archaeology; Taíno people reached Jamaica from South America by about AD 650.

namesOverTime.note: Usually translated 'land of wood and water'. The modern name is a direct descendant of it.

namesOverTime.name: Santiago
namesOverTime.note: Spain's official name for the island. Spanish rule destroyed the Taíno population within about sixty years.

geoCoverage.label: The island, with a free interior until 1740
geoCoverage.change: Jamaica's mountainous interior was held by Maroon communities that Britain could not defeat: the Cockpit Country and the Blue Mountains were outside colonial control until the treaties of 1739 and 1740, and semi-autonomous after them.

date.note: The date as recorded by the English expedition under the Julian calendar then in use in England.

acquisitions.how: Cromwell's Western Design fleet failed to take Santo Domingo in April 1655 and seized lightly defended Jamaica instead as a consolation prize; both commanders were imprisoned in the Tower of London on their return for coming home with the wrong island.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: An island it had held for 161 years and neglected: about 1,500 Spanish colonists and a cattle economy. Spanish guerrillas under Cristóbal Arnaldo Ysassi fought on from the north coast until 1660.

counterparties.name: The Africans enslaved by the Spanish, who became the first Maroons
counterparties.lost: Nothing to England — they gained. Fleeing Spanish owners freed or abandoned them, and they took to the mountains and stayed free, founding communities that fought England for eighty-five years.
counterparties.note: Juan de Bolas and Juan de Serras led the two main groups. De Bolas made terms with the English in 1660 and was killed in 1664; de Serras never did.

counterparties.name: Taíno of Xaymaca
counterparties.lost: They had already lost everything. Spanish forced labour and epidemic disease destroyed a population of perhaps 60,000 within sixty years of 1494; by 1655 almost none remained.

people.name: Oliver Cromwell
people.role: Lord Protector, who ordered the Western Design to seize Spanish America and treated Jamaica as a failure

people.name: Admiral Sir William Penn
people.role: admiral commanding the fleet; imprisoned in the Tower on his return

people.name: Robert Venables
people.role: general commanding the troops; imprisoned in the Tower on his return

people.name: Cristóbal Arnaldo Ysassi
people.role: last Spanish governor, who fought a five-year guerrilla campaign from the north coast before escaping to Cuba in 1660

people.name: Juan de Serras
people.role: leader of the Karmahaly Maroons, who fought the English from the mountains and never made terms

cost.note: Most of the English dead were the invaders themselves: of roughly 7,000 soldiers landed in 1655, disease and starvation killed thousands within the first year. Spanish and Maroon losses were not counted.

warrant.author: The Western Design’s own musters and returns
warrant.work: English musters and returns of the Western Design, 1655–56
warrant.supports: Most of the English dead were the invaders themselves: of roughly 7,000 soldiers landed in 1655, disease and starvation killed thousands within the first year. Spanish and Maroon losses were not counted.
warrant.check: State Papers Colonial and the Thurloe State Papers; CO 1 at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The invaders counted the invaders. Spanish and Maroon losses were not counted at all, which is why the only precise number here is England’s own dead.

acquisitions.resistance: Spanish guerrillas held out for five years; the freed Africans who became the Maroons fought England for eighty-five years and were never defeated, only treated with.

evidence.author: Carla Gardina Pestana
evidence.work: The English Conquest of Jamaica: Oliver Cromwell's Bid for Empire
evidence.supports: The Western Design, the failure at Hispaniola and the taking of Jamaica.

from.note: Julian dating, as recorded by the expedition.

statusPeriods.label: Military occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An army of survivors held the coast under martial law while Spanish guerrillas and Maroons held the interior; soldiers were given land to stop them leaving, and thousands died of disease.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Spanish Town, under the army command

statusPeriods.label: Planter Assembly and the greatest sugar colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor appointed in London faced an elected Assembly of planters that voted the taxes, wrote the slave code of 1664 and defended its privileges against the Crown for two centuries. Jamaica became the richest colony in the empire and the largest single destination for enslaved Africans in the British Atlantic.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Spanish Town, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: White male property-holders — about 2,000 voters in 1830 among 350,000 people. Free people of colour won the vote in 1830; property and tax qualifications kept almost all formerly enslaved people off the register after 1838.
statusPeriods.note: Port Royal, the buccaneers' base, was the richest town in English America until an earthquake dropped most of it into the sea on 7 June 1692.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony after Morant Bay
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Terrified by the Morant Bay rising, the Assembly voted itself out of existence in December 1865 rather than share power with Black Jamaicans, and London governed directly through a governor and a nominated council for the next sixty years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingston, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: None at first; a partly elected council returned in 1884, and universal adult suffrage came in 1944 after the 1938 labour rebellion.
statusPeriods.note: The 1938 rebellion — strikes and riots across the island in which police killed 46 people — produced both of Jamaica's political parties, the trade unions and, in 1944, the vote.

statusPeriods.label: Full internal self-government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Norman Manley's government ran Jamaica's internal affairs completely, with Britain keeping defence and foreign policy; the argument of these three years was not about Britain but about whether to stay in the West Indies Federation.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingston
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage since 1944.

departures.how: Jamaicans voted 54 per cent to 46 in a referendum on 19 September 1961 to leave the West Indies Federation; the Federation collapsed, and Britain legislated Jamaica into independence eleven months later.

led.name: Norman Manley
led.role: lawyer, founder of the People's National Party in 1938 and Premier; called the referendum, lost it, and then negotiated independence

led.name: Alexander Bustamante
led.role: trade union leader from the 1938 rebellion, campaigned for Jamaica to leave the Federation, and became the first Prime Minister

led.name: Marcus Garvey
led.role: founder of the Universal Negro Improvement Association in Kingston in 1914, whose Pan-African movement shaped Jamaican and world Black politics

departures.movement: Jamaica Labour Party and People's National Party, both grown out of the 1938 labour rebellion

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. The deaths that produced Jamaican mass politics came in 1938, when police killed 46 people during the labour rebellion.

warrant.author: The West India Royal Commission (the Moyne commission)
warrant.work: Report of the West India Royal Commission (Cmd. 6607)
warrant.supports: Nobody died at independence. The deaths that produced Jamaican mass politics came in 1938, when police killed 46 people during the labour rebellion.
warrant.check: Command Paper Cmd. 6607, HMSO; the commission reported in 1939 and publication was held back until the war ended.
warrant.note: The report on the 1938 killings was written in 1939 and suppressed for six years because of what it said about conditions in the colonies.

departures.borders: No line moved on the island, but Jamaica's exit destroyed the West Indies Federation: as Eric Williams put it, one from ten leaves nought, and ten separate small states left the empire instead of one large one.

slavery.note: Jamaica was the largest slave colony in the British Empire: roughly one million Africans were landed here between 1655 and 1807, and the enslaved population still never grew, because the work killed people faster than they were born.

abolitionDate.note: The Slave Trade Act ended British trafficking; Jamaica had been its largest single destination.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom in law on 1 August 1834, then four years of unpaid apprenticeship. Jamaican apprentices' resistance is a large part of why apprenticeship was abandoned two years early.

toll.money: £6.16 million was paid in 1836 to Jamaica's slave-owners for 311,070 people — the largest share of the £20 million by far. The 311,070 received nothing. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: The arrivals range is from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database; a substantial number were re-exported to Spanish America and the mainland colonies, so it overstates the number who stayed. The 1834 population count comes from the Slave Compensation Commission.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.author: Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery, University College London
warrant.work: Legacies of British Slavery database
warrant.supports: £6.16 million was paid in 1836 to Jamaica's slave-owners for 311,070 people — the largest share of the £20 million by far.
warrant.check: ucl.ac.uk/lbs — browse by colony. Every award transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission’s registers, T 71, The National Archives, Kew.

warrant.author: David Eltis and David Richardson
warrant.work: Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade
warrant.supports: The number of enslaved Africans landed in Jamaica: 900,000 to 1,200,000.
warrant.check: Yale University Press, 2010; the voyage-by-voyage data behind it is at slavevoyages.org, Estimates.

violence.note: Two Maroon wars, Tacky's Revolt in 1760, the Baptist War of 1831-32 and the Morant Bay rising of 1865: British forces killed and executed people in every one of them, and after Morant Bay killed 439 and hanged 354 more.

toll.note: A rough total across the four largest risings, based on the death counts in Craton, Brown and Heuman. No one counted enslaved dead systematically, so all such totals are minimums.

warrant.author: Vincent Brown
warrant.work: Tacky's Revolt: The Story of an Atlantic Slave War
warrant.supports: A rough total across the four largest risings, based on the death counts in Craton, Brown and Heuman.
warrant.check: Harvard University Press, 2020. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

warrant.author: Gad Heuman
warrant.work: The Killing Time: The Morant Bay Rebellion in Jamaica
warrant.supports: A rough total across the four largest risings, based on the death counts in Craton, Brown and Heuman.
warrant.check: Macmillan Caribbean, 1994. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

populationTransfer.note: About a million Africans trafficked in; 568 Trelawny Maroons deported to Nova Scotia in 1796 and on to Sierra Leone in 1800; about 36,400 Indians and 5,000 Chinese indentured after 1845; and a great emigration to Panama, Cuba, the United States and Britain after 1900.

commonwealth.note: Jamaica remains a Commonwealth realm; successive governments since 2022 have announced plans to become a republic.

retainedTerritory.note: Maroon towns — Accompong, Moore Town, Charles Town and Scott's Hall — still hold land and a measure of self-government under the treaties of 1739 and 1740, the oldest such agreements in the Americas.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar and rum for two centuries, then bananas, bauxite and tourism; the sugar estates' collapse after 1846 shaped a century of rural poverty and emigration.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, an Assembly tradition, and Jamaican Patois — a creole language with English vocabulary and West African grammar spoken by almost everyone.

peak.populationNote: 1960 census. In 1834 the island held 311,070 enslaved people and about 16,000 whites — a ratio of roughly twenty to one, which is why Jamaica's planters lived in permanent fear.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Jamaica’s largest recorded population: 1,609,814 people, counted in 1960.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Vincent Brown
evidence.work: Tacky's Revolt: The Story of an Atlantic Slave War
evidence.supports: The 1760-61 rising, its African military background and its consequences for Jamaican slave law.

evidence.author: Gad Heuman
evidence.work: The Killing Time: The Morant Bay Rebellion in Jamaica
evidence.supports: The 1865 rising, the death toll and the abolition of the Assembly.

evidence.author: Trevor Burnard
evidence.work: Mastery, Tyranny, and Desire: Thomas Thistlewood and His Slaves in the Anglo-Jamaican World
evidence.supports: Daily violence on Jamaican estates, documented from an overseer's own diaries.

contested.note: The number of Africans landed in Jamaica is an estimate from voyage records and varies with how re-exports are counted; the death toll of the Maroon wars and of Tacky's Revolt is uncertain because the deaths of enslaved people were rarely recorded.

pedagogy.hook: England took Jamaica by accident. Cromwell's fleet was sent to conquer Spanish America, failed at Santo Domingo, grabbed Jamaica instead, and its commanders were thrown in the Tower for coming home with it.

misconception.belief: Enslaved people were freed by Parliament and by British abolitionists acting on their behalf.
misconception.correction: Jamaica's Baptist War of Christmas 1831 involved about 60,000 enslaved people and was the largest rebellion in the British Caribbean. Parliament passed the Abolition Act nineteen months later. The rising cost fourteen white lives and about 540 Black ones, most of them executed afterwards, and it convinced the government that slavery could not be held down indefinitely.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Jamaica is the centre of gravity of the British Atlantic: the largest slave colony, the richest, the most rebellious, and the place where every argument about empire — profit, resistance, abolition, race and self-government — was fought out first and hardest.

date.note: Julian date as recorded by the expedition.

keyDates.what: The Western Design takes Jamaica from Spain
Cudjoe's treaty ends the First Maroon War
Tacky's Revolt begins in St Mary
Sam Sharpe's Baptist War, the largest rising in the British Caribbean
Morant Bay; 439 people killed in the suppression
