namesOverTime.name: Lucayan islands

from.note: A marker for the centuries of Lucayan settlement, dated by archaeology; the islands were settled from Hispaniola and Cuba by about AD 800.

to.note: The date the deportations ended, because there was no one left to deport.

namesOverTime.note: Guanahani, where Columbus first landed in the Americas on 12 October 1492, was a Lucayan island. Its modern identity is disputed; San Salvador is the usual candidate.

namesOverTime.name: Islas de Bajamar

from.note: Spanish charts of the early sixteenth century; the exact first usage is not fixed.

namesOverTime.note: 'Islands of the shallow sea' — the origin of the name Bahamas.

namesOverTime.name: The Bahamas
namesOverTime.note: Woodes Rogers arrived as the first royal governor in 1718 with a commission to end the pirate republic at Nassau; the islands were a crown colony from then.

geoCoverage.label: About 700 islands and 2,400 cays
geoCoverage.change: The Turks and Caicos Islands were governed from Nassau between 1799 and 1848 and are recorded here as a separate place, because they were separated again and never came back.

date.note: The Eleutheran Adventurers' expedition sailed in 1648; the month of the wreck on Eleuthera is not securely recorded.

acquisitions.how: About seventy English Puritans from Bermuda, calling themselves the Eleutheran Adventurers, wrecked on a reef off Eleuthera and founded a religious-freedom colony on islands the Spanish had emptied of people 130 years earlier.

counterparties.name: The Lucayan people
counterparties.lost: Everything, and before any English person arrived. Spain deported the entire Lucayan population — usually estimated at 40,000 or more — to work in the mines and pearl fisheries of Hispaniola and Cuba, and within about 25 years the islands were empty.
counterparties.note: This was the first mass deportation of the European colonisation of the Americas. It happened between roughly 1500 and 1520, and it is why the English found 'uninhabited' islands.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: A claim it never occupied. Spain attacked and burned Nassau repeatedly — in 1684, 1703 and 1782 — but never settled the islands.

instrument.name: Articles and Orders of the Company of Eleutherian Adventurers
instrument.note: The Articles promised religious liberty and are sometimes described as an early written constitution; the colony nearly starved and was fed by charity from Massachusetts.

people.name: William Sayle
people.role: Bermudian Puritan who led the Eleutheran Adventurers and later governed the colony

statusPeriods.label: Proprietors, wreckers and pirates
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: In law the Lords Proprietors of Carolina governed. In fact almost nobody did: the islands lived on salvaging wrecks and on privateering, and between about 1706 and 1718 Nassau was run by a self-declared republic of pirates.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Charles Town, later Nassau, under proprietors in London who never came
statusPeriods.franchise: None.
statusPeriods.note: In law the islands belonged to the six Lords Proprietors of Carolina from 1 November 1670. In fact nobody governed: Spain burned Nassau in 1684 and 1703, and from about 1706 to 1718 the town was held by an alliance of pirates including Benjamin Hornigold, Charles Vane and Anne Bonny.

statusPeriods.label: Royal government and an assembly
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A royal governor took over from the proprietors, cleared out the pirates, and called the first House of Assembly in 1729; the islands remained poor, living on salt, wrecking and the sea.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The status is crown colony because the Crown had taken the government from the proprietors, but from 1729 an elected Assembly existed, so control was in practice shared. The default degree is kept because the governor's authority in this period was real and unchallenged.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nassau
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders; the first Assembly of 1729 had 24 members.
statusPeriods.note: Woodes Rogers arrived on 26 July 1718 with a royal pardon and a commission; he pardoned most of the pirates, hanged eight in December 1718, and gave the colony its motto, Expulsis Piratis, Restituta Commercia. The proprietors sold their remaining property rights to the Crown for £12,000 in 1787.

statusPeriods.label: Spanish occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Spanish expedition from Havana took Nassau without a fight in May 1782 and governed for eleven months, until an American Loyalist, Andrew Deveaux, retook the town with about 220 men and a fleet of fishing boats.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Spain governed and Britain had no authority; degree 0 rather than the default 5, which describes British occupation of another power's territory.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nassau, under the Spanish governor

statusPeriods.label: Loyalists, cotton, and the Bay Street Boys
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor and an Assembly elected on a property franchise governed together; from the 1830s to the 1960s a small group of white Nassau merchants known as the Bay Street Boys controlled the Assembly and, through it, the islands.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nassau
statusPeriods.franchise: A property franchise, with plural voting for property owners in more than one district and a company vote, that kept the Black majority out of power until 1967. Women got the vote only in 1962.
statusPeriods.note: American Loyalists arriving after 1783 brought about 5,700 enslaved people and tripled the population, turning a wrecking economy briefly into a cotton one; the crop failed within twenty years and many owners left, leaving the enslaved population behind.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The 1964 constitution gave the Bahamas a Premier and cabinet government; in 1967 the Progressive Liberal Party won and Lynden Pindling became the first Black head of government — the event Bahamians call Majority Rule.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nassau
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage, after the company vote and plural voting were abolished in 1964 and constituency boundaries were redrawn.

departures.how: Six years after Majority Rule ended white minority government, Lynden Pindling's government took the Bahamas to independence at a London conference in December 1972, and the flag changed at midnight in Nassau.

led.name: Lynden Pindling
led.role: leader of the Progressive Liberal Party and first Prime Minister; threw the Speaker's mace out of the window of the House of Assembly in April 1965 to protest at gerrymandered constituencies

led.name: Milo Butler
led.role: PLP member who threw the hourglass out of the window on the same day; became the first Bahamian Governor-General in 1973

led.name: Doris Johnson
led.role: led the suffrage movement that won Bahamian women the vote in 1962

cost.note: No one died at independence. The turning point was the general strike of January 1958, which shut Nassau for 19 days and forced Britain to impose a fairer franchise.

departures.borders: No border moved, but the archipelago's shape is its history: 700 islands strung along the route from Florida to Cuba, which made the Bahamas rich from blockade running in the 1860s, from Prohibition rum in the 1920s, and from offshore banking afterwards.

slavery.note: The Bahamas never had a plantation economy that worked: cotton failed by 1810, so enslaved Bahamians were hired out, fished, sailed and farmed, and by 1834 many were living almost independently on the outer islands.

abolitionDate.note: The Slave Trade Act. It made the Bahamas a landing place for 'liberated Africans': roughly 6,000 people taken off intercepted slave ships were landed and settled here between 1811 and 1860.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom in law in 1834, then four years of apprenticeship.

toll.money: £128,296 was paid in 1836 to Bahamian slave-owners for 10,086 people. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: Slave Compensation Commission records digitised by University College London's Legacies of British Slavery database.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.author: Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery, University College London
warrant.work: Legacies of British Slavery database
warrant.supports: £128,296 was paid in 1836 to Bahamian slave-owners for 10,086 people.
warrant.check: ucl.ac.uk/lbs — browse by colony. Every award transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission’s registers, T 71, The National Archives, Kew.

populationTransfer.note: The Lucayans deported to extinction by Spain before 1520; American Loyalists with 5,700 enslaved people after 1783; and about 6,000 Africans landed from intercepted slave ships after 1808.

toll.note: Estimates of the Lucayan population deported to Hispaniola and Cuba between about 1500 and 1520 range widely; the figures come from Spanish colonial accounts and modern archaeological reconstructions, and no count was made at the time.

consequences.economicLegacy: Wrecking, then blockade running for the Confederacy, then Prohibition rum-running, then tourism and offshore banking: the Bahamas has repeatedly grown rich on other countries' laws.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, a House of Assembly meeting since 1729 — one of the oldest in the western hemisphere — and a Bahamian dialect with strong Loyalist-era American roots.

peak.populationNote: 1970 census. In 1783 the islands held about 4,000 people; the Loyalist influx tripled that within three years.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: The Bahamas’s largest recorded population: 168,812 people, counted in 1970.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Michael Craton and Gail Saunders
evidence.work: Islanders in the Stream: A History of the Bahamian People
evidence.supports: The whole narrative from Lucayan settlement through Loyalists, slavery and Majority Rule.

evidence.author: Colin Woodard
evidence.work: The Republic of Pirates
evidence.supports: The pirate republic at Nassau and Woodes Rogers's suppression of it.

evidence.author: B. W. Higman
evidence.work: A Concise History of the Caribbean
evidence.supports: The Lucayan deportations and comparative Caribbean demography.

pedagogy.hook: The first place Columbus landed in the Americas was a Bahamian island. Within thirty years Spain had shipped every single Lucayan away to die in the mines of Hispaniola, and the islands stood empty for over a century.

misconception.belief: Caribbean islands that Europeans called 'uninhabited' had always been empty.
misconception.correction: The Bahamas were home to tens of thousands of Lucayan people when Columbus arrived in 1492. Spain deported all of them between about 1500 and 1520 to replace the labour it had already worked to death on Hispaniola. The English who arrived in 1648 found empty islands because a deportation had emptied them, not because nobody had ever lived there.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Bahamas is where the American story starts, and where the pattern starts too: a people removed, islands repopulated by force, and a colony that lived for three centuries on the edges of other countries' laws — wrecking, piracy, blockade running, rum and offshore banking.

keyDates.what: Columbus lands at Guanahani, a Lucayan island
The Eleutheran Adventurers found an English colony
Woodes Rogers arrives and ends the pirate republic
Andrew Deveaux retakes Nassau from Spain
Majority Rule: Pindling's PLP takes office
Independence

from.note: A marker for the centuries of Lucayan settlement; archaeology shows villages on Middle Caicos with a ball court, the only one found in the Bahamian archipelago.

to.note: The date the Spanish deportations had emptied the islands.

from.note: The names appear in English usage as the Bermudian salt trade develops; 'Turk' is usually said to come from a cactus resembling a fez, and 'Caicos' from a Lucayan word.
Bermudian salt rakers were working the islands seasonally by the 1670s; 1678 is the conventional date for the start of continuous English use.

geoCoverage.label: Eight main islands and about forty cays

date.note: The islands were used seasonally from the 1660s; a permanent Bermudian presence is documented from about 1678.

acquisitions.how: Bermudian salt rakers came down every year to work the natural salt ponds of Grand Turk and Salt Cay, raking sea salt to sell to the cod fisheries of Newfoundland and New England, and eventually stayed.

counterparties.name: The Lucayan people
counterparties.lost: Everything, before any English arrival: Spain deported the entire population of the Bahamian archipelago, these islands included, to the mines of Hispaniola between about 1500 and 1520.

counterparties.name: Spain and France
counterparties.lost: Claims neither occupied. The French drove the salt rakers off in 1706, 1753 and 1764, and Spanish forces raided in 1710, but neither settled.

contested.note: There is no founding document. Seasonal Bermudian salt raking shaded into permanent settlement across the 1670s and 1680s, and different accounts give dates between 1668 and 1681.

from.note: See how it was taken: the start of continuous English use is approximate.

statusPeriods.label: Bermudian salt ponds
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: There was no government. Bermudian salt rakers organised themselves and answered, loosely, to Bermuda's assembly; the Bahamas claimed jurisdiction and the rakers ignored it.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Nominally within the Bermudian and then Bahamian sphere, but in practice almost ungoverned; the default degree is kept because no other authority existed either.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bermuda, in principle
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Annexed to the Bahamas
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The islands were annexed to the Bahamas and given two seats in the Nassau assembly; American Loyalists had arrived in the 1780s with about 1,000 enslaved people to grow cotton, and the crop failed within a generation.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nassau, Bahamas
statusPeriods.franchise: White male property-holders only.

statusPeriods.label: Separate colony with its own council
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After petitioning against Bahamian taxation, the islands were separated and given a president and legislative board of their own under the Governor of Jamaica.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Grand Turk, under the Governor of Jamaica
statusPeriods.franchise: A narrow property franchise.

statusPeriods.label: Dependency of Jamaica
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The islands became a dependency of Jamaica, administered by a commissioner in Grand Turk under the Governor at Kingston, 750 kilometres away, with almost no revenue of their own.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Grand Turk, under the Governor of Jamaica
statusPeriods.franchise: None until the twentieth century; universal adult suffrage came in 1961.

statusPeriods.label: Colony in its own right after Jamaican independence
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: When Jamaica became independent the islands were left behind as a separate colony, briefly attached to the Bahamas from 1965, and given their own governor when the Bahamas went independent in 1973.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Grand Turk, then Cockburn Town
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.
statusPeriods.note: In 1917 the Canadian prime minister Robert Borden suggested annexing the islands to Canada, and a private member's bill to the same effect was introduced in Ottawa in 1974. Neither went anywhere, and the idea is still raised periodically.

statusPeriods.label: British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor appointed in London holds defence, external affairs, internal security and the public service; an elected House of Assembly runs the rest — except between 2009 and 2012, when Britain suspended the constitution and ruled directly.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cockburn Town, Grand Turk
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage; British citizenship was restored to Turks and Caicos Islanders by the British Overseas Territories Act 2002.
statusPeriods.note: A commission of inquiry under Sir Robin Auld reported in 2009 that there was a high probability of systemic corruption in the territory's government. Britain suspended ministerial government and the House of Assembly on 14 August 2009 and governed directly until elections in November 2012.

stillBritish.note: The Turks and Caicos Islands are still British, and were governed directly from London as recently as 2009 to 2012 after a corruption inquiry.

departures.how: The islands never left. They were passed between Bermuda, the Bahamas and Jamaica for two centuries, and were left as a colony each time their administering neighbour became independent.

slavery.note: Slavery here meant salt and cotton, not sugar: Loyalist planters arrived in the 1780s with about 1,000 enslaved people, the cotton failed, and most owners left, abandoning the enslaved population on the islands.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom in law in 1834, then four years of apprenticeship, applied through the Bahamas.

toll.money: Compensation for the islands' enslaved people was paid through the Bahamas award, which covered 10,086 people across the whole archipelago. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: The Turks and Caicos figures are not separately itemised in the Slave Compensation Commission returns, so no separate money figure can be given honestly.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.author: Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery, University College London
warrant.work: Legacies of British Slavery database
warrant.supports: Compensation for the islands' enslaved people was paid through the Bahamas award, which covered 10,086 people across the whole archipelago.
warrant.check: ucl.ac.uk/lbs — browse by colony. Every award transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission’s registers, T 71, The National Archives, Kew.

populationTransfer.note: The Lucayans deported to extinction by Spain before 1520; Bermudian salt rakers from the 1670s; Loyalists with about 1,000 enslaved people in the 1780s; and Haitian migration since the 1980s.

commonwealth.note: Represented by the United Kingdom; an associate member of CARICOM.

consequences.economicLegacy: Salt for 250 years, until the industry closed in 1964; then offshore finance and tourism, and a population that has grown ninefold since 1970.
consequences.borderLegacy: Passed between four administering neighbours in three centuries — Bermuda, the Bahamas, Jamaica, then the Bahamas again — the islands ended up British by default each time a neighbour left.

peak.populationNote: 2022 estimate. The population was about 5,700 in 1970, before tourism.

evidence.author: Michael J. Jarvis
evidence.work: In the Eye of All Trade: Bermuda, Bermudians, and the Maritime Atlantic World, 1680-1783
evidence.supports: The Bermudian salt trade that created the settlement and its Atlantic markets.

evidence.author: Michael Craton and Gail Saunders
evidence.work: Islanders in the Stream: A History of the Bahamian People
evidence.supports: The Lucayan deportations, the Loyalist influx and the Bahamian administration of the islands.

contested.note: The date of first permanent settlement is uncertain, and the islands' enslaved population and compensation payments were recorded under the Bahamas rather than separately, so several figures cannot be given precisely.

pedagogy.hook: Britain suspended this territory's elected government and ruled it directly from London for three years — not in 1909, but from 2009 to 2012.

misconception.belief: The British Empire is entirely in the past.
misconception.correction: Fourteen British Overseas Territories still exist, and Britain still exercises real power in them. After a commission of inquiry reported probable systemic corruption in 2009, the British government suspended the Turks and Caicos constitution, dissolved the House of Assembly, and governed through its governor until elections in 2012.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: These islands show what happens to the small pieces of empire: passed from Bermuda to the Bahamas to Jamaica for administrative convenience, left behind whenever a neighbour became independent, and still governed under a constitution London can suspend.

date.note: The start of continuous settlement is approximate.

keyDates.what: Bermudian salt rakers settle Grand Turk and Salt Cay
Annexed to the Bahamas
Made a dependency of Jamaica
Left behind as a colony when Jamaica becomes independent
Britain suspends the constitution and imposes direct rule

namesOverTime.name: Las Tortugas

to.note: The name changed gradually on Spanish charts during the early sixteenth century.

namesOverTime.note: Columbus named them 'the turtles' on his fourth voyage, for the sea turtles that covered the water. The turtles were hunted to near-extinction to feed passing ships.

namesOverTime.name: Caymanas

from.note: The name appears on charts through the sixteenth century.

namesOverTime.note: From a Carib word for a marine crocodile; the islands did once have crocodiles.

namesOverTime.name: The Cayman Islands
namesOverTime.note: Spain recognised English possession at the Treaty of Madrid in 1670; the English spelling has been the official one since.

geoCoverage.label: Grand Cayman, Cayman Brac and Little Cayman

acquisitions.how: Spain recognised English possession of Jamaica and its dependencies, the Cayman Islands among them, at the Treaty of Madrid; permanent settlement followed only in the 1730s, when the first land grants were made on Grand Cayman.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Three uninhabited islands it had charted in 1503 and never settled, ceded as part of the general recognition of English Jamaica.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.note: The Cayman Islands are one of the few places in the Caribbean with no evidence of permanent pre-Columbian settlement: no Indigenous village site has been found, and the islands appear to have been visited but not inhabited.

instrument.name: Treaty of Madrid (1670)
instrument.note: Also called the Godolphin Treaty. Spain recognised English possessions in the Americas in exchange for England suppressing buccaneering — a promise England did not keep, as Henry Morgan sacked Panama six months later.

statusPeriods.label: Turtlers, wreckers and a self-run settlement
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nobody governed the Caymans for most of two centuries. Settlers from Jamaica took land grants from the 1730s, elected their own magistrates and vestry from 1831, and lived on turtling, wrecking, shipbuilding and cotton.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The elected vestry of 1831 was a local invention, not a colonial grant, and Jamaica's governor took almost no interest; the default degree is kept because no rival authority existed.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bodden Town, then George Town, nominally under Jamaica
statusPeriods.franchise: Male householders; the vestry was elected by the settlers themselves from 1831.

statusPeriods.label: Dependency of Jamaica
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An act of 1863 made the islands a formal dependency of Jamaica, run by a commissioner from 1898 under the Governor at Kingston; the islands paid no direct taxes and Britain spent almost nothing on them.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: George Town, under the Governor of Jamaica
statusPeriods.franchise: A property franchise; universal adult suffrage came in 1957.
statusPeriods.note: The population lived largely on remittances from Caymanian men working as seamen on foreign merchant ships — at one point a majority of adult men were at sea.

statusPeriods.label: Separate colony after Jamaican independence
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Caymanians chose to stay British rather than go with Jamaica; an administrator, later a governor, held the reserved powers while an elected Legislative Assembly grew steadily stronger.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: George Town, Grand Cayman
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage since 1957.
statusPeriods.note: Banking and company registration law passed in 1966 turned an island of seamen and turtlers into an offshore financial centre within twenty years.

statusPeriods.label: British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor appointed in London keeps defence, external affairs, internal security and the courts; an elected Parliament and a Premier run everything else, including one of the world's largest financial sectors.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: George Town, Grand Cayman
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage; British citizenship restored by the British Overseas Territories Act 2002.

stillBritish.note: The Cayman Islands stayed British when Jamaica became independent in 1962, and there has never been a serious independence movement.

departures.how: The islands never left, and chose not to: when Jamaica went independent in 1962 Caymanians opted to remain a British colony rather than join the new state.

slavery.note: Slavery in the Caymans was small and domestic: about 950 enslaved people in 1834, on an island with no plantations, working in households, on small farms, in boatbuilding and at sea.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom in law in 1834 with apprenticeship to 1838, applied through Jamaica. Emancipation day is still marked in Cayman as a public occasion.

toll.note: The 1834 registration counted 985 enslaved people in a total population of about 2,000 — roughly half the islanders. The figures come from the Jamaican slave registration returns.

warrant.author: The Slave Registration Office, Jamaica
warrant.work: Jamaican slave registration returns for the Cayman Islands, 1834
warrant.supports: The 1834 registration counted 985 enslaved people in a total population of about 2,000 — roughly half the islanders. The figures come from the Jamaican slave registration returns.
warrant.check: The registers are in T 71 at The National Archives, Kew, and are indexed award by award in the Legacies of British Slavery database at ucl.ac.uk/lbs.
warrant.note: Registration existed to protect owners’ property in people. It is the most precise count on this page for exactly that reason.

populationTransfer.note: Settlers came from Jamaica, from disbanded soldiers and from shipwrecks; the islands' modern population is over half foreign-born, drawn by the financial sector.

commonwealth.note: Represented by the United Kingdom.

consequences.economicLegacy: Turtling and seafaring until the 1950s, then banking, insurance and investment funds: the Cayman Islands now host tens of thousands of registered companies and funds — far more entities than people.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law with an appeal to the Privy Council, and a body of company and trust law written from the 1960s onwards that made a British territory of 80,000 people central to global finance.

peak.populationNote: 2023 estimate. The population was about 2,000 in 1834 and roughly 8,000 in 1960, before the financial sector.

evidence.author: Michael Craton
evidence.work: Founded upon the Seas: A History of the Cayman Islands and Their People
evidence.supports: Settlement, the turtling and wrecking economy, slavery, and the twentieth-century transformation.

evidence.author: B. W. Higman
evidence.work: A Concise History of the Caribbean
evidence.supports: The islands' place among the Jamaican dependencies and the growth of Caribbean offshore finance.

contested.note: The famous story that Caymanians were rewarded with freedom from taxation for rescuing the crews of the Wreck of the Ten Sail in 1794 — supposedly including a royal prince — has no documentary support; no prince was aboard and no such grant exists. It is still repeated locally and in guidebooks.

pedagogy.hook: The Cayman Islands have more registered companies than people, and until the 1950s most Caymanian men earned their living as sailors on other countries' ships.

misconception.belief: Caymanians won permanent freedom from taxation from King George III for rescuing a royal prince from a shipwreck in 1794.
misconception.correction: Ten ships were wrecked on the Grand Cayman reef in February 1794 and Caymanians did rescue the crews, losing not a single life. But no prince was aboard, no royal grant exists in any archive, and the islands' lack of direct taxation dates from ordinary nineteenth-century colonial practice. The legend is a good story that explains a real fact with an invented cause.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Cayman shows the empire's afterlife most sharply: a poor dependency of Jamaica that chose to stay British in 1962, then wrote company and banking law that made a British territory of 80,000 people one of the largest financial centres on earth.

keyDates.what: Spain cedes the islands with Jamaica at the Treaty of Madrid
The first land grant on Grand Cayman; permanent settlement begins
The Wreck of the Ten Sail; every crew saved
Formally made a dependency of Jamaica
Caymanians choose to stay British as Jamaica leaves
Banking and company laws create the offshore financial centre

territories.name: British Honduras (Belize)
territories.formalName: Colony of British Honduras, renamed Belize in 1973

from.note: A marker for the Classic Maya period; Caracol, Lamanai, Xunantunich and Altun Ha are all in modern Belize, and Lamanai was still occupied when the Spanish arrived.

namesOverTime.name: The Settlement of Belize in the Bay of Honduras

from.note: The founding date is traditional and unverifiable; English logwood cutting in the bay is documented from the 1650s and 1660s.

namesOverTime.note: The careful official name of a place Britain spent two centuries insisting was not a colony.

modernSuccessors.name: Belize
modernSuccessors.note: Guatemala still claims all or part of Belize; both states agreed to refer the claim to the International Court of Justice after referendums in 2018 and 2019.

from.note: The traditional founding date; continuous English cutting is documented from the 1650s.

geoCoverage.label: Cutting rights, not territory
geoCoverage.change: Britain's treaty rights covered only the coastal strip between the Hondo and, after 1786, the Sibun rivers. Settlers pushed south to the Sarstoon anyway, which is why Guatemala disputes the southern half of Belize to this day.

geoCoverage.label: Colony of British Honduras
geoCoverage.change: Britain finally claimed sovereignty over the whole territory to the Sarstoon, 76 years after signing a convention that said the land was Spain's.

date.note: The 1638 date is a settlement tradition with no documentary basis; English and Scottish logwood cutters, many of them former buccaneers, are documented in the Bay of Honduras from the 1650s.

acquisitions.how: English logwood cutters, many of them buccaneers put out of work by the peace with Spain, moved into the mangrove creeks of the Bay of Honduras to cut dyewood on land Spain claimed and did not occupy.

counterparties.name: Maya peoples of the Belize lowlands
counterparties.lost: Their forests and, over two centuries, their land. The Maya had already fought the Spanish for a century; British cutters pushed them inland, and colonial land law in the 1860s and 1870s treated Maya villages as squatters on Crown land.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Nothing in law for 224 years — Spain kept formal sovereignty until its American empire collapsed — but it lost control of the ground almost immediately and attacked the settlement repeatedly, in 1717, 1730, 1754, 1779 and 1798.

acquisitions.resistance: Spanish expeditions destroyed the settlement several times and the cutters simply came back; the Maya fought the settlers and the colonial government into the 1870s, and San Pedro Maya communities were attacked by British troops in 1867.

contested.note: The traditional founding date of 1638, and the story of a shipwrecked buccaneer named Wallace giving Belize its name, are both unsupported by any contemporary document. Assad Shoman treats them as national myth-making.

acquisitions.how: Britain signed a convention accepting that the land belonged to Spain, in exchange for the right to cut mahogany as far south as the Sibun and to appoint a superintendent — and promised to build no forts and set up no government.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Effective control, while keeping sovereignty on paper. Spain also gained: Britain agreed in the same convention to evacuate the Mosquito Coast, and about 2,000 settlers and their enslaved workers were moved from there to Belize.

instrument.name: Convention of London (1786)
instrument.note: The convention explicitly barred Britain from erecting fortifications or any system of government in the settlement. Britain did both anyway.

acquisitions.how: Britain declared the settlement a colony under the Governor of Jamaica, claiming sovereignty over territory it had spent two centuries formally admitting was Spanish, and over Maya land it had never treated with anyone about.

counterparties.name: Guatemala
counterparties.lost: Its claim as Spain's successor. Guatemala had signed a boundary treaty with Britain in 1859 in exchange for a road to the coast that Britain never built, and has argued ever since that the treaty is therefore void.

counterparties.name: Maya communities of the interior
counterparties.lost: Legal title to land they lived on. Crown land legislation from the 1860s made Maya villages tenants at will, and the reservations created afterwards were held at the government's pleasure.

instrument.name: Wyke-Aycinena Treaty with Guatemala
instrument.note: Article 7 committed both states to build a road from Guatemala City to the Caribbean coast. It was never built, and Guatemala treats the whole treaty as void in consequence.

from.note: The founding date is traditional; see how it was taken.

statusPeriods.label: Baymen on Spanish soil
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: There was no British government here at all. The cutters made their own law in a public meeting, wrote Burnaby's Code in 1765, elected magistrates, and were disowned by London whenever Spain complained.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: The Public Meeting at Belize Town, disowned by London
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-owning white cutters. Burnaby's Code of 1765 was written by the settlers for themselves, and the Public Meeting continued to run the settlement until 1854.

statusPeriods.label: British superintendent, Spanish sovereignty
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British superintendent governed alongside the settlers' Public Meeting on land Britain had signed a convention admitting was Spain's; after the Battle of St George's Caye in 1798 Spain never returned, and Britain simply stayed.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Degree 4 rather than the default 5 for occupation: Britain administered the settlement through a superintendent but formally disclaimed sovereignty, and the settlers' own Public Meeting held real power until 1854.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Belize Town, under the Superintendent and the Public Meeting
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-owning white settlers; the free coloured population won the vote in 1808 but under a property bar most could not meet.
statusPeriods.note: In 1832 about 200 Garifuna arrived from Honduras — descendants of the people Britain had deported from St Vincent in 1797. Their landing on 19 November is now Belize's Garifuna Settlement Day.

statusPeriods.label: Colony of British Honduras
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A lieutenant-governor under Jamaica until 1884, then a governor of a separate crown colony, ruled with a nominated council; the elected assembly the settlers had run for a century was gone.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Belize Town, under the Governor of Jamaica until 1884, then directly under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1936, when a narrow franchise returned; universal adult suffrage came in 1954.
statusPeriods.note: The 1931 hurricane killed about 2,500 people in Belize Town, and the government's response — a loan on condition of stricter British control of the colony's finances — helped produce the labour movement of the 1930s under Antonio Soberanis.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government under George Price
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Belizeans ran their own government from 1964 under a Premier; Britain kept defence and foreign affairs, and kept a garrison, because Guatemala had massed troops on the border more than once and threatened to invade.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Belize City, then Belmopan after the capital moved inland in 1970
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage since 1954.

departures.how: Belize became independent seventeen years after internal self-government, delayed by Guatemala's claim; Britain left 1,500 troops, Harrier jets and a radar station behind because Guatemala refused to recognise the new state.

led.name: George Cadle Price
led.role: leader of the People's United Party from 1956 and first Prime Minister; campaigned for independence for 31 years

led.name: Philip Goldson
led.role: nationalist and later opposition leader, jailed with Price in 1951, who broke with him over the terms proposed for settling the Guatemalan claim

led.name: Antonio Soberanis Gómez
led.role: barber and labour organiser whose Unemployed Brigade led the 1934 protests that began modern Belizean politics

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. The cost was measured in delay and in soldiers: Guatemala's claim held independence up for years, and British forces stayed until 1994.

departures.borders: The border with Guatemala is the one Britain drew in the 1859 treaty, in exchange for a road it never built. Guatemala has claimed all or part of Belize ever since, and the case is now before the International Court of Justice.

slavery.note: Belize's enslaved people cut mahogany, not cane: small gangs working deep in the forest for months, which gave them more autonomy and more chance to escape than any sugar colony allowed, and produced revolts in 1765, 1768, 1773 and 1820.

abolitionDate.note: End of the British slave trade.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom in law in 1834, then four years of apprenticeship. Debt peonage and the advance-and-truck system kept mahogany workers tied to their employers long afterwards.

toll.money: £53,690 was paid in 1836 to Belize slave-owners for 1,923 people. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: Slave Compensation Commission records, digitised by University College London's Legacies of British Slavery database.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.author: Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery, University College London
warrant.work: Legacies of British Slavery database
warrant.supports: £53,690 was paid in 1836 to Belize slave-owners for 1,923 people.
warrant.check: ucl.ac.uk/lbs — browse by colony. Every award transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission’s registers, T 71, The National Archives, Kew.

populationTransfer.note: Africans trafficked in to cut mahogany; about 2,000 settlers and enslaved people moved from the Mosquito Coast in 1787; Garifuna from Honduras in 1802 and 1832; and Yucatec Maya and Mestizo refugees fleeing the Caste War of Yucatán after 1847.

violence.note: British troops burned San Pedro Maya villages in 1867 after the Maya leader Marcos Canul raided a mahogany camp; Canul was killed attacking Orange Walk in 1872.

consequences.borderLegacy: Guatemala's claim, resting on Britain's failure to build a road promised in 1859, is unresolved after 165 years and is now before the International Court of Justice.
consequences.economicLegacy: Logwood, then mahogany, then chicle for chewing gum, then sugar and citrus: an extractive forest economy that left the country with almost no infrastructure at independence.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law and English as the official language, in a country where most people speak Belizean Kriol, Spanish, or one of three Maya languages, and where Garifuna is a recognised national heritage.

peak.populationNote: 1980 census. The settlement held about 4,000 people in 1790, of whom roughly three quarters were enslaved.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: British Honduras (Belize)’s largest recorded population: 145,353 people, counted in 1980.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
areaWarrant.supports: British Honduras (Belize)’s greatest extent, 22,966 km² in 1981: the 1 map unit this atlas draws it holding that year measure 22,373 km², within 2.6% of it.
areaWarrant.check: Open the atlas at that year and select this territory: the outline you see IS the figure. Its units are listed under `geoCoverage` in the shard and measured in app/data/geo/units.index.json, from Natural Earth 1:10m boundaries — public domain, naturalearthdata.com.
areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: Assad Shoman
evidence.work: Thirteen Chapters of a History of Belize
evidence.supports: The settlement's legal ambiguity, the St George's Caye myth, the Guatemalan claim and the independence movement.

evidence.author: O. Nigel Bolland
evidence.work: The Formation of a Colonial Society: Belize, from Conquest to Crown Colony
evidence.supports: Mahogany slavery, Maya dispossession and the making of the colony in 1862.

pedagogy.hook: For two centuries Britain insisted Belize was not a colony. It signed a treaty in 1786 promising Spain it would build no forts and set up no government there — and then did both.

misconception.belief: At the Battle of St George's Caye in 1798, Belizean settlers and the people they enslaved fought side by side against Spain, and that is where the nation was born.
misconception.correction: Enslaved men certainly fought — the settlement had no one else to man the boats — but the story of a shared national founding was written up in the 1890s by a colonial establishment that wanted a loyal origin myth. Assad Shoman and other Belizean historians point out that the men who fought were still property the next morning, and that emancipation came 40 years later.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Belize shows the empire operating without a legal foundation for 224 years: a settlement Britain denied governing, on land it admitted was Spain's, taken from Maya people nobody negotiated with — and a border dispute from 1859 that is still in court.

keyDates.what: Burnaby's Code: the settlers write their own law
The Convention of London: rights to cut wood, no right to govern
The Battle of St George's Caye; Spain never returns
Britain finally declares a colony
Soberanis's Unemployed Brigade begins modern Belizean politics
Independence, with British troops staying until 1994

namesOverTime.name: Guiana

from.note: A marker for the pre-colonial period; the name is an Indigenous word, usually glossed 'land of many waters'.

namesOverTime.note: The Lokono (Arawak), Kalina (Carib), Warao, Wapishana, Macushi, Akawaio, Patamona, Arekuna, Wai Wai and Pemon peoples lived here before, during and after Dutch and British rule; about 10 per cent of Guyanese are Indigenous today.

namesOverTime.name: Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice
namesOverTime.note: Three separate Dutch colonies: Essequibo from 1616, Berbice from 1627, Demerara from 1745. Their names survive as Guyanese counties and rivers.

modernSuccessors.name: Guyana
modernSuccessors.note: Venezuela claims the Essequibo region — about 159,500 square kilometres, roughly two thirds of Guyana — on the ground that the 1899 arbitration of the British boundary was rigged. The case is before the International Court of Justice.

to.note: The colonies were handed back to the Batavian Republic during 1802 under the Peace of Amiens; the exact handover dates differ between the three colonies.

geoCoverage.label: First British occupation of the three Dutch colonies
geoCoverage.change: British forces took Demerara, Essequibo and Berbice from the Dutch in April 1796. Only the coastal strip was under any European control; the interior belonged to Indigenous nations.

geoCoverage.label: British Guiana
geoCoverage.change: Britain retook the three colonies in 1803 and bought them at the 1814 settlement. The colony's western boundary was drawn by a British surveyor and remained disputed with Venezuela for the whole of British rule and ever since.

acquisitions.how: A British squadron from Barbados took Demerara, Essequibo and Berbice from the Batavian Republic without serious fighting, helped by the fact that most of Demerara's planters were already British.

counterparties.name: The Batavian Republic (the Netherlands under French control)
counterparties.lost: Three colonies the Dutch West India Company had built over 180 years, with their sugar and coffee estates and about 70,000 enslaved people.

counterparties.name: The Kalina, Lokono, Warao, Akawaio and Macushi nations of the Guianas
counterparties.lost: Nothing immediately — the Dutch had governed by alliance and trade, and the Kalina and Lokono had been treaty partners rather than subjects — but they lost that status as British planters pushed inland during the nineteenth century.
counterparties.note: The Dutch relied on Indigenous allies to recapture people who escaped from the plantations, a role written into treaty and paid for in trade goods.

acquisitions.how: Britain retook the three colonies fifteen months after handing them back at Amiens, and this time kept them.

counterparties.name: The Batavian Republic
counterparties.lost: The colonies for good; it never governed them again.

acquisitions.how: Britain paid the restored Kingdom of the Netherlands £6 million and kept Demerara, Essequibo, Berbice and the Cape of Good Hope, handing back Java, Suriname and Curaçao — a straight purchase of colonies with people on them.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of the Netherlands
counterparties.lost: Its Guiana colonies and the Cape, sold under pressure at the settlement of the Napoleonic wars; the Dutch got Suriname, Java and Curaçao back, and £6 million, of which £2 million was earmarked for fortresses in the Low Countries.

counterparties.name: The enslaved people of Demerara, Essequibo and Berbice
counterparties.lost: They were bought and sold with the colonies. About 100,000 people changed sovereign without being consulted, and the sale price counted their labour as an asset.

instrument.name: Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814 (Convention of London)
instrument.note: The £6 million was not paid for the Guianas alone: it covered the Cape as well and included £2 million for the barrier fortresses. The treaty is the clearest example in the empire of colonies being bought like property.

to.note: The handover to the Batavian Republic took place during 1802 and on different dates in each colony.

statusPeriods.label: First British occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British military governors ran three Dutch colonies under Dutch law and Dutch institutions — the Court of Policy and the College of Kiezers — leaving the planters, who were mostly British anyway, entirely in place.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Stabroek, later Georgetown
statusPeriods.franchise: Plantation owners, under the Dutch electoral system Britain kept.

statusPeriods.label: Second occupation, then purchase
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned the three colonies to the Batavian Republic during 1802 under the Peace of Amiens, and retook them in September 1803.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Military occupation became legal ownership when Britain bought the colonies in 1814, but the Dutch constitution stayed: a Court of Policy of officials and planters governed, and Roman-Dutch law survived here into the twentieth century.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Georgetown
statusPeriods.franchise: Plantation owners only.

statusPeriods.label: British Guiana under the Court of Policy
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The three colonies were united as British Guiana under a governor and a Combined Court in which planters voted the budget; the sugar interest ran the colony, and used its control of taxation to fund the immigration of indentured Indians.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Georgetown
statusPeriods.franchise: A high property and income qualification; in 1891 there were about 4,000 voters in a population of 280,000.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1838 and 1917 about 239,000 people were brought from India under indenture — more than to any other British Caribbean colony — together with 32,000 Portuguese from Madeira and about 14,000 Chinese.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain abolished the Dutch-derived constitution and made British Guiana a crown colony with a nominated majority, taking financial control away from the planters — and from everyone else.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Georgetown, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: A property franchise until 1953, when universal adult suffrage was introduced for the first election under a new constitution.

to.note: Full internal self-government followed the August 1961 election; the constitution came into force during that year.

statusPeriods.label: Constitution suspended; British troops in Georgetown
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: 133 days after the People's Progressive Party won the colony's first universal-suffrage election, Britain suspended the constitution, landed troops from HMS Superb and governed by an interim commission. Cheddi Jagan was jailed in 1954.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Georgetown, under an interim government appointed by the Governor
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage, suspended in 1953 and restored for elections in 1957.
statusPeriods.note: Declassified British and American records show that Britain and the United States worked to split the PPP and to remove Jagan, and that Britain changed the electoral system to proportional representation in 1964 knowing it would put Forbes Burnham in office instead.

from.note: The new constitution came into force during 1961, after the August election.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An elected premier ran internal affairs while Britain kept defence, external affairs and internal security, and used them: British troops were deployed during the racial violence of 1962 to 1964.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Georgetown
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage; the voting system was changed from first-past-the-post to proportional representation in 1964.

date.note: The three colonies were handed back to the Batavian Republic during 1802 on different dates.

departures.how: Britain gave Demerara, Essequibo and Berbice back to the Batavian Republic under the Peace of Amiens, and retook them fifteen months later when the war resumed.

becomes.name: Dutch Guiana colonies under the Batavian Republic

led.name: Robert Jenkinson, Lord Hawkesbury
led.role: British foreign secretary who negotiated the Peace of Amiens

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. About 70,000 enslaved people were transferred with the colonies, as property.

departures.borders: No line moved; the colonies changed hands whole, and the western boundary with Spanish, later Venezuelan, territory remained undefined.

departures.how: Guyana became independent under Forbes Burnham, after Britain had suspended the constitution in 1953, jailed Cheddi Jagan, and changed the voting system in 1964 to make sure the party it preferred was in office when the flag came down.

led.name: Cheddi Jagan
led.role: dentist and Marxist, founder of the People's Progressive Party; won the elections of 1953, 1957 and 1961 and was out of office at independence

led.name: Forbes Burnham
led.role: co-founder of the PPP who broke away in 1955, was preferred by Britain and the United States, and became first Prime Minister

led.name: Janet Jagan
led.role: American-born co-founder of the PPP, jailed in 1955, later President of Guyana

led.name: Duncan Sandys
led.role: British Colonial Secretary who imposed proportional representation in 1964, knowing it would remove Jagan

Counts come from the 1965 International Commission of Jurists report and later scholarship.

departures.borders: Guyana inherited two disputes: Venezuela claims the Essequibo region west of the 1899 arbitration line, about two thirds of the country, and Suriname claims the New River Triangle in the south-east. Both lines were drawn by European powers.

evidence.author: Colin A. Palmer
evidence.work: Cheddi Jagan and the Politics of Power: British Guiana's Struggle for Independence
evidence.supports: The 1953 suspension, Anglo-American intervention and the change to proportional representation.

slavery.note: Demerara's sugar estates were among the deadliest in the Americas: the coastal plantations were built on land below sea level, and enslaved people dug and maintained thousands of kilometres of sea defences and canals by hand.

abolitionDate.note: End of the British slave trade. Demerara had been importing captives at a great rate right up to the deadline.

emancipationDate.note: Freedom in law in 1834, then four years of apprenticeship. Freed Guyanese pooled wages to buy abandoned estates outright — the village movement — and by 1848 about 44,000 people lived in villages they owned.

toll.money: £4.29 million was paid in 1836 to British Guiana's slave-owners for 84,915 people — the second-largest award after Jamaica, and the highest per person anywhere. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.

commonwealth.note: Guyana became a republic on 23 February 1970 and remains in the Commonwealth.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Schomburgk Line, drawn by a German-born British surveyor in 1840 and confirmed by a Paris arbitration in 1899, is still rejected by Venezuela; oil discoveries offshore since 2015 have made the dispute urgent again.
consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar, then bauxite and rice, and since 2019 one of the fastest oil booms in the world — in the waters Venezuela claims.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law grafted onto Roman-Dutch law, with Dutch county names, an Indian-descended plurality, and a politics still organised along the ethnic lines the sugar economy created.

peak.populationNote: 1970 census. In 1834 the three colonies held 84,915 enslaved people; by 1911 the Indian-descended population alone was over 126,000.

evidence.author: Emilia Viotti da Costa
evidence.work: Crowns of Glory, Tears of Blood: The Demerara Slave Rebellion of 1823
evidence.supports: The 1823 rising, the trial of the missionary John Smith and its effect on British opinion.

evidence.author: Walter Rodney

evidence.author: Colin A. Palmer

contested.note: The number of Africans landed in the three colonies is an estimate; the death toll of the 1962-64 violence is disputed; and the validity of the 1899 boundary arbitration is the subject of a live case at the International Court of Justice, with Venezuela relying on a 1949 memorandum by one of the arbitration lawyers alleging a deal between the British and Russian judges.

pedagogy.hook: The enslaved man who led the 1823 Demerara rebellion was owned by John Gladstone — father of a future British prime minister, and the man who fifteen years later shipped the first indentured Indians to the same estates.

misconception.belief: Britain left its colonies when the people there voted for independence.
misconception.correction: In British Guiana, Britain suspended the constitution in October 1953, 133 days after the first universal-suffrage election, and landed troops. It jailed Cheddi Jagan, worked with the United States to split his party, and imposed proportional representation in 1964 specifically to remove him. Independence came in 1966 under the leader Britain preferred. Britain set the terms and chose the winner.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Guyana holds both halves of the Caribbean story in one country: the deadliest slave plantations in the British Atlantic, and the largest importation of indentured Indians anywhere — and a politics still shaped by the divide those two systems created.

territories.name: The Mosquito Coast
territories.formalName: The Mosquito Shore and the Mosquito Reserve

namesOverTime.name: Mosquitia

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact period; the Miskitu, Mayangna (Sumu) and Rama peoples lived along this coast and its rivers.

namesOverTime.note: The name has nothing to do with the insect: it comes from the Miskitu people, whose own name may derive from the muskets English traders sold them in the seventeenth century.

namesOverTime.name: The Mosquito Reserve
namesOverTime.note: The self-governing reserve created by the Treaty of Managua when Britain handed the coast to Nicaragua. Nicaragua annexed it by force in 1894.

modernSuccessors.name: Nicaragua
modernSuccessors.note: The coast is now the North and South Caribbean Autonomous Regions of Nicaragua, created in 1987 — the Miskitu got a form of self-government back 127 years after Britain signed it away.

geoCoverage.label: The Mosquito Shore protectorate
geoCoverage.change: Britain's superintendency covered the coastal settlements and the Miskitu king's alliance; the interior belonged to Mayangna and Rama communities that neither Britain nor the Miskitu governed.

geoCoverage.label: The revived protectorate
geoCoverage.change: Britain declared a protectorate over the Mosquito kingdom again in 1844 and seized the port of San Juan del Norte in 1848, to keep control of the Atlantic end of any future canal across Nicaragua.

date.note: Robert Hodgson was appointed superintendent in 1749; English alliance with the Miskitu dates from the 1630s and the crowning of Miskitu kings under British auspices from 1687.

acquisitions.how: Britain appointed a superintendent to a coast it had traded with and armed for a century, formalising an alliance in which Miskitu kings were crowned in Jamaica or Belize and Miskitu raiders were supplied with British guns.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Any prospect of controlling the Caribbean coast of Central America, which it claimed and had never occupied; Spanish expeditions against the shore failed in 1782 and the coast remained outside Spanish rule until Spain left America altogether.

counterparties.name: The Mayangna (Sumu), Rama and Pech peoples
counterparties.lost: Their safety. Miskitu raiders armed by British traders captured Mayangna, Rama and other Indigenous people and sold them into slavery in Jamaica, a trade that ran for most of the eighteenth century.

counterparties.name: The Miskitu kingdom
counterparties.lost: Nothing at first — this was an alliance the Miskitu wanted, and it made them the dominant power on the coast — but they lost their sovereignty by degrees, and lost it completely when Britain handed the coast to Nicaragua in 1860.

people.name: Robert Hodgson
people.role: first British superintendent of the Mosquito Shore

people.name: King Jeremy
people.role: Miskitu ruler taken to Jamaica in 1687 and crowned there, beginning the practice of British-sponsored Miskitu kingship

contested.note: Whether the Mosquito Shore was ever legally a British possession is exactly what Spain, and later Nicaragua and the United States, disputed. Britain called it a protectorate over an allied kingdom; its opponents called it an occupation of Spanish territory.

acquisitions.how: Fifty-seven years after evacuating the coast, Britain declared a protectorate over the Mosquito kingdom again and seized San Juan del Norte in 1848, renaming it Greytown, to hold the Atlantic end of any canal across Nicaragua.

counterparties.name: Nicaragua
counterparties.lost: Its claim to its own Caribbean coast, and the port at the mouth of the San Juan river, which Britain took by force in January 1848.

counterparties.name: The Miskitu kingdom
counterparties.lost: Independent decision-making. The Miskitu king was now a British client, and in 1860 Britain traded away his kingdom without asking him.

from.note: The superintendency dates from 1749; the alliance is a century older.

statusPeriods.label: The Mosquito Shore superintendency
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British superintendent advised a Miskitu king whose crown came from Jamaica, while British and Jamaican settlers cut mahogany and grew provisions with enslaved African labour along the shore.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Black River (Río Tinto), under the Governor of Jamaica
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The settlers had an elected council from 1774; the Miskitu had their own kingship and councils, which Britain treated as a foreign court.

statusPeriods.label: The revived protectorate
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain evacuated the Mosquito Shore in 1787 under the Convention of London, moving about 2,650 settlers and enslaved people to Belize; for 57 years it exercised no authority here at all.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British consul-general and a Royal Navy squadron backed a Miskitu king against Nicaragua; Britain's real interest was the San Juan river, the best route for a canal between the Atlantic and the Pacific.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bluefields, under a British consul-general and the Governor of Jamaica
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

departures.how: Britain evacuated the Mosquito Shore under the Convention of London, shipping about 2,650 settlers and the people they had enslaved to Belize, and abandoning the Miskitu allies it had armed for 150 years.

becomes.name: Spanish Central America, in law; the Miskitu kingdom, in fact

led.name: Robert Hodgson the younger
led.role: last superintendent of the Mosquito Shore, who organised the evacuation

led.name: King George II Frederic
led.role: Miskitu king at the time of the evacuation, left without the ally that had crowned him

cost.note: British returns count about 2,650 people removed to Belize, of whom roughly two thirds were enslaved. They had no say in the move. Figures come from the superintendency's evacuation returns.

warrant.author: The British superintendency of the Mosquito Shore, in its evacuation returns
warrant.work: Evacuation returns of the Mosquito Shore, 1787
warrant.supports: British returns count about 2,650 people removed to Belize, of whom roughly two thirds were enslaved. They had no say in the move. Figures come from the superintendency's evacuation returns.
warrant.check: Transport, embarkation and evacuation returns are in the ADM, CO and T series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The returns count people moved. They record no consent because none was asked.

departures.borders: Britain traded the coast for a better legal position in Belize: the same convention that made it leave Mosquitia gave it the right to cut mahogany as far south as the Sibun.

departures.how: Under pressure from the United States, Britain signed the coast over to Nicaragua and left the Miskitu a self-governing reserve inside it; Nicaragua sent troops and abolished the reserve in 1894.

becomes.name: Nicaragua, with a self-governing Mosquito Reserve

led.name: Charles Lennox Wyke
led.role: British minister who negotiated the treaties that handed both the Mosquito Coast and the Bay Islands to Central American states

led.name: Máximo Jerez
led.role: Nicaraguan negotiator of the Treaty of Managua

led.name: Robert Charles Frederick's successors, the Miskitu hereditary chiefs
led.role: rulers of the Mosquito Reserve, who were not parties to the treaty that disposed of their kingdom

cost.note: No one died at the signing. The cost came in 1894, when Nicaraguan troops occupied Bluefields, abolished the reserve and imposed Spanish-language government on a Miskitu- and English-speaking coast.

departures.borders: Britain drew the Miskitu a reserve inside Nicaragua and then had no way to defend it. The Miskitu regained autonomy only in 1987, and the boundary of today's Caribbean autonomous regions still follows the shape of the 1860 reserve.

instrument.name: Treaty of Managua
instrument.note: Signed in the shadow of the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty of 1850, in which Britain and the United States had agreed that neither would colonise Central America or control a canal alone.

slavery.note: The Mosquito Shore's British settlers held enslaved Africans on mahogany and provision grounds, and their Miskitu allies raided inland to capture Mayangna and Rama people to sell in Jamaica.

toll.note: No reliable count exists of the Indigenous people taken and sold from the Central American interior through the Miskitu trade; the historians who have worked on it treat it as thousands over more than a century, not a figure that can be given precisely.

populationTransfer.note: About 2,650 settlers and enslaved people were moved from the shore to Belize in 1787, and the Garifuna deported from St Vincent in 1797 settled along this same coast from Roatán westwards.

commonwealth.note: The coast is part of Nicaragua, which has never been a Commonwealth member.

consequences.borderLegacy: A British protectorate over an Indigenous kingdom became, by treaty, a minority region inside a Spanish-speaking republic; the Miskitu fought the Sandinista government in the 1980s and won the autonomous regions in 1987.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English-based Creole and Miskitu are still spoken along the coast, and Moravian churches — a legacy of German missionaries invited under the British protectorate — remain the dominant denomination.

peak.populationNote: Contemporary estimates of the population of the whole Mosquito protectorate in the mid-nineteenth century range widely; 15,000 is an order of magnitude, not a census figure.

populationWarrant.work: The 1850 census of The Mosquito Coast
populationWarrant.supports: The Mosquito Coast’s largest recorded population: 15,000 people, counted in 1850.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Robert A. Naylor
evidence.work: Penny Ante Imperialism: The Mosquito Shore and the Bay of Honduras, 1600-1914
evidence.supports: The Mosquito Shore superintendency, the 1787 evacuation, the 1844 protectorate and the Treaty of Managua.

evidence.author: Michael D. Olien
evidence.work: The Miskito Kings and the Line of Succession
evidence.supports: The British-sponsored Miskitu kingship and its succession from 1687.

contested.note: Whether Britain's relationship with the Miskitu was a protectorate over a sovereign kingdom or a thin cover for occupying Spanish territory was disputed at the time by Spain, and later by Nicaragua and the United States. Population figures for the coast are estimates, not counts.

pedagogy.hook: For 150 years Britain crowned the kings of an Indigenous nation in Central America, armed them, and then in 1860 signed their country over to Nicaragua without asking them.

misconception.belief: The British Empire is a story of Britain acting on people who had no choices.
misconception.correction: The Miskitu chose the alliance. They used British guns to dominate the coast, took Miskitu kings to Jamaica to be crowned, raided their neighbours and sold captives to British buyers, and were for a century the strongest power on this shore. Then Britain's interest changed, and the alliance was worth nothing. Being an ally of an empire is not the same as being safe from it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Mosquito Coast shows informal empire at work: no colony, no governor, no map colouring — just guns, trade and a client king — and it shows what informal empire is worth to the client when the empire's priorities move on.

date.note: The superintendency dates from 1749.

namesOverTime.name: Guanaja, Roatán and Utila

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact period; Columbus met a large Maya trading canoe off Guanaja in 1502.

namesOverTime.note: Spain deported the islands' Indigenous population to work in the mines of Hispaniola in the 1520s and 1530s.

from.note: English usage settles as Caymanian settlers arrive; English buccaneers had used the islands from the 1640s.

namesOverTime.name: Islas de la Bahía
namesOverTime.note: A department of Honduras since Britain handed the islands over under the Wyke-Cruz Treaty, signed on 28 November 1859 and carried out in 1860.

modernSuccessors.name: Honduras

since.note: The handover under the Wyke-Cruz Treaty took effect during 1860 and was resisted by settlers into 1861.

modernSuccessors.note: The Bay Islands are a department of Honduras where English and Bay Islands Creole are still widely spoken.

from.note: Caymanian settlement built up through the 1830s; the date is approximate.

to.note: The transfer to Honduras took effect during 1860.

geoCoverage.label: Roatán, Utila, Guanaja and their smaller neighbours

date.note: Settlement built up over the 1830s from the Cayman Islands and Belize; there is no founding date.

acquisitions.how: Settlers from the Cayman Islands and Belize moved onto islands the Spanish had emptied three centuries earlier, joining the Garifuna whom Britain had deported from St Vincent and landed on Roatán in 1797.

counterparties.name: The Republic of Central America, later Honduras
counterparties.lost: Islands it claimed as Spain's successor and did not occupy; Honduras protested continuously from the 1830s and got them back in 1860.

counterparties.name: The Garifuna of Roatán
counterparties.lost: Not the islands, which they had been dumped on in 1797 and largely left, but any prospect of being consulted about who governed them; most had already moved to the Central American mainland.

contested.note: Britain's title was contested from the start. Honduras and the United States both argued that Britain had renounced any claim to Central American territory in the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty of 1850, and Britain declared the colony in 1852 anyway.

acquisitions.how: Britain declared the Colony of the Bay Islands, formally annexing islands Honduras claimed and the United States said Britain had already promised not to colonise.

counterparties.name: Honduras
counterparties.lost: Formal possession of the islands for eight years, and turned the dispute into a diplomatic quarrel that reached the United States Senate.

counterparties.name: The United States
counterparties.lost: Its reading of the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty. Washington's objection was the main reason Britain gave the islands back in 1860.

instrument.name: Order in Council constituting the Colony of the Bay Islands

from.note: The date settlement built up; there is no founding event.

statusPeriods.label: English-speaking settlers, no government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nobody governed. Caymanian settlers farmed, fished and cut timber on islands Honduras claimed and Britain had not annexed, occasionally visited by the superintendent of Belize.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Nowhere; occasionally visited from Belize
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

to.note: The colony was ceded to Honduras during 1860 and settler resistance delayed the handover into 1861.

statusPeriods.label: Colony of the Bay Islands
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A superintendent under the Governor of Jamaica governed a colony of about 2,000 English-speaking settlers, which existed for eight years and was abolished under American diplomatic pressure.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Coxen Hole, Roatán, under the Governor of Jamaica
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

date.note: The Wyke-Cruz Treaty was signed on 28 November 1859; ratifications were exchanged and the transfer took effect during 1860, with settler resistance delaying the handover into 1861.

departures.how: Britain gave the islands to Honduras under the Wyke-Cruz Treaty, after the United States insisted that keeping them broke the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty; the settlers petitioned against it and were ignored.

led.name: Charles Lennox Wyke
led.role: British minister who negotiated the cession, as he did for the Mosquito Coast and the Belize boundary

led.name: Carlos Gutiérrez
led.role: Honduran negotiator

cost.note: Nobody died. About 2,000 English-speaking settlers became citizens of a Spanish-speaking republic without being asked, and the treaty promised them religious liberty and property rights in return.

departures.borders: The treaty made Britain's Central American retreat complete: the Bay Islands to Honduras in 1860, the Mosquito Coast to Nicaragua in the same year, and only Belize kept, on a boundary Britain had already agreed with Guatemala in 1859.

slavery.note: Slavery had been abolished throughout the British Empire in 1834, before the colony existed; the settlers who came from the Cayman Islands after 1830 included both former owners and formerly enslaved people.

populationTransfer.note: Roatán received the surviving Garifuna deported from St Vincent in April 1797 — the origin of the Garifuna population of Central America — and then Caymanian settlers from the 1830s.

toll.note: British transport returns record 4,338 Garifuna landed on Roatán in April 1797, but many died or moved to the mainland within months; contemporary Spanish counts of those remaining on the island are far lower. Both figures come from the shipping and colonial returns.

warrant.note: The ships’ returns and the Spanish counts of who was still on Roatán months later do not agree, and the record prints both.

commonwealth.note: The islands are part of Honduras, which has never been a Commonwealth member.

consequences.borderLegacy: The colony lasted eight years and left an English-speaking, Protestant department inside Spanish-speaking Catholic Honduras.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English and Bay Islands Creole are still spoken on Roatán, Utila and Guanaja, and the islands are legally and culturally distinct from mainland Honduras.

peak.populationNote: Contemporary estimates of the colony's population in the 1850s cluster around 2,000; no census was taken.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1856 census of The Bay Islands
populationWarrant.supports: The Bay Islands’s largest recorded population: 2,000 people, counted in 1856.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Robert A. Naylor
evidence.work: Penny Ante Imperialism: The Mosquito Shore and the Bay of Honduras, 1600-1914
evidence.supports: The Bay Islands colony, the Clayton-Bulwer dispute and the Wyke-Cruz Treaty.

evidence.author: William V. Davidson
evidence.work: Historical Geography of the Bay Islands, Honduras
evidence.supports: Caymanian settlement, the Garifuna landing of 1797 and the islands' English-speaking population.

contested.note: Exact dates for the 1860 handover differ between accounts because settler resistance delayed it, and no census fixes the colony's population.

pedagogy.hook: Britain created a colony in Honduras in 1852 and gave it away eight years later, because the United States told it to.

misconception.belief: The British Empire expanded steadily until decolonisation began after 1945.
misconception.correction: Britain gave territory back throughout its imperial history when it was cheaper to do so. It evacuated the Mosquito Coast in 1787, abolished the Bay Islands colony in 1860, and handed the Mosquito Coast to Nicaragua in the same year — all under pressure from Spain and then the United States, and all a century before decolonisation.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Bay Islands are the point where the British Empire ran into the Monroe Doctrine and backed off: after 1860 Britain kept Belize and left the rest of Central America to the Americans.
