territories.name: Havana under British occupation
territories.formalName: British occupation of Havana and western Cuba

modernSuccessors.name: Cuba
modernSuccessors.note: Spain returned in 1763 and held Cuba until 1898; the eleven British months are still treated by Cuban historians as the moment the island's sugar and slave economy began.

geoCoverage.label: Havana and the west of the island
geoCoverage.change: The British occupation reached Havana, Matanzas and the western plains. Santiago and the east were never taken, and Spanish authority continued there throughout.

acquisitions.how: The largest amphibious expedition Britain had ever sent — over 200 ships and about 14,000 troops — besieged Havana for two months, blew a mine under the Morro castle, and forced the surrender of the city and the Spanish Caribbean fleet in it.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Its greatest fortress and naval base in the Americas, twelve ships of the line, and the port through which the treasure fleets sailed; Spain got Havana back only by giving Britain Florida.

counterparties.name: The enslaved and free Black militias of Havana
counterparties.lost: Heavily. Free Black and enslaved men dug the defences and fought in the militia; the Spanish crown afterwards freed some in recognition, and the British occupation trafficked thousands more Africans into the island.

people.name: George Keppel, Earl of Albemarle
people.role: British commander of the expedition and governor of Havana during the occupation

people.name: Luis Vicente de Velasco
people.role: Spanish naval officer who defended the Morro castle and was killed in its final assault; Spain has kept a ship named for him ever since

people.name: José Antonio Aponte
people.role: free Black Havana carpenter whose grandfather served in the Black militia against the British; he led an anti-slavery conspiracy in 1812

cost.note: British combat losses were around 700; disease, mainly yellow fever, killed several thousand more within months. Spanish and enslaved casualties were not counted. Figures come from the expedition's own returns as analysed by Elena Schneider and by Fred Anderson.

warrant.author: Elena A. Schneider
warrant.work: The Occupation of Havana: War, Trade, and Slavery in the Atlantic World
warrant.supports: British combat losses were around 700; disease, mainly yellow fever, killed several thousand more within months.

warrant.author: Fred Anderson
warrant.work: Crucible of War: The Seven Years' War and the Fate of Empire in British North America, 1754-1766
warrant.supports: British combat losses were around 700; disease, mainly yellow fever, killed several thousand more within months.
warrant.check: Alfred A. Knopf, 2000. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

acquisitions.resistance: Havana held out for two months and was defended by regular troops, militia and enslaved and free Black volunteers; the countryside outside the city was never brought under British control.

evidence.author: Elena A. Schneider
evidence.work: The Occupation of Havana: War, Trade, and Slavery in the Atlantic World
evidence.supports: The siege, the Black militias, and the slave trade the occupation opened.

statusPeriods.label: Eleven months of British Havana
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military governor ran Havana under Spanish law with the existing town council, opened the port to British and North American shipping, and licensed a flood of slave ships.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Havana, under a British military governor
statusPeriods.franchise: None; the Spanish cabildo continued to sit under British authority.

departures.how: Britain handed Havana back to Spain at the Treaty of Paris in exchange for Florida — trading the richest port in the Spanish Caribbean for a swamp, because the sugar lobby in London did not want another sugar island competing with Jamaica.

led.name: John Stuart, Earl of Bute
led.role: British prime minister who chose Florida over Havana at the peace and was burned in effigy for the terms he accepted

led.name: Charles III of Spain
led.role: Spanish king who ceded Florida to recover Havana

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. The lasting cost fell on Africa and on Cuba: the occupation's eleven months of open trade began the sugar-and-slavery expansion that made Cuba the largest slave society in the Spanish empire.

departures.borders: The swap redrew North America: Spain gave up Florida to get Havana back, and France had already given Spain Louisiana, so the Mississippi became the line between the British and Spanish empires.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris
instrument.note: Signed in February; Havana was formally handed back on 6 July 1763.

slavery.note: In eleven months British traders landed several thousand enslaved Africans in Havana — comparable to the whole preceding decade of Spanish imports — and showed Cuban planters what an open slave trade could do for sugar.

toll.note: Estimates of the number landed during the occupation vary widely between contemporary British merchant records and Spanish port records; Elena Schneider gives a range rather than a figure, and says the point is the change in scale, not the exact count.

warrant.author: Elena A. Schneider
warrant.work: The Occupation of Havana: War, Trade, and Slavery in the Atlantic World
warrant.supports: Estimates of the number landed during the occupation vary widely between contemporary British merchant records and Spanish port records; Elena Schneider gives a range rather than a figure, and says the point is the change in scale, not the exact count.
warrant.check: University of North Carolina Press, 2018. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

consequences.economicLegacy: Cuban historians treat 1762 as the hinge of their island's modern history: the year Havana was opened to free trade and mass slave imports, which turned Cuba into the world's largest sugar producer within two generations.
consequences.borderLegacy: Britain traded Havana for Florida, so an eleven-month occupation of Cuba is the reason Florida was British between 1763 and 1783.

peak.populationNote: Havana and its immediate region held roughly 35,000 to 45,000 people in 1762; the occupation never reached most of the island's 150,000 or so inhabitants.

evidence.author: Elena A. Schneider
evidence.work: The Occupation of Havana: War, Trade, and Slavery in the Atlantic World
evidence.supports: The siege, the occupation government, the slave trade and the Black militias of Havana.

evidence.author: Fred Anderson
evidence.work: Crucible of War: The Seven Years' War and the Fate of Empire in British North America, 1754-1766
evidence.supports: The expedition, its losses to disease, and the bargaining at the Treaty of Paris.

contested.note: The number of enslaved Africans landed during the occupation is genuinely uncertain: British merchants had reasons to overstate and Spanish officials to understate, and the surviving records do not agree.

pedagogy.hook: Britain captured Havana in 1762 and gave it back eleven months later in exchange for Florida — because London's sugar planters did not want a rival sugar island inside the empire.

misconception.belief: Empires always wanted more territory, and gave land back only when forced to.
misconception.correction: At the peace of 1763 Britain had captured Havana, Manila, Guadeloupe and Martinique, and handed back every one of them. The West India lobby in Parliament actively campaigned against keeping the sugar islands, because more sugar inside the empire meant lower prices for their own crops. Britain chose Canada and Florida instead, and Voltaire mocked it for preferring 'a few acres of snow'.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is where you see the empire's decisions being made by interest groups rather than by a map: the sugar lobby got its way, Cuba stayed Spanish and became the largest slave society in the Americas, and Florida became British for twenty years.

keyDates.what: The British fleet arrives off Havana
A mine breaches the Morro castle; Velasco is killed
Havana surrenders with the Spanish Caribbean fleet
Britain hands Havana back in exchange for Florida

modernSuccessors.name: Haiti
modernSuccessors.note: The first state in the world founded by formerly enslaved people, and the second independent republic in the Americas. Britain's expulsion in 1798 was one of its early victories.

geoCoverage.label: Ports and coastal districts only
geoCoverage.change: Britain held Jérémie, Môle-Saint-Nicolas, Saint-Marc, Léogâne and, from June 1794, Port-au-Prince. It never held the interior, the north, or the majority of the colony's people.

acquisitions.how: A small British force from Jamaica landed at Jérémie at the invitation of French royalist planters, five weeks after the French Republic's commissioner had freed the colony's enslaved people, with the declared aim of taking the richest colony in the world and restoring slavery in it.

counterparties.name: The French Republic
counterparties.lost: Control of its most valuable colony, which produced roughly two fifths of the world's sugar and half its coffee, for five years.

counterparties.name: The formerly enslaved people of Saint-Domingue
counterparties.lost: Their freedom wherever British troops arrived. Britain's explicit war aim was to restore the slave regime the Republic had abolished in August 1793, and it re-established slavery in the districts it held.

counterparties.name: The royalist planters of Saint-Domingue
counterparties.lost: Everything, in the end. They invited the British in to save slavery and signed away their colony's sovereignty by the Whitehall accords; five years later Britain left and they lost their estates for good.

instrument.name: The Whitehall Accords
instrument.note: An agreement between French royalist planter representatives and the British government, promising British protection and the preservation of slavery in exchange for the colony.

people.name: Toussaint Louverture
people.role: formerly enslaved coachman turned general, who joined the French Republic in 1794 and drove the British out of Saint-Domingue

people.name: Thomas Maitland
people.role: British commander who negotiated the evacuation directly with Toussaint in 1798

people.name: Léger-Félicité Sonthonax
people.role: French commissioner who proclaimed emancipation in the north on 29 August 1793, before Paris did

people.name: Jean-Jacques Dessalines
people.role: general under Toussaint who declared Haitian independence on 1 January 1804

cost.note: David Geggus's count from the regimental returns gives over 12,700 British soldiers dead in Saint-Domingue between 1793 and 1798, the great majority of yellow fever rather than combat. Deaths among the colony's own population were far higher and were never counted.

warrant.author: David Patrick Geggus
warrant.work: Slavery, War and Revolution: The British Occupation of Saint Domingue, 1793-1798
warrant.supports: The invasion, its aims, its casualties and the negotiated evacuation.
warrant.check: Clarendon Press

acquisitions.resistance: The armies of formerly enslaved people that had risen in 1791 fought the British throughout; Toussaint Louverture's forces took the interior in 1794-97 and reduced the British to a few coastal towns.

evidence.author: David Patrick Geggus
evidence.work: Slavery, War and Revolution: The British Occupation of Saint Domingue, 1793-1798
evidence.supports: The invasion, its aims, its casualties and the negotiated evacuation.

statusPeriods.label: British-held ports in a revolution
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British commanders governed the towns they held under French colonial law, restored slavery where they could, and depended on royalist planter militias and on troops who were dying of yellow fever faster than they could be replaced.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Degree 3 rather than the default 5: Britain governed a handful of coastal towns and never the interior, the north, or most of the population. Calling this an occupation of Saint-Domingue overstates what Britain ever held.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port-au-Prince and Môle-Saint-Nicolas, under the Governor of Jamaica
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

departures.how: Britain was beaten. Toussaint Louverture's army of formerly enslaved people took town after town, and General Maitland negotiated a withdrawal directly with Toussaint — a British general treating with a man who had been a slave nine years earlier.

becomes.name: Saint-Domingue under Toussaint Louverture, nominally French

led.name: Toussaint Louverture
led.role: commander of the army that defeated the British; negotiated the evacuation and a secret trade convention with Maitland

led.name: Thomas Maitland
led.role: British commander who signed the evacuation and the convention

led.name: André Rigaud
led.role: free-coloured general in the south who fought the British throughout the occupation

departures.movement: The armies of the Haitian Revolution

cost.note: British military deaths over five years, mostly from yellow fever, on Geggus's count from the regimental returns. It was the costliest single campaign of the French revolutionary wars for the British army.

warrant.author: David Patrick Geggus
warrant.work: Slavery, War and Revolution: The British Occupation of Saint Domingue, 1793-1798
warrant.supports: British military deaths over five years, mostly from yellow fever, on Geggus's count from the regimental returns.
warrant.check: Clarendon Press, 1982. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

departures.borders: Britain left the island entirely. Six years later Saint-Domingue became Haiti, and Britain — which had invaded to save slavery there — became one of the first states to trade with the new republic while refusing to recognise it.

instrument.name: Convention between Maitland and Toussaint Louverture
instrument.note: The public convention arranged the evacuation; a secret annexe opened trade between Jamaica and Toussaint's Saint-Domingue and promised Britain would not attack again.

slavery.note: Britain invaded Saint-Domingue in order to restore slavery there, and re-established it in the districts it held. This is the clearest evidence that Britain's abolition of the slave trade in 1807 was a change of policy, not a settled national character.

toll.note: The occupation cost the British army over 12,000 dead and shipped an unknown number of people back into slavery in the districts it held; neither Britain nor France counted the colony's own dead.

violence.note: Five years of war between British troops, royalist planters, free-coloured forces and armies of formerly enslaved people, in which disease killed far more than combat on every side.

commonwealth.note: Haiti has never been a Commonwealth member; it is a member of CARICOM.

consequences.economicLegacy: The war destroyed the world's most productive colony. Saint-Domingue had supplied about two fifths of the world's sugar; Haiti never regained that position, and in 1825 France extracted an indemnity of 150 million francs as the price of recognition.
consequences.borderLegacy: British failure here made British Caribbean planters permanently afraid: the Haitian Revolution is the shadow behind every slave code, militia law and rebellion trial in the British islands after 1804.

peak.populationNote: A rough estimate of the population of the districts Britain held at its greatest extent in 1796; the colony as a whole had held about 500,000 enslaved people in 1789.

evidence.author: David Patrick Geggus
evidence.work: Slavery, War and Revolution: The British Occupation of Saint Domingue, 1793-1798
evidence.supports: The whole occupation: aims, campaigns, casualties and the 1798 evacuation.

evidence.author: Laurent Dubois
evidence.work: Avengers of the New World: The Story of the Haitian Revolution
evidence.supports: The revolution, emancipation in 1793-94, and Toussaint's campaigns against the British.

pedagogy.hook: Britain sent an army to Haiti in 1793 to put slavery back. Over 12,000 British soldiers died there, and the man who beat them had himself been enslaved nine years earlier.

misconception.belief: Britain led the world in ending slavery.
misconception.correction: In 1793, fourteen years before it abolished the slave trade, Britain invaded Saint-Domingue explicitly to overturn the French Republic's emancipation decree and restore the plantation system. It failed, at a cost of more than 12,000 British lives. Abolition in 1807 came after this defeat, not before it — and the fear of another Haiti is one reason it came at all.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Haitian Revolution is the event that frightened every slave-owning power in the Atlantic. It defeated Spain, Britain and then Napoleonic France, and every British Caribbean rebellion after 1804 was read by planters, and by London, in its light.

keyDates.what: The rising in the north begins the Haitian Revolution
Sonthonax proclaims emancipation in the north
British troops land at Jérémie to restore slavery
The last British troops leave; Maitland has treated with Toussaint
Haiti declares independence

modernSuccessors.name: France (Martinique)
modernSuccessors.note: Martinique has been an overseas department of France since 1946 and is part of the European Union.

geoCoverage.label: Second British occupation
geoCoverage.change: Britain took the island in 1794 at the invitation of royalist planters who preferred British rule to the French Republic's abolition of slavery, and held it for eight years.

geoCoverage.label: Third British occupation
geoCoverage.change: Britain took Martinique again in 1809 as part of the blockade of Napoleon's empire, and returned it at the general peace in 1814.

acquisitions.how: General Monckton's expedition took Fort Royal and the island surrendered within weeks; Britain gave it back a year later at the Treaty of Paris, keeping Canada instead.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Its administrative capital in the Caribbean and, for a year, the richest French sugar island after Saint-Domingue.

acquisitions.how: Grey and Jervis took the island after a two-month campaign, invited by royalist planters who wanted British rule rather than the French Republic's emancipation decree; slavery was maintained throughout the eight-year occupation.

counterparties.name: The French Republic
counterparties.lost: The island for eight years, and with it the chance to apply its emancipation decree of February 1794 here at all.

counterparties.name: The enslaved people of Martinique
counterparties.lost: The emancipation that reached Guadeloupe and Saint-Domingue in 1794 never reached Martinique, because Britain held it. Martinique's enslaved population was freed only in 1848, by France.

acquisitions.how: A British expedition of 10,000 men took Martinique in three weeks to close the last French naval base in the eastern Caribbean; Britain held it for five years and handed it back at the peace.

counterparties.name: Napoleonic France
counterparties.lost: Its last secure Caribbean base, and the privateers operating from it.

statusPeriods.label: First occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military governor left French law, the French planters and the plantation system untouched, and opened the ports to British trade for a year.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Royal, under a British military governor

statusPeriods.label: Second occupation: slavery preserved
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned Martinique to France at the Treaty of Paris in 1763 and did not hold it again for 31 years.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain governed with the royalist planters who had invited it, kept French colonial law including the Code Noir, and guaranteed that the Republic's abolition of slavery would not apply here.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Royal, renamed Fort Edward under the occupation
statusPeriods.franchise: None; the planters' colonial assembly sat by British permission.

statusPeriods.label: Third occupation
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned Martinique to France at the Peace of Amiens in 1802, and Napoleon used it as a naval base until Britain retook it in 1809.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military government again ran the island under French law, and again left slavery in place, until the general peace returned it to France.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Royal, under a British military governor

departures.how: Britain returned Martinique and Guadeloupe to France at the Treaty of Paris and kept Canada, in the most argued-over trade of the eighteenth century.

led.name: John Stuart, Earl of Bute
led.role: British prime minister who preferred Canada to the sugar islands

led.name: Étienne-François, duc de Choiseul
led.role: French foreign minister who recovered the sugar islands at the peace

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. Around 70,000 enslaved people on Martinique changed sovereign without being consulted, twice in two years.

departures.borders: The 1763 trade set the shape of the modern Americas: France kept its sugar islands and gave up Canada, and Britain took a continent instead of two islands.

departures.how: Britain handed Martinique back at the Peace of Amiens, and the island passed to a French government that was in the same months restoring slavery across the French Caribbean.

led.name: Robert Jenkinson, Lord Hawkesbury
led.role: British foreign secretary at Amiens

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover; because Britain had held the island since 1794, the enslaved people of Martinique had never been freed at all.

departures.borders: No line moved; the island simply reverted, and Britain took it again seven years later.

departures.how: Britain returned Martinique to the restored French monarchy at the Treaty of Paris, keeping St Lucia and Tobago instead, and never held it again.

led.name: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh
led.role: British foreign secretary who set the colonial terms of the 1814 settlement

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. Martinique's enslaved population, kept enslaved through eight years of British rule, waited another 34 years for the French emancipation of 1848.

departures.borders: The 1814 settlement fixed the Caribbean map that still exists: Britain kept St Lucia, Tobago, Trinidad and the Guianas; France kept Martinique, Guadeloupe and French Guiana.

slavery.note: Britain held Martinique for eight years specifically so that the French Republic's abolition of slavery would not apply there, and enslaved Martinicans were freed only by France in 1848.

commonwealth.note: Martinique is part of France and of the European Union.

consequences.economicLegacy: British occupation opened the island's sugar to British and North American markets and left French planters with a habit of trading outside the French empire.
consequences.borderLegacy: Everything Britain took in the Caribbean between 1793 and 1810 it gave back except St Lucia, Tobago, Trinidad and the Guianas — a reminder that conquest and possession are different things.

peak.populationNote: Roughly 96,000 people at the turn of the nineteenth century, of whom about 80,000 were enslaved.

evidence.supports: Why emancipation reached Guadeloupe and not Martinique, and what British occupation meant for enslaved people.

contested.note: Exact handover dates in 1802 differ between accounts because the Peace of Amiens was implemented island by island over several months.

pedagogy.hook: Enslaved people on Guadeloupe were freed in 1794 and enslaved people on Martinique, 40 kilometres away, were not — because Britain occupied Martinique to make sure the French abolition decree never landed there.

misconception.belief: Whether you were free depended on when history moved forward.
misconception.correction: It depended on which flag flew over your island in a particular month. Guadeloupe's enslaved population was freed by the French Republic in 1794 and re-enslaved by Napoleon in 1802. Martinique's was never freed at all, because Britain held it from 1794 to 1802 for exactly that purpose, and had to wait for the French abolition of 1848.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Martinique is the control case that proves the point about St Lucia and Guadeloupe: the difference between freedom and slavery in the 1790s Caribbean was often a naval campaign, not a moral awakening.

Britain occupies to prevent emancipation reaching the island
Third British occupation begins

modernSuccessors.name: France (Guadeloupe)

since.note: The final British handover after the Hundred Days took place during 1816.

modernSuccessors.note: An overseas department of France since 1946 and part of the European Union.

geoCoverage.label: Eight months, then expelled
geoCoverage.change: Britain took Guadeloupe in April 1794 and lost it in December to Victor Hugues, who landed with the Republic's emancipation decree, freed the enslaved population and armed them against the British.

to.note: Guadeloupe was restored to France under the 1814 settlement; the handover took place during that year.

geoCoverage.label: Third British occupation
geoCoverage.change: Britain took Guadeloupe again in 1810 and, in 1813, promised it to Sweden as the price of Swedish support against Napoleon — a promise unwound in 1814 when the island went back to France.

to.note: The final handover to France took place during 1816; accounts differ on the month.

geoCoverage.label: Fourth and last British occupation
geoCoverage.change: Guadeloupe declared for Napoleon during the Hundred Days, so British and Swedish forces retook it in August 1815 and handed it to the restored French monarchy the following year.

acquisitions.how: After bombarding Basse-Terre into ruins, a British expedition took the island in a four-month campaign, and the planters signed a capitulation that guaranteed their property, their religion and their enslaved workforce.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Its second sugar island for four years — and got it back in a peace treaty that many in Britain thought was a mistake.

acquisitions.how: Grey and Jervis took Guadeloupe in April 1794 as part of the campaign to seize France's sugar colonies and stop the Republic's abolition decree spreading; they held it for less than eight months.

counterparties.name: The French Republic
counterparties.lost: The island briefly, and then took it back in the only French reconquest of a British-held colony in the Caribbean during the entire war.

acquisitions.how: A British force from Martinique took the last French colony in the Caribbean, completing the blockade of Napoleon's overseas empire.

counterparties.name: Napoleonic France
counterparties.lost: Its last colonial possession in the Americas.

counterparties.name: Sweden
counterparties.lost: Sweden did not lose Guadeloupe — it gained it, briefly and on paper. Britain promised the island to Sweden in 1813 to bring Bernadotte into the coalition, and bought it back in 1814 with an annuity known as the Guadeloupe Fund.

instrument.name: Treaty of Stockholm (1813)
instrument.note: Britain ceded Guadeloupe to Sweden in exchange for Swedish troops against Napoleon. Sweden never took possession, and returned the claim in 1814 in exchange for an annuity that the French crown eventually paid off.

acquisitions.how: Guadeloupe's governor declared for Napoleon during the Hundred Days, so a British and Swedish force retook the island in August 1815 and held it until it could be handed to Louis XVIII's government.

counterparties.name: Bonapartist France
counterparties.lost: Its last overseas foothold, three months after Waterloo.

statusPeriods.label: First occupation: the sugar boom
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military governor guaranteed the planters everything and opened the island to British slave ships and British credit; in four years the planters imported tens of thousands of enslaved Africans and sugar output rose sharply.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basse-Terre, under a British military governor
statusPeriods.franchise: None; the French colonial council continued under British authority.

statusPeriods.label: Eight months, ended by an army of freed people
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned Guadeloupe to France at the Treaty of Paris in 1763 and did not hold it again for 31 years.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British commanders held the forts with a garrison being destroyed by yellow fever, while Victor Hugues landed with the emancipation decree, freed and armed the enslaved population, and drove the British into the sea.

statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basse-Terre, then nowhere

statusPeriods.gapReason: From December 1794 to February 1810 Guadeloupe was French: first a republic that had abolished slavery, then, after 1802, a colony where Napoleon restored it by force.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military governor ran the island under French law with slavery restored, while in Europe Britain promised the island to Sweden and then bought the promise back.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basse-Terre, under a British military governor

to.note: The final handover to France took place during 1816.

statusPeriods.label: Fourth occupation, after the Hundred Days
statusPeriods.gapReason: Guadeloupe was restored to France in 1814 and declared for Napoleon during the Hundred Days in 1815, which is why Britain took it a fourth time.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A short military occupation under British and Swedish command, ended by handing the island to the restored Bourbon government.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Basse-Terre, under a British military governor

departures.how: Britain gave Guadeloupe back to France at the Treaty of Paris and kept Canada instead — a choice ridiculed at the time by people who thought a sugar island worth more than a frozen continent.

led.name: John Stuart, Earl of Bute

departures.how: Britain did not hand Guadeloupe over: it was driven off the island by an army Victor Hugues raised from the people he had just freed, in the only French reconquest of a British-held Caribbean colony in the whole war.

led.role: British foreign secretary who arranged both the cession to Sweden and its reversal

led.name: Charles XIV John of Sweden
led.role: formerly Marshal Bernadotte; accepted Guadeloupe in 1813 and gave it up in 1814 for an annuity

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. Slavery, restored by Napoleon in 1802 and maintained by Britain after 1810, continued until France abolished it in 1848.

departures.borders: The 1814 settlement returned Guadeloupe and Martinique to France and kept St Lucia, Tobago and Trinidad British, drawing the eastern Caribbean map that still exists.

date.note: The final handover took place during 1816; accounts differ on the month.

departures.how: Britain handed Guadeloupe to Louis XVIII's government for the last time, ending 57 years in which the island had changed hands six times.

led.name: James Leith
led.role: British commander in the Leeward Islands who took Guadeloupe in 1815 and oversaw the handover

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. Guadeloupe's people had been enslaved, freed in 1794, re-enslaved in 1802, and remained enslaved until 1848.

departures.borders: No line moved. Guadeloupe has been French ever since, and is today part of the European Union.

slavery.note: British occupation in 1759-63 trebled the island's slave imports and built its sugar economy; British occupation in 1810-14 kept slavery in place after Napoleon had restored it. Both times Britain was the guarantor of the plantation, not its enemy.

commonwealth.note: Guadeloupe is part of France and of the European Union.

consequences.economicLegacy: The four years of British rule after 1759 turned Guadeloupe into a first-rank sugar island, financed by British credit and supplied by British slave ships.
consequences.borderLegacy: In 1813 Britain gave Guadeloupe to Sweden by treaty. It is the only time a Caribbean island was used as payment for a European alliance, and the annuity Sweden received in exchange was still being argued about decades later.

peak.populationNote: Roughly 100,000 people at the end of the eighteenth century, about 85,000 of them enslaved.

pedagogy.hook: In 1813 Britain gave Guadeloupe to Sweden to buy a Swedish army, then bought it back a year later with an annuity and handed the island to France.

misconception.belief: Britain's Caribbean colonies were the empire's minor possessions.
misconception.correction: In 1762 the British Parliament seriously debated whether to keep Guadeloupe — 1,600 square kilometres — or Canada. Guadeloupe produced more taxable revenue than all of New France. Britain chose Canada partly because its own sugar planters lobbied against admitting a rival. Sugar islands were the most valuable real estate in the eighteenth-century world.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Guadeloupe is where the reader can see what empire was actually worth in money, and where an army of formerly enslaved people beat a British force in open war — the only French reconquest of a British-held Caribbean colony in the entire revolutionary war.

territories.name: Suriname (Willoughbyland and the occupations)
territories.formalName: Willoughbyland, later the British occupations of Dutch Surinam

namesOverTime.name: Willoughbyland
namesOverTime.note: Named for Francis, Lord Willoughby, governor of Barbados, who founded and paid for the colony.

namesOverTime.name: Suriname
namesOverTime.note: Independent from the Netherlands on 25 November 1975; the older English spelling Surinam went out of official use with it.

modernSuccessors.name: Suriname
modernSuccessors.note: Independent from the Netherlands in 1975. Sranan Tongo, its national creole, still carries seventeenth-century English words from the Willoughbyland years.

geoCoverage.label: Willoughbyland: the English colony
geoCoverage.change: The English colony was a strip along the Suriname and Commewijne rivers; the interior belonged to Indigenous nations and, increasingly, to people escaping the plantations.

to.note: Surinam was returned to the Batavian Republic during 1802 under the Peace of Amiens; the handover date is given variously.

geoCoverage.label: First British occupation
geoCoverage.change: Britain took the Dutch colony in August 1799, 132 years after losing its own colony on the same rivers to the Dutch at the Treaty of Breda.

geoCoverage.label: Second British occupation
geoCoverage.change: Britain retook the colony in 1804 and held it for twelve years, handing it back to the Netherlands under the 1814 treaty.

date.note: Willoughby's expedition sailed from Barbados during 1650; no founding day is recorded.

acquisitions.how: Francis, Lord Willoughby, governor of Barbados, sent settlers to the Suriname river to found a colony for planters squeezed out of an island already full of sugar estates, and within fifteen years it held about 4,000 people.

counterparties.name: The Kalina, Lokono and Trio peoples of the Suriname rivers
counterparties.lost: Riverbank land, and their independence from European demands for labour; a war with the colonists between 1678 and 1686 ended in a peace the Dutch had to concede.

counterparties.name: The Dutch and the Zeeland traders
counterparties.lost: Nothing yet — they took the colony seventeen years later, and kept it for three centuries.

instrument.name: Letters patent to Francis, Lord Willoughby, for the colony of Surinam
instrument.note: The grant was made twelve years after Willoughby had founded the colony at his own expense — and five years before it was lost to the Dutch.

people.name: Francis Willoughby, 5th Baron Willoughby of Parham
people.role: governor of Barbados who founded and financed the colony

acquisitions.how: A British squadron took Surinam from the Batavian Republic without a fight; the Dutch planters preferred a British garrison to a French one and surrendered on terms that guaranteed their property.

counterparties.name: The Batavian Republic
counterparties.lost: Its richest colony after Java, together with about 50,000 enslaved people and the largest sugar and coffee plantations on the South American coast.

acquisitions.how: Britain retook Surinam in 1804 after handing it back at Amiens, and governed it for twelve years — long enough for the 1807 abolition of the slave trade to apply here, which is why Dutch Surinam's slave imports stopped when they did.

counterparties.name: The Batavian Republic
counterparties.lost: The colony for a second time; it was returned in 1816 under the Anglo-Dutch settlement.

statusPeriods.label: Willoughbyland
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Lord Willoughby owned and governed the colony from Barbados, appointing the governor and taking rent; a planters' assembly met from 1662, and English, Irish, Jewish and Dutch settlers grew sugar with enslaved African labour.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Torarica, on the Suriname river, under the proprietor in Barbados
statusPeriods.franchise: Male planters. The colony's Portuguese Jewish community, granted unusual religious and civil liberties in 1665, kept them under Dutch rule and still holds the oldest synagogue in the Americas at Jodensavanne.

to.note: Returned to the Batavian Republic during 1802.

statusPeriods.label: First British occupation
statusPeriods.gapReason: The Dutch took Surinam in 1667 and held it, apart from these two occupations, until 1975; Britain had no authority here for 132 years.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military governor ran the colony under Dutch law with the Dutch planter council in place, and opened its trade to British merchants.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Paramaribo, under a British military governor

statusPeriods.label: Second British occupation
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned Surinam to the Batavian Republic during 1802 under the Peace of Amiens and retook it in May 1804.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Twelve years of British military government under Dutch law; the British slave trade ban of 1807 applied, so the colony's imports of enslaved Africans effectively stopped six years before it went back to the Netherlands.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Paramaribo, under a British military governor

departures.how: A Zeeland fleet took the colony in February 1667, and at the Treaty of Breda England kept New Netherland — New Amsterdam, now New York — and let the Dutch keep Surinam, which at the time looked like the better half of the bargain for the Dutch.

led.name: Abraham Crijnssen
led.role: Zeeland admiral who captured the colony in February 1667

led.name: William Byam
led.role: English governor who surrendered Fort Willoughby

led.name: Aphra Behn
led.role: English writer who had lived in the colony and set her 1688 novel Oroonoko there — one of the first English works to make an enslaved African its hero

cost.note: Most English planters left for Jamaica and Barbados, taking enslaved people with them. Those who stayed became Dutch subjects. No reliable casualty figures survive for the 1667 fighting.

departures.borders: This is the swap that made New York English: at Breda each side kept what it held, so the Dutch kept Surinam and England kept New Amsterdam.

instrument.name: Treaty of Breda
instrument.note: The principle was uti possidetis — each side keeps what it holds. It settled New York and Surinam in a single clause.

date.note: The handover to the Batavian Republic took place during 1802; accounts give different months.

departures.how: Britain handed Surinam back to the Batavian Republic at the Peace of Amiens, and retook it two years later when the war resumed.

becomes.name: Dutch Surinam under the Batavian Republic

led.name: Robert Jenkinson, Lord Hawkesbury
led.role: British foreign secretary at Amiens

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover; about 50,000 enslaved people were transferred with the colony as property.

departures.borders: No line moved. The colony's frontier with British Guiana — the Corantijn river — was not fixed, and the New River Triangle is still disputed between Guyana and Suriname today.

departures.how: Britain handed Surinam back to the Kingdom of the Netherlands under the 1814 treaty, keeping Demerara, Essequibo and Berbice next door and paying £6 million for them.

led.name: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh
led.role: British foreign secretary who negotiated which Dutch colonies Britain would keep and which it would return

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. Slavery continued in Suriname until 1863 — 25 years after it ended in the neighbouring British colonies, which is why people escaped across the Corantijn in the opposite direction from usual.

departures.borders: Britain kept the three colonies west of the Corantijn and gave back the one to the east. The line it chose is the modern Guyana-Suriname border, and its southern section is still disputed.

slavery.note: Suriname's plantations were among the deadliest in the Americas, and more people escaped them successfully than anywhere else: the Saramaka, Ndyuka and other Maroon nations of the interior forced the Dutch to sign peace treaties with them in the 1760s.

abolitionDate.note: The British Slave Trade Act applied here because Britain was in occupation, which cut off the colony's imports of enslaved Africans years before Dutch law would have.

emancipationDate.note: The Netherlands abolished slavery in Suriname 25 years after Britain did in its own colonies, and imposed ten years of compulsory state supervision afterwards.

populationTransfer.note: Enslaved Africans under English and then Dutch rule, and after 1873 about 34,000 indentured Indians and 33,000 Javanese — the Dutch copying the system Britain had invented next door in Guiana.

commonwealth.note: Suriname is a member of CARICOM but not of the Commonwealth.

consequences.languageAndLaw: Sranan Tongo, Suriname's national language, is an English-based creole — the direct linguistic descendant of seventeenth-century Willoughbyland, still spoken by a country that has been Dutch-speaking for 300 years.
consequences.borderLegacy: Britain's choice in 1814 of which Guiana colonies to keep drew the Guyana-Suriname border, and the New River Triangle in the south is still claimed by both states.

peak.populationNote: Roughly 50,000 to 60,000 people during the second British occupation, the great majority enslaved; the Maroon nations of the interior were counted by nobody.

evidence.author: Matthew Parker
evidence.work: Willoughbyland: England's Lost Colony
evidence.supports: The English colony of 1650-67, its planters, and the exchange for New York at Breda.

evidence.author: Richard Price
evidence.work: First-Time: The Historical Vision of an African American People
evidence.supports: The Saramaka Maroons, their escape from the plantations and their own account of that history.

contested.note: Handover dates for the 1802 restitution differ between accounts, and population figures for the occupations are estimates from planter returns that never counted the Maroon nations of the interior.

pedagogy.hook: In 1667 England swapped Suriname for New Amsterdam. The Dutch thought they had the better end of the deal — a sugar colony for a fur-trading town that became New York.

misconception.belief: Colonies were valued for their size and their future potential.
misconception.correction: They were valued for what they produced that year. In 1667 a sugar colony on the Suriname river earned far more than a small port on the Hudson, and the Treaty of Breda simply let each side keep what it held. Nobody involved imagined New Amsterdam becoming New York. Judging imperial decisions by what we know now hides how those decisions were actually made.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Suriname is the empire's road not taken, and its creole language still carries the seventeenth-century English of the colony England gave up — the clearest evidence anywhere of how deep a seventeen-year colony can cut.

keyDates.what: Barbadian planters found Willoughbyland on the Suriname river
The Treaty of Breda: the Dutch keep Surinam, England keeps New York

territories.name: Curaçao and Aruba under British occupation
territories.formalName: British occupations of Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire

modernSuccessors.name: Curaçao
modernSuccessors.note: A constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands since the dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles in 2010.

modernSuccessors.name: Aruba
modernSuccessors.note: A constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands since 1986.

geoCoverage.label: Second British occupation
geoCoverage.change: Four British frigates sailed into Sint Anna Bay at dawn on New Year's Day 1807 and took Fort Amsterdam before the garrison was awake; Britain held the islands for nine years.

acquisitions.how: Dutch officials on Curaçao, fearing a French takeover and a rising by the island's enslaved majority, invited a British squadron in; Britain occupied the island and its dependencies Aruba and Bonaire for two and a half years.

counterparties.name: The Batavian Republic
counterparties.lost: The great Caribbean entrepôt of the Dutch empire, whose harbour at Willemstad had transshipped enslaved Africans to Spanish America for a century and a half.

counterparties.name: The enslaved population of Curaçao
counterparties.lost: Their moment. A major rising led by Tula in August 1795 had been crushed with great violence; the change of flag brought them nothing.

acquisitions.how: Captain Charles Brisbane sailed four frigates straight into the narrow harbour of Willemstad at dawn on New Year's Day, ran them alongside the fort, and demanded surrender within five minutes; the island was taken with fewer than ten casualties.

counterparties.name: The Batavian Republic
counterparties.lost: Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire for nine years, and with them the last Dutch naval position in the Caribbean.

people.name: Charles Brisbane
people.role: British captain who took Curaçao in a dawn raid and was knighted for it

statusPeriods.label: First British occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British garrison held Fort Amsterdam and left the Dutch council, Dutch law and the merchant houses of Willemstad in place; the harbour went on doing what it had always done.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Willemstad, under a British military governor

statusPeriods.label: Second British occupation
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned the islands to the Batavian Republic under the Peace of Amiens in 1803 and retook them by surprise attack in January 1807.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nine years of British military government under Dutch law. The British slave trade ban of 1807 applied, closing down the transshipment trade that had been Curaçao's business for 150 years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Willemstad, under a British military governor

departures.how: Britain handed the islands back to the Batavian Republic under the Peace of Amiens, and took them again by surprise four years later.

led.name: Robert Jenkinson, Lord Hawkesbury
led.role: British foreign secretary at Amiens

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover; the enslaved population of the three islands changed sovereign without being consulted for the second time in three years.

departures.borders: No line moved. The Leeward Antilles stayed a Dutch enclave 60 kilometres off the Venezuelan coast, as they still are.

departures.how: Britain returned Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire to the Kingdom of the Netherlands under the 1814 treaty, keeping the Guiana colonies and the Cape instead.

led.name: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh
led.role: British foreign secretary who chose which Dutch colonies to keep

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. Slavery on the islands lasted until the Dutch abolition of 1863.

departures.borders: Britain kept the Dutch colonies that grew sugar and gave back the ones that traded it. Curaçao's value had been its harbour, and by 1816 the trade that harbour served — selling enslaved Africans to Spanish America — had been made illegal by Britain itself.

slavery.note: Curaçao was the Dutch empire's slave market: for about 150 years captives were landed at Willemstad and sold on to Spanish America, and the island's own enslaved population rose against it under Tula in 1795.

abolitionDate.note: The British Slave Trade Act applied during the occupation, which is why Curaçao's transshipment trade ended when it did rather than in 1863.

emancipationDate.note: The Netherlands abolished slavery in its Caribbean colonies in 1863, 25 years after Britain.

commonwealth.note: Curaçao and Aruba are constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

consequences.economicLegacy: Willemstad's deep harbour outlasted the trade it was built for: it became an oil-refining and bunkering port after Venezuelan oil was found in 1914.

peak.populationNote: Roughly 20,000 to 24,000 people on Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire during the second occupation; about half of those on Curaçao were enslaved.

pedagogy.hook: On New Year's Day 1807 four British frigates sailed into Willemstad harbour at dawn, tied up alongside the fort, and captured a Dutch island before most of the garrison was out of bed.

misconception.belief: The British Empire consisted of the places coloured pink on the map.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Napoleonic wars made Britain, briefly, the master of the entire Caribbean — and then it chose what to keep. Understanding what it kept and what it returned tells you what the empire was actually for.

territories.name: Sint Eustatius, Saba and Bonaire under British occupation
territories.formalName: British occupations of the Dutch Windward Islands and Bonaire

namesOverTime.name: The Golden Rock

from.note: A nickname, not an official name; it describes Sint Eustatius at the height of its free-port trade.

namesOverTime.note: In the 1770s more than 3,000 ships a year called at an island of 21 square kilometres.

namesOverTime.name: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba
namesOverTime.note: Special municipalities of the Netherlands since the dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles on 10 October 2010.

modernSuccessors.name: Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba)
modernSuccessors.note: Special municipalities of the Netherlands since the Netherlands Antilles were dissolved in 2010.

geoCoverage.label: Rodney's occupation of Sint Eustatius
geoCoverage.change: Britain took Sint Eustatius and Saba in February 1781. Bonaire, at the other end of the Caribbean, was not involved.

to.note: Returned to the Batavian Republic during 1802 under the Peace of Amiens.

geoCoverage.label: Second British occupation
geoCoverage.change: France had retaken Sint Eustatius from Britain in November 1781 and returned it to the Dutch in 1784; Britain occupied the islands again in 1801, and by now there was almost nothing left to take.

geoCoverage.label: Third British occupation
geoCoverage.change: By 1810 Britain held all three islands, Bonaire included, and returned them together under the 1814 settlement.

acquisitions.how: Admiral George Rodney took the island without a shot being fired, then seized every ship, warehouse and private fortune on it, expelled the Jewish merchant community after stripping them, and kept the Dutch flag flying for a month to lure in more shipping.

counterparties.name: The Dutch Republic
counterparties.lost: The busiest free port in the Atlantic, and the merchant capital in it. Britain had declared war on the Dutch two months earlier largely because Sint Eustatius was supplying the American rebels with gunpowder.

counterparties.name: The merchants of Sint Eustatius, including its Jewish community
counterparties.lost: Everything they owned. Rodney's men confiscated goods valued at £3 million or more, held an auction that ran for months, and deported 101 Jewish men after searching them for hidden money.

counterparties.name: The enslaved people of Sint Eustatius
counterparties.lost: They were inventoried and sold with the rest of the property; several hundred were shipped off the island in the disposal of the prize.

people.name: George Brydges Rodney
people.role: British admiral who seized and looted the island; sued in the English courts for years afterwards by merchants whose goods he had taken

people.name: Johannes de Graeff
people.role: Dutch governor who in November 1776 ordered Fort Oranje to return the salute of the American brig Andrew Doria — often called the first foreign salute to the flag of the United States

people.name: Edmund Burke
people.role: Member of Parliament who denounced the plunder of Sint Eustatius in the Commons in 1781 as a violation of the law of nations

cost.money: Goods and shipping valued in contemporary claims at between £3 million and £4 million were confiscated; much of the convoy carrying the loot to Britain was captured by the French on the way.
cost.note: The valuations come from the merchants' own claims in the English courts and from Rodney's prize accounts, and the two sets of figures do not agree.

warrant.author: The merchants’ claims in the English prize courts, and Rodney’s prize accounts
warrant.work: Prize court claims and accounts for the seizure of St Eustatius
warrant.supports: The valuations come from the merchants' own claims in the English courts and from Rodney's prize accounts, and the two sets of figures do not agree.
warrant.check: High Court of Admiralty prize papers, HCA series, The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: Two sets of figures by two interested parties, and they do not agree. The record prints the gap rather than splitting it.

acquisitions.resistance: There was none. The garrison of about 60 men surrendered immediately; the resistance came afterwards, in the English courts and in Parliament.

evidence.author: Andrew Jackson O'Shaughnessy
evidence.work: An Empire Divided: The American Revolution and the British Caribbean
evidence.supports: Rodney's seizure of Sint Eustatius, its trade with the American rebels and the political row that followed.

acquisitions.how: Britain occupied the Dutch Windward Islands again during the war with the Batavian Republic, and returned them at the Peace of Amiens a year later.

counterparties.name: The Batavian Republic
counterparties.lost: The islands for a year; by now Sint Eustatius's trade had never recovered from 1781 and there was little left to take.

acquisitions.how: Britain took the Dutch Windward Islands for a third time, and by then also held Bonaire, so all three of today's Caribbean Netherlands were under British administration until 1816.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Holland under Napoleon
counterparties.lost: Its last Caribbean possessions for six years.

statusPeriods.label: Rodney's occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Rodney governed by inventory: the island was treated as captured property, its warehouses emptied and auctioned, its merchants deported, and its trade destroyed. A French force took it back in November.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Oranje, Sint Eustatius, under the British admiral

to.note: Returned to the Batavian Republic during 1802.

statusPeriods.label: Second occupation
statusPeriods.gapReason: France retook Sint Eustatius in November 1781 and returned it to the Dutch in 1784; Britain had no authority here for nearly twenty years.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A small British garrison held the forts; the free port never recovered its trade and there was little to govern.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Oranje, Sint Eustatius

statusPeriods.label: Third occupation
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned the islands to the Batavian Republic under the Peace of Amiens in 1802 and retook them in 1810.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Six years of British military government over three small islands, ended by handing them to the Kingdom of the Netherlands under the 1814 treaty.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Oranje, Sint Eustatius

departures.how: A French force under the Marquis de Bouillé retook Sint Eustatius by surprise in November 1781 and handed it back to the Dutch in 1784; Rodney's loot had already sailed, and much of it was captured at sea by the French.

becomes.name: Sint Eustatius under France, returned to the Dutch Republic in 1784

led.name: François Claude de Bouillé
led.role: French general who retook the island

cost.note: Casualties in the November 1781 action were light on the French and British sides; the cost of the year fell on the island's merchants and its enslaved population, who had been sold as part of the prize.

departures.borders: No line moved, but the Golden Rock never recovered. Sint Eustatius went from 3,000 ships a year to a village, and today has about 3,100 residents.

date.note: The handover under the Peace of Amiens took place during 1802.

departures.how: Britain handed the islands back to the Batavian Republic at the Peace of Amiens, and took them again eight years later.

becomes.name: Dutch Windward Islands under the Batavian Republic

led.name: Robert Jenkinson, Lord Hawkesbury
led.role: British foreign secretary at Amiens

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover.

departures.borders: No line moved.

departures.how: Britain returned Sint Eustatius, Saba and Bonaire to the Kingdom of the Netherlands under the 1814 treaty, along with Curaçao, Aruba and Suriname.

led.name: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh
led.role: British foreign secretary who negotiated the return of the Dutch Caribbean

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. Slavery on the islands continued until the Dutch abolition of 1863.

departures.borders: Britain gave back every Dutch island and kept the three Guiana colonies on the mainland, because sugar land was worth more than harbours once the slave trade was illegal.

slavery.note: Enslaved people on Sint Eustatius were confiscated and sold as part of Rodney's prize in 1781, one of the few occasions when a British force treated an entire island's population as captured goods in a formal legal process.

commonwealth.note: The islands are special municipalities of the Netherlands.

consequences.economicLegacy: Sint Eustatius was the busiest free port in the Atlantic before 1781 and never traded again at anything like that scale; the ruined warehouses along its shoreline are now underwater.
consequences.borderLegacy: Britain declared war on the Dutch Republic in December 1780 largely because Sint Eustatius was supplying the American rebels — a Caribbean island of 21 square kilometres helped keep the American Revolution supplied with gunpowder.

peak.populationNote: Sint Eustatius alone held roughly 8,000 to 12,000 people in 1780, most of them enslaved, on 21 square kilometres; today about 3,100 people live there.

evidence.author: Andrew Jackson O'Shaughnessy
evidence.work: An Empire Divided: The American Revolution and the British Caribbean
evidence.supports: Sint Eustatius's trade with the American rebels, Rodney's seizure and the political fallout in Britain.

evidence.author: Ronald Hurst
evidence.work: The Golden Rock: An Episode of the American War of Independence, 1775-1783
evidence.supports: The free port, the 1781 seizure and the disposal of the confiscated property.

contested.note: The value of the property Rodney confiscated is disputed: merchants' claims and Rodney's prize accounts give different totals, and much of it was recaptured at sea before it reached Britain.

pedagogy.hook: In 1781 a British admiral captured a Dutch island of 21 square kilometres and took three million pounds' worth of other people's property off it — and spent the rest of his life being sued for it in English courts.

misconception.belief: The American Revolution was fought in North America.
misconception.correction: It was an Atlantic war. Sint Eustatius, a free port in the Leeward Islands, sold the American rebels the gunpowder they could not make, and Britain declared war on the Dutch Republic in December 1780 largely to stop it. Rodney's fleet was in the Caribbean, not off the American coast, when Washington and Rochambeau were closing on Yorktown — one reason the French fleet got there first.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Sint Eustatius shows the empire's law working exactly as its critics said it did: what was called prize at sea was called robbery in Parliament, and Edmund Burke said so in the Commons within months.

keyDates.what: Fort Oranje returns the salute of an American brig
Rodney seizes and strips the island
A French force retakes it
Britain returns the islands to the Netherlands for the last time

territories.name: The Danish West Indies under British occupation
territories.formalName: British occupations of St Thomas, St John and St Croix

modernSuccessors.name: United States Virgin Islands
modernSuccessors.note: The United States bought the islands from Denmark in 1917 for $25 million in gold, to keep them out of German hands.

geoCoverage.label: Second British occupation
geoCoverage.change: Britain occupied the Danish islands again after bombarding Copenhagen and seizing the Danish fleet, and held them for seven years.

acquisitions.how: Britain occupied St Thomas, St John and St Croix without fighting, to stop Denmark's neutral shipping being used to supply France; the islands were returned within a year.

counterparties.name: Denmark-Norway
counterparties.lost: Its Caribbean colonies for eleven months, taken because Denmark had joined the League of Armed Neutrality against British searches of neutral shipping.

counterparties.name: The enslaved people of St Croix, St Thomas and St John
counterparties.lost: Nothing, and that is the point: Britain governed under Danish law and left slavery exactly as it found it. They were freed only on 3 July 1848, by Denmark, after a rising at Frederiksted led by John Gottlieb, called General Buddhoe.
counterparties.note: St John had seen one of the longest slave revolts in the Americas in 1733-34, when Akwamu people held most of the island for six months.

acquisitions.how: Months after bombarding Copenhagen and carrying off the Danish fleet, Britain occupied the Danish West Indies again and held them for seven years, running them under Danish law with the Danish planters in place.

counterparties.name: Denmark-Norway
counterparties.lost: Its Caribbean colonies for seven years, and — after the bombardment of Copenhagen — its navy. Denmark got the islands back in 1815 and sold them to the United States a century later.

statusPeriods.label: First British occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British garrison held the forts and left Danish law, Danish officials and the plantation system untouched; St Thomas's free port went on trading, now under British protection.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Charlotte Amalie, St Thomas, under a British military governor

statusPeriods.label: Second British occupation
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned the islands to Denmark under the Peace of Amiens in 1802 and reoccupied them at the end of 1807 after the bombardment of Copenhagen.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Seven years of British military government under Danish law. Denmark had already banned the transatlantic slave trade from 1803 — the first country in the world to do so — and the British ban of 1807 applied here too.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Charlotte Amalie, St Thomas, under a British military governor

departures.how: Britain returned the islands to Denmark as the Peace of Amiens took shape, and occupied them again less than six years later.

led.name: Henry Addington
led.role: British prime minister whose government made the peace with the northern powers and with France

cost.note: Nobody died in either the occupation or the handover. The islands' roughly 35,000 enslaved people were unaffected either way.

departures.borders: No line moved. The Virgin Islands stayed split between Danish and British halves, which is why there are two sets of Virgin Islands today, one American and one British.

departures.how: Britain handed the islands back to Denmark at the end of the Napoleonic wars, as part of the settlement in which Denmark lost Norway to Sweden and Heligoland to Britain.

led.name: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh
led.role: British foreign secretary who settled the Danish territorial questions at Vienna

cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. Denmark abolished slavery in the islands in 1848, after a mass rising on St Croix led by John Gottlieb, known as General Buddhoe, forced the governor's hand in a single day.

departures.borders: Britain kept Heligoland from Denmark and gave back the Caribbean islands. A century later Denmark sold them to the United States, which is why the American flag flies four kilometres from a British territory.

slavery.note: Denmark banned the transatlantic slave trade from 1803, the first country in the world to do so, four years before Britain; slavery itself continued in these islands until a rising forced emancipation in 1848.

abolitionDate.note: The Danish ban of 1792 took effect on 1 January 1803, making Denmark the first state to end its transatlantic slave trade.

emancipationDate.note: Enslaved people on St Croix gathered in their thousands at Frederiksted under John Gottlieb, called General Buddhoe, and the Danish governor proclaimed emancipation the same day rather than face them.

commonwealth.note: The islands are an unincorporated territory of the United States.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Virgin Islands were split between Denmark and Britain in the seventeenth century, and the split survives: the British Virgin Islands are a British Overseas Territory and the United States Virgin Islands lie four kilometres away.

peak.populationNote: Roughly 35,000 to 40,000 people during the second occupation, the great majority enslaved on the sugar estates of St Croix.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
areaWarrant.supports: The Danish West Indies under British occupation’s greatest extent, 346 km² in 1810: the 1 map unit this atlas draws it holding that year measure 356 km², within 2.9% of it.
areaWarrant.check: Open the atlas at that year and select this territory: the outline you see IS the figure. Its units are listed under `geoCoverage` in the shard and measured in app/data/geo/units.index.json, from Natural Earth 1:10m boundaries — public domain, naturalearthdata.com.
areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: Neville A. T. Hall
evidence.work: Slave Society in the Danish West Indies: St Thomas, St John and St Croix
evidence.publisher: University of the West Indies Press
evidence.supports: The islands' slave society, the British occupations and the 1848 emancipation.

evidence.author: Michael Duffy
evidence.work: Soldiers, Sugar, and Seapower: The British Expeditions to the West Indies and the War against Revolutionary France
evidence.supports: British strategy towards neutral colonies in the Caribbean during the wars with France.

contested.note: Exact dates for the 1802 and 1815 handovers vary between accounts, and population estimates for the occupation years come from Danish plantation returns of uneven quality.

pedagogy.hook: Denmark banned the transatlantic slave trade in 1803, four years before Britain — and Britain then occupied the Danish islands twice, without changing anything about how they worked.

misconception.belief: Britain was the first country to abolish the slave trade.
misconception.correction: Denmark passed its ban in 1792 to take effect on 1 January 1803, and it did. Britain's Act came in 1807. Britain's abolition mattered far more in practice, because Britain was the biggest carrier and had the navy to enforce a ban on others — but 'first' belongs to Denmark, and knowing that changes what Britain's 1807 Act was actually for.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: These islands are the reason there are two Virgin Islands today, and they show how neutral powers' colonies were treated in a total war: occupied when convenient, returned when convenient, and never consulted.

keyDates.what: Denmark's ban on the transatlantic slave trade takes effect
Britain occupies the Danish islands for seven years
Britain hands them back to Denmark
A rising on St Croix forces Danish emancipation in a day
Denmark sells the islands to the United States

events.title: The killing at Bloody Point

date.note: The month is not securely recorded; contemporary accounts place the attack in 1626, two years after the English landed.

events.summary: English and French settlers on St Kitts, told that the Kalinago were gathering fighters to expel them, attacked at night and killed the Kalinago leader Tegremante and most of his people at a place still called Bloody Point.
events.significance: It is the founding act of the British Caribbean: the first English colony in the region was two years old, and it secured itself by destroying the people who had fed it through its first winter. The same pattern followed on Nevis, Antigua and Montserrat within a decade.

places.name: Bloody Point, St Kitts
places.note: At the mouth of the Stone Fort river, near Old Road Town.

people.name: Tegremante
people.role: Kalinago leader of Liamuiga, who had allowed the English to settle and was killed in the attack

people.name: Thomas Warner
people.role: English governor of St Kitts who ordered the attack

people.name: Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc
people.role: French commander who joined the attack alongside the English

toll.note: The figure of 2,000 dead comes from a later French account and is often repeated; other contemporary sources suggest a much smaller number, perhaps 100 to 120. Nobody counted, and the range reflects genuine uncertainty rather than caution.

pedagogy.hook: The first English colony in the Caribbean survived its first year because the Kalinago fed it. In its third year it killed them.

misconception.belief: European settlers and Indigenous Caribbean peoples were separated by a wide technological gap that made resistance hopeless.
misconception.correction: The Kalinago were a serious military power in the Lesser Antilles for another 170 years. They destroyed English settlements on Antigua, Montserrat and Tobago, forced Britain and France to declare Dominica and St Vincent neutral territory in 1660, and held Dominica until 1763. What happened at Bloody Point was a surprise attack, not an inevitability.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It sets the terms for everything that follows in this region: Indigenous people were not absent from the British Caribbean, they were removed from it, and the removal has dates and names.

evidence.author: Richard S. Dunn
evidence.work: Sugar and Slaves: The Rise of the Planter Class in the English West Indies, 1624-1713
evidence.supports: The founding of St Kitts and the destruction of its Kalinago population.

contested.note: The death toll rests on hostile and much later European accounts and cannot be verified; estimates range from about a hundred to two thousand.

events.title: Cromwell's Western Design

date.note: The fleet sailed from Portsmouth on 25 December 1654.

endDate.note: The Spanish surrender of Jamaica, dated by the English expedition under the Julian calendar.

events.summary: Oliver Cromwell sent 38 ships and 7,000 men to seize Spanish America. They were beaten at Santo Domingo in April 1655, losing over a thousand men, and took lightly defended Jamaica instead. Both commanders were imprisoned in the Tower for it.
events.significance: It was the first time an English government sent a state fleet to conquer other people's colonies rather than licensing private adventurers, and it began the shift from a Caribbean of settlements to an empire of conquest. Jamaica became the empire's richest colony and its largest slave society.

places.name: Santo Domingo
places.note: Where the expedition was defeated in April 1655.

places.name: Passage Fort, Jamaica
places.note: Where the English landed on 10 May 1655.

people.name: Oliver Cromwell
people.role: Lord Protector, who conceived the Design and treated its outcome as a divine judgement on England

people.name: Admiral Sir William Penn
people.role: admiral of the fleet, imprisoned in the Tower on his return

people.name: Robert Venables
people.role: general of the land forces, imprisoned in the Tower on his return

people.name: Cristóbal Arnaldo Ysassi
people.role: Spanish governor who fought a guerrilla campaign in Jamaica until 1660

people.name: Juan de Bolas
people.role: leader of formerly enslaved Africans in Jamaica's mountains who made terms with the English in 1660 and was killed in 1664

toll.note: Over a thousand died in the failed assault on Santo Domingo; thousands more of the 7,000 who landed on Jamaica died of disease and hunger in the first year. Spanish and African deaths were not counted. Figures are from the expedition's own returns as used by Carla Gardina Pestana.

pedagogy.hook: England conquered Jamaica by accident, as a consolation prize after losing a battle it expected to win — and jailed the men who brought it home.

misconception.belief: The British Empire was built by deliberate long-term planning.
misconception.correction: The Western Design was planned, and it failed. Its target was Hispaniola, and the fleet was beaten there by a much smaller Spanish force. Jamaica was a substitute nobody wanted, and Cromwell was so angry he imprisoned both commanders. The empire's most valuable Caribbean colony was the by-product of a defeat.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It marks the moment the English state itself went into the conquest business in the Americas, and it created the colony that would dominate the British Atlantic for the next 150 years.

evidence.author: Carla Gardina Pestana
evidence.work: The English Conquest of Jamaica: Oliver Cromwell's Bid for Empire
evidence.supports: The expedition, its failure at Hispaniola, its losses and its consequences.

events.title: Prince Klaas's conspiracy, Antigua

date.note: The date the first executions began; the alleged plot was uncovered on 15 October by the planters' own account, and the dating in the court record is inconsistent.

events.summary: Antiguan planters uncovered what they said was a plan by enslaved people to blow up a ball attended by the island's white elite and seize the island. Eighty-eight people were executed: five broken on the wheel, six hung in chains to starve, and 77 burned alive.
events.significance: It is the best-documented case in the British Caribbean of a slave society punishing an intention rather than an act, and the court record — kept by the planters themselves — is one of the fullest sources historians have for how enslaved communities organised on a British island.

places.name: St John's, Antigua
places.note: Where the trials and most of the executions took place.

people.name: Court, called Prince Klaas
people.role: Akan-born enslaved man named by the court as the intended king of a free Antigua; broken on the wheel

people.name: Tomboy
people.role: enslaved carpenter named as the man who would set the gunpowder; executed

toll.note: The count of 88 executions comes from the planters' own court records, analysed by David Barry Gaspar. Whether a plot existed at the scale the court described is disputed; the executions are documented beyond doubt.

pedagogy.hook: Eighty-eight people were executed in Antigua in 1736 for a rebellion that never happened.

misconception.belief: Slave societies were stable places where rebellion was rare.
misconception.correction: They were societies organised around permanent fear. Antigua's 3,700 white residents lived among 24,400 enslaved people, and the response to a rumour was 88 public executions designed to be watched. Historians disagree about whether the 1736 plot was real; nobody disagrees that the planters believed one was always possible.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the machinery of a slave society under stress: the courts, the punishments and the public theatre that held the system together when the numbers did not.

evidence.author: David Barry Gaspar
evidence.work: Bondmen and Rebels: A Study of Master-Slave Relations in Antigua
evidence.supports: The conspiracy, the trials and the executions, from the Antiguan court records.

contested.note: Historians differ over whether the conspiracy was as organised as the court found, or whether the evidence was produced by torture and the expectations of frightened planters.

events.title: The Jamaican Maroon treaties

endDate.note: The second treaty, with the Windward Maroons under Quao.

events.summary: After a decade of war it could not win, Britain signed treaties with the Jamaican Maroons: Cudjoe's Leeward Maroons got land, autonomy and freedom in March 1739, and Quao's Windward Maroons in June 1740. In exchange the Maroons agreed to return people who escaped from the plantations.
events.significance: A European empire formally conceded territory and self-government to a community of formerly enslaved Africans, 96 years before it abolished slavery. The treaties still have legal force in Jamaica, and the clause requiring the Maroons to return runaways is the hardest thing in Caribbean history to teach honestly.

places.name: Trelawny Town (Cudjoe's Town)
places.note: Where the 1739 treaty was signed, in the Cockpit Country.

places.name: Nanny Town, Portland
places.note: The Windward Maroon settlement associated with Nanny, destroyed by British forces in 1734.

people.name: Cudjoe
people.role: leader of the Leeward Maroons who fought the British to a standstill and signed the 1739 treaty

people.name: Nanny
people.role: Windward Maroon leader, Jamaica's only female National Hero, remembered as a military and spiritual leader in the war

people.name: Quao
people.role: leader of the Windward Maroons who signed the second treaty in 1740

people.name: Edward Trelawny
people.role: Governor of Jamaica who authorised the treaties because the war could not be won

pedagogy.hook: In 1739 the British Empire signed a peace treaty with an army of people who had escaped slavery — and one of the terms was that they would catch others who escaped and hand them back.

misconception.belief: Resistance to slavery was always a straightforward struggle between the enslaved and their owners.
misconception.correction: The Maroons won their freedom and their land by fighting, and they kept it by agreeing to hunt down other people seeking the same thing. Historians and Jamaicans still argue about this. It is not a reason to admire the Maroons less; it is a reason to see how completely a slave society could shape even the choices of the people who had escaped it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The treaties are still in force, Maroon towns still hold their land, and the compromise inside them shows what freedom cost when it had to be negotiated with an empire.

evidence.author: Mavis C. Campbell
evidence.work: The Maroons of Jamaica 1655-1796: A History of Resistance, Collaboration and Betrayal
evidence.supports: The First Maroon War, the treaties and their terms.

events.title: The St Patrick's Day rising, Montserrat
events.summary: Enslaved Montserratians planned to seize the island's arms while the Irish planters celebrated St Patrick's Day at Government House. The plan was betrayed; nine men were executed and about thirty transported off the island.
