events.significance: Montserrat now keeps St Patrick's Day as a national holiday commemorating this rising, not the saint — the only place in the world where the day belongs to enslaved Africans rather than to the Irish, on an island the Irish had been sent to colonise.

places.name: Plymouth, Montserrat
places.note: The colonial capital, buried by pyroclastic flows in 1997.

people.name: Cudjoe
people.role: named in the trial records as one of the leaders; executed

toll.note: Nine men were executed and about thirty transported, according to the colonial trial records; those records are the only source and were made by the men the rising was aimed at.

pedagogy.hook: Montserrat's St Patrick's Day is a public holiday about a slave rebellion, on an island founded by Irish Catholics who by then owned 6,000 enslaved Africans.

misconception.belief: Irish people in the Caribbean were fellow victims of the English, not participants in the slave system.
misconception.correction: Montserrat was settled by Irish Catholics escaping Protestant St Kitts, and within two generations they were the island's planter class. By 1729 they owned about 6,000 enslaved people. Being oppressed at home did not stop people becoming owners abroad, and the enslaved Montserratians of 1768 planned their rising for the day their Irish owners would be drunk.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest single case in the empire of colonised people becoming colonisers, and Montserrat has chosen to remember it rather than the comfortable version.

evidence.author: Donald Harman Akenson
evidence.work: If the Irish Ran the World: Montserrat, 1630-1730
evidence.supports: Irish settlement, Irish slave-ownership and the society the 1768 rising took place in.

contested.note: The rising is documented only in the colonial trial records; details of its plan and leadership come from confessions obtained under threat of execution.

events.title: Tacky's Revolt

endDate.note: Fighting continued in scattered risings for eighteen months; no single end date is recorded.

events.summary: Enslaved Akan people in St Mary, Jamaica, led by a man the records call Tacky, seized the fort at Port Maria and rose across the island in a war that lasted eighteen months. About 60 white and 400 Black people were killed in the fighting, and hundreds more were executed.
events.significance: It was the largest slave rising in the British Empire before 1831 and cost Jamaica more than the island's annual revenue. It produced the harshest slave code in the British Caribbean, and the Maroons fought for the government under their 1739 treaties.

places.name: Port Maria, St Mary
places.note: Where the rising began with the seizure of Fort Haldane's arms.

people.name: Tacky
people.role: Akan leader of the rising in St Mary, killed by a Maroon marksman

people.name: Wager, also called Apongo
people.role: leader of the Westmoreland rising; said to have been a military commander in West Africa before he was enslaved

people.name: Sir Henry Moore, 1st Baronet
people.role: Lieutenant-Governor of Jamaica who directed the suppression

toll.note: Contemporary accounts give about 60 white deaths and 400 enslaved killed in the fighting, with 100 or more executed and 500 transported. Vincent Brown treats these figures as approximations from planter sources; nobody counted carefully.

pedagogy.hook: The men who led Jamaica's greatest eighteenth-century rising had been soldiers in West Africa before they were enslaved, and they fought it like a campaign, not a riot.

misconception.belief: Slave revolts were spontaneous explosions of despair.
misconception.correction: Vincent Brown's reconstruction shows Tacky's Revolt as a coordinated war fought over eighteen months across the island by people with military experience from the wars of the Gold Coast. They took a fort, held territory, and were defeated by regular troops, sailors and Maroon allies. It was a campaign in an Atlantic war, not an outburst.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It changed Jamaican law for a century, and it shows enslaved people carrying African political and military history with them across the Atlantic and using it.

evidence.author: Vincent Brown
evidence.work: Tacky's Revolt: The Story of an Atlantic Slave War
evidence.supports: The course of the rising, its African military background and its suppression.

contested.note: Casualty figures come from planter accounts written to justify the response, and the identity and role of 'Tacky' himself are known only through those hostile sources.

events.title: The Treaty of Paris, 1763
events.summary: The treaty ending the Seven Years' War handed Britain Canada, Florida, Grenada, Dominica, St Vincent and Tobago, and handed back Guadeloupe, Martinique, St Lucia and Havana. Britain's West India lobby had campaigned against keeping the sugar islands.
events.significance: This is the settlement that made the British Empire the dominant power in the Americas, and the moment its own sugar planters argued successfully against expansion because more sugar inside the empire meant lower prices for them. Empire was shaped by interest groups, not just by generals.

places.name: Paris
places.note: Where the treaty was signed.

people.name: John Stuart, Earl of Bute
people.role: British prime minister who made the peace and was burned in effigy for its terms

people.name: Étienne-François, duc de Choiseul
people.role: French foreign minister who kept the sugar islands and gave up Canada

people.name: William Pitt the Elder
people.role: argued in Parliament that giving back Guadeloupe and Martinique threw away the war's real prizes

pedagogy.hook: In 1763 Parliament seriously debated whether Canada or the island of Guadeloupe was worth more. Guadeloupe produced more revenue.

misconception.belief: Empires always took as much territory as they could get.
misconception.correction: Britain ended the Seven Years' War holding Havana, Manila, Guadeloupe and Martinique, and gave every one of them back. The West India interest in Parliament — the sugar planters and merchants — lobbied hard against keeping rival sugar islands, because more supply meant lower prices. What Britain kept was decided partly by who had votes in the House of Commons.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest place in the empire's history to see economic self-interest overriding territorial ambition, and it redrew both the Caribbean and North America in a single document.

evidence.author: Fred Anderson
evidence.work: Crucible of War: The Seven Years' War and the Fate of Empire in British North America, 1754-1766
evidence.supports: The peace negotiations, the Canada-versus-Guadeloupe debate and the terms of the treaty.

events.title: The Berbice rebellion

endDate.note: Resistance was broken over the first months of 1764; there is no single surrender date.

events.summary: Enslaved people in the Dutch colony of Berbice, led by a man called Cuffy, took over almost the whole colony and held it for nearly a year, offering to divide it with the Dutch. Troops from Suriname, Barbados and British and French ships put the rising down.
events.significance: It was the largest slave rebellion in the Guianas and the closest anyone came to founding a free state on the South American mainland before Haiti. Cuffy is Guyana's national hero, and 23 February is Guyana's Republic Day.

places.name: Fort Nassau, Berbice river
places.note: The colony's capital, abandoned by the Dutch during the rising.

people.name: Cuffy (Kofi)
people.role: Akan-born enslaved cooper who led the rising, declared himself Governor of Berbice and proposed partitioning the colony with the Dutch; died in 1763

people.name: Akara
people.role: rival rebel leader whose split with Cuffy weakened the rising

people.name: Wolphert Simon van Hoogenheim
people.role: Dutch governor who held on at the river mouth and negotiated for time while waiting for troops

toll.note: Perhaps half the colony's 4,000 to 5,000 enslaved people died in the fighting, of hunger, or by execution afterwards; 125 or more were executed in the reprisals. The figures come from Dutch colonial records and are approximate.

pedagogy.hook: For almost a year in 1763 an enslaved cooper called Cuffy governed a European colony in South America and wrote to the Dutch offering to split it in half.

misconception.belief: Enslaved rebels wanted to destroy plantation society and had no political programme.
misconception.correction: Cuffy's letters to Governor van Hoogenheim proposed a negotiated partition of Berbice, with the Africans keeping the upper river and the Dutch the coast. He signed himself Governor. This was a bid for a state, made in writing, thirty years before the Haitian Revolution.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the precedent for Demerara in 1823 and for everything the Guianese working class did afterwards; Guyana dates its republic from the day the rising began.

evidence.author: Marjoleine Kars
evidence.work: Blood on the River: A Chronicle of Mutiny and Freedom on the Wild Coast
evidence.supports: The rising, Cuffy's negotiations and the suppression, reconstructed from Dutch archives.

contested.note: Death tolls are estimates from Dutch colonial records; the internal politics of the rebel leadership are known mainly from interrogations of captured rebels.

events.title: Rodney sacks Sint Eustatius
events.summary: Admiral George Rodney took the Dutch free port of Sint Eustatius without a shot, confiscated every warehouse and ship on the island, deported its Jewish merchants after searching them for money, and kept the Dutch flag flying to trap incoming vessels.
events.significance: Britain had declared war on the Dutch Republic mainly because this island was supplying the American rebels with gunpowder. The plunder was denounced in Parliament by Edmund Burke, tied Rodney up in litigation for years, and kept his fleet in the Leewards while the French sailed for Chesapeake Bay.

places.name: Oranjestad, Sint Eustatius
places.note: The lower town's warehouses ran for more than a kilometre along the shore.

people.name: George Brydges Rodney
people.role: British admiral who seized the island and disposed of its property as prize

people.name: Johannes de Graeff
people.role: Dutch governor whose salute to an American brig in 1776 became a symbol of the island's role in the American Revolution

people.name: Edmund Burke
people.role: denounced the plunder in the House of Commons as a breach of the law of nations

toll.money: Property valued in contemporary claims at £3 million to £4 million was confiscated; a large part of the convoy carrying it to Britain was captured at sea by the French.
toll.note: Merchants' claims in the English courts and Rodney's own prize accounts give different totals, and neither is disinterested.

pedagogy.hook: A Dutch island of 21 square kilometres kept the American Revolution supplied with gunpowder, and Britain went to war with the Netherlands to stop it.

misconception.belief: Britain lost the American war on the American mainland.
misconception.correction: It lost it in an Atlantic and Caribbean war. Rodney's fleet spent months at Sint Eustatius disposing of loot while the French fleet under de Grasse sailed north; de Grasse's blockade of the Chesapeake made Yorktown possible. British commanders in 1781 were fighting a global war with limited ships, and the Caribbean was where most of them were.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows imperial law from the inside: what a fleet called prize, Parliament called robbery, and the courts spent a decade deciding.

evidence.author: Andrew Jackson O'Shaughnessy
evidence.work: An Empire Divided: The American Revolution and the British Caribbean
evidence.supports: The seizure, the island's trade with the American rebels and the political fallout in Britain.

contested.note: The value of the confiscated property is disputed between the merchants' claims and Rodney's accounts, and much of it never reached Britain.

events.title: The Battle of the Saintes
events.summary: Rodney's fleet broke the French line in the channel between Guadeloupe and Dominica, captured the French flagship and its admiral, and destroyed a Franco-Spanish plan to invade Jamaica.
events.significance: It saved Jamaica and let Britain negotiate the 1783 peace from strength in the Caribbean, recovering most of the islands France had taken. The British Empire lost thirteen American colonies in that war and kept almost all of its sugar islands, which is why 1783 did not end it.

places.name: Îles des Saintes
places.note: The islets between Guadeloupe and Dominica that give the battle its name.

people.name: George Brydges Rodney
people.role: British admiral commanding the fleet

people.name: François Joseph Paul de Grasse
people.role: French admiral, victor at the Chesapeake six months earlier, captured with his flagship at the Saintes

toll.note: French dead and wounded are usually put at around 2,000 to 3,000, British at about 1,000. Naval casualty returns of this period count crews unevenly, and prisoners are often included in the totals.

pedagogy.hook: Six months after helping win American independence at the Chesapeake, the French admiral de Grasse was captured with his flagship in the channel between Guadeloupe and Dominica.

misconception.belief: Britain was defeated in 1783 and its empire went into decline.
misconception.correction: Britain lost the thirteen colonies and kept nearly everything else. At the Saintes it destroyed the fleet that was to invade Jamaica, and at the peace it recovered St Kitts, Nevis, Montserrat, Dominica, St Vincent and Grenada. Within twenty years it had conquered Trinidad, the Guianas, the Cape and Ceylon. The empire after 1783 was larger, not smaller.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the pivot on which the myth of 1776 as the end of the British Empire breaks: the Caribbean and Asian empire that came after was bigger than the one lost.

evidence.author: Andrew Jackson O'Shaughnessy
evidence.work: An Empire Divided: The American Revolution and the British Caribbean
evidence.supports: The Caribbean campaigns of 1780-83 and the terms of the 1783 settlement.

events.title: Fédon's rebellion, Grenada
events.summary: Julien Fédon, a free man of colour, raised the French Republic's flag over Grenada, took the lieutenant-governor hostage and held most of the island for fifteen months with thousands of enslaved and free-coloured fighters, demanding citizenship and emancipation.
events.significance: It was the most serious internal challenge to British rule in the Caribbean outside Jamaica, and it was explicitly political: the rebels fought under a republic that had abolished slavery in 1794. Britain needed 15 months and thousands of troops to defeat it, and Fédon was never found.

places.name: Belvidere estate, Grenada
places.note: Fédon's own estate, the rebellion's headquarters and the place where 48 British hostages were killed.

people.name: Julien Fédon
people.role: free coloured planter who led the rising; never captured, and his fate is unknown

people.name: Ninian Home
people.role: Lieutenant-Governor of Grenada, taken hostage and killed with 47 others in April 1795

people.name: Victor Hugues
people.role: French republican commissioner at Guadeloupe who supplied the rebellion with arms, officers and the emancipation decree

people.name: Ralph Abercromby
people.role: British general whose troops finally broke the rising in June 1796

toll.note: Contemporary British estimates put the enslaved dead at around 7,000 out of about 28,000 on the island, from fighting, hunger and executions. Modern historians treat these as orders of magnitude: no one counted the dead among the enslaved.

pedagogy.hook: For fifteen months in 1795 and 1796, Grenada was governed from a plantation in the mountains by a free Black planter flying the flag of the French Republic.

misconception.belief: The French Revolution was a European event.
misconception.correction: Its most radical decision — abolishing slavery in the colonies in February 1794 — turned the Caribbean into a battlefield of ideas. Fédon in Grenada, Chatoyer in St Vincent, the Brigands in St Lucia and Hugues in Guadeloupe all fought under that decree. Britain sent tens of thousands of soldiers to the Caribbean in the 1790s, and most of them died there, to stop it spreading.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest evidence that enslaved and free coloured people in the British islands were following Atlantic politics closely, and acted on it the moment a door opened.

evidence.author: Michael Craton
evidence.work: Testing the Chains: Resistance to Slavery in the British West Indies
evidence.supports: The rebellion's course and its place in Caribbean slave resistance.

evidence.author: Edward L. Cox
evidence.work: Free Coloreds in the Slave Societies of St. Kitts and Grenada, 1763-1833
evidence.supports: The political exclusion of free people of colour that produced the rising.

contested.note: The death toll among the enslaved comes from British estimates made after the event, and Fédon's fate is genuinely unknown — accounts have him drowned, escaped to Cuba, or living in Trinidad.

events.title: The Second Carib War, St Vincent
events.summary: The Garifuna of St Vincent, allied with French republicans, rose against British settlement of their land under their paramount chief Joseph Chatoyer. Chatoyer was killed on Dorsetshire Hill on 14 March 1795; the war ground on for another fifteen months until British troops burned the Garifuna's food supplies.
events.significance: It was the last stand of an independent Indigenous polity in the eastern Caribbean, and the British answer to it was not a treaty but a deportation. It ended Kalinago and Garifuna landholding on St Vincent for good.

places.name: Dorsetshire Hill, St Vincent
places.note: Where Chatoyer was killed on 14 March 1795; there is a monument there now.

people.name: Joseph Chatoyer
people.role: paramount chief of the Garifuna, killed on Dorsetshire Hill; St Vincent's national hero since 2002

people.name: Duvalle
people.role: Garifuna commander who fought on after Chatoyer's death and surrendered in 1796

people.name: Ralph Abercromby
people.role: British general who ended the war by destroying Garifuna provision grounds

toll.note: Deaths in the fighting were never counted on either side; most of the mortality came afterwards, on Balliceaux, where roughly half of about 5,000 detained Garifuna died over the winter of 1796-97.

pedagogy.hook: The last independent Indigenous nation in the eastern Caribbean was beaten not in battle but by burning its food.

misconception.belief: Indigenous Caribbean peoples had disappeared long before the age of the British Empire.
misconception.correction: The Garifuna were still fighting Britain for their own country in 1796 — 300 years after Columbus. They allied with the French Republic, held most of St Vincent for a year, and were removed only by a campaign that destroyed their provision grounds and then deported the survivors.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It links directly to Central America: the people defeated here in 1796 are the ancestors of the Garifuna communities of Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua today.

evidence.author: Christopher Taylor
evidence.work: The Black Carib Wars: Freedom, Survival, and the Making of the Garifuna
evidence.supports: The war, Chatoyer's leadership and the British campaign against Garifuna food supplies.

events.title: The Second Maroon War and the Nova Scotia deportation
events.summary: The Trelawny Town Maroons went to war after two of their men were flogged by a workhouse slave. Britain brought in bloodhounds from Cuba, and the Maroons surrendered on terms. The terms were broken: 568 people were deported to Nova Scotia, and in 1800 sent on to Sierra Leone.
events.significance: It is the clearest documented case of a British colonial government breaking a surrender agreement it had signed, and it connects the Caribbean directly to West Africa: the Trelawny Maroons helped found Freetown's Maroon Town, where their descendants live today.

places.name: Trelawny Town, Cockpit Country
places.note: The Maroon town whose people were deported.

places.name: Freetown, Sierra Leone
places.note: Where the deportees were landed in 1800; the district is still called Maroon Town.

people.name: Montague James
people.role: colonel of the Trelawny Town Maroons who negotiated the surrender and was deported with his people

people.name: George Walpole
people.role: British commander who gave the Maroons his word that they would not be deported, and resigned his commission and refused a sword of honour when Jamaica's assembly broke it

people.name: Alexander Lindsay, Earl of Balcarres
people.role: Governor of Jamaica who imported the bloodhounds and insisted on the deportation

toll.note: The figure of 568 deported to Nova Scotia in 1796 comes from the transport returns. Deaths in the fighting were low among the Trelawny Maroons and the British alike; the cost of this war was measured in exile.

pedagogy.hook: Britain promised the Trelawny Maroons they would not be deported if they surrendered. They surrendered, and were shipped to Nova Scotia — and then to Sierra Leone.

misconception.belief: Colonial governments were bound by the treaties and terms they signed.
misconception.correction: General Walpole gave the Maroons his personal word, in writing, that surrender would not mean deportation. Jamaica's assembly deported them anyway. Walpole resigned and refused the sword of honour the assembly voted him. The record of what was promised, and by whom, survives — which is why this case is used to teach how imperial promises actually worked.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the empire as one connected system: a war in the Jamaican mountains ends with families landing in Halifax in the snow and then in Freetown, and their descendants live in all three places.

evidence.author: Mavis C. Campbell
evidence.work: The Maroons of Jamaica 1655-1796: A History of Resistance, Collaboration and Betrayal
evidence.supports: The war, the surrender terms and the deportation to Nova Scotia and Sierra Leone.

events.title: The deportation of the Garifuna

date.note: The convoy sailed from Balliceaux in March 1797; sources give slightly different sailing dates.

events.summary: After the Second Carib War, Britain held about 5,000 Garifuna on the barren islet of Balliceaux, where roughly half died of typhus and dysentery over the winter. In March 1797 the survivors — 4,338 by the transport returns — were shipped 3,000 kilometres to Roatán, off Honduras.
events.significance: It is the largest forced removal of an Indigenous people carried out by Britain in the Americas, and it created a nation: today roughly 300,000 Garifuna live in Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua, and UNESCO lists their language, dance and music as intangible cultural heritage.

places.name: Balliceaux, Grenadines
places.note: The waterless islet where about half the detained Garifuna died over the winter of 1796-97.

places.name: Roatán, Bay Islands
places.note: Where the survivors were landed on 12 April 1797.

people.name: Duvalle
people.role: Garifuna commander deported with his people

people.name: Ralph Abercromby
people.role: British general who ordered the removal

people.name: William Young
people.role: St Vincent planter and commissioner whose writings pressed the case for removing the Garifuna from the island entirely

toll.note: British commissary returns count 4,338 people landed on Roatán out of roughly 5,000 held on Balliceaux; the difference is the winter's death toll from typhus and dysentery. The numbers come from the transport and commissary records, made by the people who carried out the removal.

pedagogy.hook: Balliceaux is a waterless island of two square kilometres. Britain held five thousand people on it for one winter, and half of them died.

misconception.belief: Mass forced removals of Indigenous peoples were an American, not a British, policy.
misconception.correction: Britain removed the entire Garifuna population of St Vincent in 1797, thirty-three years before the United States passed the Indian Removal Act. It was carried out by the army, recorded in official returns, and justified as a security measure. Garifuna people still travel to Balliceaux each March to commemorate it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: One British decision in 1797 explains why there are Garifuna communities along 700 kilometres of Central American coast, and why the Garifuna landing at Dangriga on 19 November is a national holiday in Belize.

evidence.author: Christopher Taylor
evidence.work: The Black Carib Wars: Freedom, Survival, and the Making of the Garifuna
evidence.supports: Balliceaux, the transport returns and the landing on Roatán.

evidence.author: Nancie L. González
evidence.work: Sojourners of the Caribbean: Ethnogenesis and Ethnohistory of the Garifuna
evidence.supports: The Garifuna dispersal across Central America after 1797.

contested.note: The number held on Balliceaux is estimated rather than counted; the 4,338 landed at Roatán is a firm figure from the transport returns, so the death toll is a difference between a firm number and an estimated one.

events.title: The Slave Trade Act 1807 in the Caribbean
events.summary: From 1 May 1807 no British ship could land another African in the Caribbean. Nearly 800,000 people already enslaved in the British islands stayed enslaved for 27 more years, and Trinidad became the test case for a register that recorded every one of them by name in order to police the ban.
events.significance: Britain had carried roughly 3.1 million Africans across the Atlantic, of whom about 2.7 million survived the crossing, and the Caribbean was where most of them landed. Ending the trade without ending slavery forced planters to keep people alive rather than replace them, and produced the registries that are now the best surviving record of who those people were.

places.name: Palace of Westminster, London
places.note: Where the Act passed the Commons by 283 votes to 16.

people.name: Olaudah Equiano
people.role: formerly enslaved writer whose 1789 autobiography sold nine editions in his lifetime and made the trade real to British readers

people.name: Ottobah Cugoano
people.role: formerly enslaved Ghanaian-born abolitionist in London who in 1787 demanded not just an end to the trade but the abolition of slavery itself

people.name: Thomas Clarkson
people.role: researcher and organiser of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade, who collected the evidence from the ports

people.name: William Wilberforce
people.role: Member of Parliament who put the abolition bills before the Commons for twenty years

people.name: Toussaint Louverture
people.role: led the revolution in Saint-Domingue that destroyed the richest slave colony in the world and made planters everywhere afraid

toll.note: Estimates of the number of Africans carried in British ships across the whole period, from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database. Around 400,000 to 600,000 died on the crossing. These figures are reconstructions from voyage records and carry real margins of error.

pedagogy.hook: The 1807 Act did not free a single enslaved person in the Caribbean. It made it illegal to bring any more, and nearly 800,000 people stayed enslaved for another 27 years.

misconception.belief: Britain abolished slavery in 1807.
misconception.correction: It abolished the trade, not slavery. Slavery in the British colonies ended in 1834 and, after four years of unpaid apprenticeship, in 1838. Denmark had banned its own trade from 1803. And the 1807 Act came after Britain had spent five years and 12,000 lives trying to restore slavery in Saint-Domingue. Abolition was a hard-fought political victory, not a national character trait.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the hinge of the whole Atlantic story, and getting the difference between the trade and slavery right is the single most useful thing a student can take from this region.

evidence.author: Christopher Leslie Brown
evidence.work: Moral Capital: Foundations of British Abolitionism
evidence.supports: Why abolitionism became politically possible in Britain when it did.

evidence.author: David Eltis and David Richardson
evidence.work: Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade
evidence.supports: The scale of the British trade and the voyage data behind the figures.

contested.note: Historians disagree about why abolition succeeded in 1807: Eric Williams argued the West Indian economy was already declining and abolition served British interests; Seymour Drescher's data show the trade was still highly profitable, which makes the moral and political campaign, and the pressure of slave resistance, the better explanation.

events.title: Bussa's Rebellion, Barbados
events.summary: On Easter Sunday 1816, enslaved people across southern and eastern Barbados rose and burned cane on more than seventy estates. Martial law and the West India Regiment crushed the rising in four days, and the executions went on for months.
events.significance: It was the first of the three great British Caribbean risings — Barbados 1816, Demerara 1823, Jamaica 1831 — that convinced Parliament slavery could not be held down indefinitely, and it took place on the island planters had always called the most secure in the empire.

places.name: Bayley's plantation, St Philip
places.note: Where the rising began.

places.name: Bridgetown
places.note: Seat of the governor who declared martial law.

people.name: Bussa
people.role: African-born ranger at Bayley's plantation who led the rising and was killed in the fighting; a National Hero of Barbados

people.name: Nanny Grigg
people.role: enslaved woman at Simmons plantation who, witnesses testified, told others that freedom had already been granted in England and would have to be taken

people.name: Washington Franklin
people.role: free man of colour tried and executed as an organiser

people.name: James Leith
people.role: governor who declared martial law and directed the suppression

toll.note: About fifty enslaved people died fighting, roughly seventy were executed in the field and around three hundred after trial; 170 more were transported off the island. Two people died on the militia's side. Accounts differ, and the figures come from the planters' own inquiry of 1818.

pedagogy.hook: The rebels of 1816 believed that freedom had already been granted in London and that the planters were hiding it from them.

misconception.belief: Enslaved people were freed by Parliament and by abolitionists acting on their behalf.
misconception.correction: Freedom was fought for from below as well as argued for in London. Barbados 1816, Demerara 1823 and Jamaica 1831-32 each raised the cost of holding slavery in place, and the Abolition Act followed the Jamaican rising by eighteen months. The enslaved were following British politics closely — that is why the 1816 rebels thought emancipation had already been passed.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows resistance as a cause of abolition rather than a footnote to it, on the island planters thought was the safest in the empire.

evidence.author: Hilary McD. Beckles
evidence.work: Bussa: The 1816 Revolution in Barbados
evidence.publisher: University of the West Indies, Department of History
evidence.supports: The rising, its leaders and its suppression.

contested.note: The death toll and Bussa's own role come mostly from the planters' inquiry of 1818, a hostile source; the number executed after trial is especially uncertain.

events.title: The Demerara rebellion
events.summary: Between 10,000 and 13,000 enslaved people on the east coast of Demerara rose after hearing that new orders from London were being withheld. They locked up their overseers rather than kill them. Troops killed over 200 in two days, and dozens were executed afterwards.
events.significance: The trial and death in prison of the English missionary John Smith turned British public opinion decisively: within months there were mass meetings and petitions, and the anti-slavery movement changed from a lobby into a campaign. Emancipation was ten years away.

places.name: Plantation Success, East Coast Demerara
places.note: Where the rising began; Quamina was a deacon at the nearby Bethel chapel.

places.name: Georgetown
places.note: Where the courts martial were held and John Smith died in jail.

people.name: Quamina
people.role: African-born cooper and church deacon, hunted down and shot in the bush three weeks after the rising; his body was hung in chains

people.name: Jack Gladstone
people.role: Quamina's son and a leader of the rising; he was owned by John Gladstone, father of the future British prime minister, and was transported to St Lucia rather than executed

people.name: John Smith
people.role: London Missionary Society minister sentenced to death for not warning the authorities; he died of tuberculosis in a Georgetown jail before the reprieve arrived

people.name: John Murray
people.role: Governor of Demerara who withheld the London despatch that triggered the rising and directed the suppression

toll.note: Over 200 enslaved people were killed in the two days of suppression, and at least 45 were executed after courts martial, some with their heads displayed publicly. Three white people died. Counts come from the colony's own returns and from Emilia Viotti da Costa's reconstruction.

pedagogy.hook: The rebels of 1823 locked their overseers in the stocks instead of killing them. The British response killed over two hundred people in two days.

misconception.belief: Slave rebellions were violent uprisings that justified violent suppression.
misconception.correction: In Demerara the rebels deliberately restrained themselves: they seized weapons, put overseers in the stocks their own people had been punished in, and killed three people in total. The suppression killed over two hundred, and the trials produced more deaths still. British newspapers noticed the difference, and that is one reason the rising changed opinion at home.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The death of John Smith in a Georgetown jail did more to build the mass anti-slavery movement in Britain than any pamphlet, and the man who owned the rising's other leader was the father of a future prime minister.

evidence.author: Emilia Viotti da Costa
evidence.work: Crowns of Glory, Tears of Blood: The Demerara Slave Rebellion of 1823
evidence.supports: The rising, its restraint, the suppression and the trial of John Smith.

events.title: The Baptist War (Christmas Rebellion), Jamaica

endDate.note: Organised resistance collapsed in early January; trials and executions continued into the spring.

events.summary: Samuel Sharpe, a literate Baptist deacon in Montego Bay, organised a general strike for wages after Christmas. It became the largest rebellion in the British Caribbean: about 60,000 people took part, 200 estates burned, 14 white people and over 500 Black people died.
events.significance: It broke the planters' argument that slavery was stable. Eighteen months later Parliament passed the Abolition Act. Sharpe's own words to a missionary before he was hanged — that he would rather die than live in slavery — are among the very few first-person statements of purpose by a rebel leader to survive.

places.name: Montego Bay
places.note: Where Sharpe organised and where he was hanged on 23 May 1832; the square is named for him.

places.name: Kensington estate, St James
places.note: Where the first fire was set on 27 December 1831.

people.name: Samuel Sharpe
people.role: Baptist deacon who organised the strike and the rising; hanged on 23 May 1832, and a National Hero of Jamaica

people.name: Thomas Burchell
people.role: Baptist missionary whose chapel Sharpe preached in; imprisoned after the rising, and his chapel destroyed by the planters' Colonial Church Union

people.name: Somerset Lowry-Corry, Earl Belmore
people.role: Governor of Jamaica who declared martial law and presided over the courts martial

toll.note: About 200 enslaved people were killed in the fighting and between 312 and 340 executed afterwards, mostly by court martial; 14 white people died. The counts are from the colonial returns and from Michael Craton and Mary Reckord's work; the number executed varies between accounts.

pedagogy.hook: It began as a strike. Sixty thousand enslaved Jamaicans refused to return to work after Christmas 1831 unless they were paid.

misconception.belief: Abolition happened because British opinion changed.
misconception.correction: British opinion mattered, and it changed partly because of what enslaved people did. The Baptist War made Jamaica ungovernable, cost more than a million pounds in damage, and was followed by planters burning Baptist chapels — which turned British nonconformist congregations into an anti-slavery army overnight. Parliament passed the Abolition Act eighteen months after Sharpe was hanged.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the strongest single piece of evidence that the enslaved were agents of their own emancipation, and it began as a demand for wages rather than a call to arms.

evidence.author: Michael Craton
evidence.work: Testing the Chains: Resistance to Slavery in the British West Indies
evidence.supports: The rising, its scale and its suppression.

evidence.author: Mary Reckord
evidence.work: The Jamaica Slave Rebellion of 1831
evidence.supports: The organisation of the strike, Sharpe's role and the missionary connection.

events.title: The Slavery Abolition Act 1833

endDate.note: The date the Act took effect across the British Caribbean.

events.summary: Parliament abolished slavery in most of the British Empire, to take effect on 1 August 1834. It freed about 800,000 people, paid their owners £20 million in compensation, paid the freed nothing, and required most of them to work unpaid for their former owners for four more years as 'apprentices'.
events.significance: The £20 million was around 40 per cent of the government's annual expenditure, borrowed and added to the national debt. The loan was not fully redeemed until 2015. No compensation of any kind was paid to the people who had been enslaved.

people.name: Samuel Sharpe
people.role: led the Jamaican rising of 1831-32 whose scale made the Act politically unavoidable; hanged in May 1832

people.name: Mary Prince
people.role: Bermudian-born woman whose 1831 account of her own enslavement was the first by a Black woman published in Britain and was used directly in the abolition campaign

people.name: Thomas Fowell Buxton
people.role: led the parliamentary campaign for abolition after Wilberforce retired

people.name: Elizabeth Heyrick
people.role: Leicester Quaker whose 1824 pamphlet demanded immediate, not gradual, abolition, against the leadership of the anti-slavery society

toll.money: £20 million was paid to about 46,000 claimants who had owned people. Nothing was paid to the roughly 800,000 people freed.
toll.note: The number freed under the Act is from the Slave Compensation Commission's registers, which counted people in order to value them. India, Ceylon and St Helena were excluded from the Act; slavery there ended later.

pedagogy.hook: British taxpayers finished paying off the loan that compensated slave-owners in 2015. Descendants of the people who were enslaved helped pay it.

misconception.belief: Britain abolished slavery, so Britain was on the right side of it.
misconception.correction: Britain built the largest slave-trading operation of the eighteenth century and then dismantled it, under pressure from the enslaved and from its own abolitionists. When it did, it paid £20 million to the owners and nothing to the owned, and made the freed work unpaid for four more years. Abolition is a real achievement inside a system Britain made. Both clauses stay in the sentence.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: University College London's Legacies of British Slavery database has traced where the £20 million went: into country houses, railways, banks, insurance firms and family fortunes that are still identifiable today.

evidence.author: Catherine Hall, Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland, Katie Donington and Rachel Lang
evidence.work: Legacies of British Slave-ownership: Colonial Slavery and the Formation of Victorian Britain
evidence.supports: The compensation, who received it, and what they did with it.

evidence.author: Nicholas Draper
evidence.work: The Price of Emancipation: Slave-ownership, Compensation and British Society at the End of Slavery
evidence.supports: The £20 million, the 46,000 claimants and the structure of the compensation scheme.

events.title: The £20 million paid to slave-owners

date.note: The Slave Compensation Commission began issuing awards in the autumn of 1835; most Caribbean payments were made during 1836.

endDate.note: The last awards were settled in the early 1840s, many after litigation between claimants.

events.summary: The Slave Compensation Commission valued 800,000 enslaved people, priced by colony and by the kind of work they did, and paid about £20 million to roughly 46,000 claimants. Jamaica's owners got £6.16 million, British Guiana's £4.29 million. The people themselves got nothing.
events.significance: It was the largest state payout in British history until the bank bailouts of 2009, financed by a loan that appeared on the national accounts until 2015. Its records name every claimant, which is why the flow of slavery money into British institutions can now be traced street by street.

places.name: The National Debt Office, London
places.note: Where the compensation loan was administered.

people.name: John Gladstone
people.role: Liverpool merchant and the largest single claimant, awarded about £106,000 for 2,508 people in British Guiana and Jamaica; father of the prime minister William Ewart Gladstone

people.name: Nicholas Draper
people.role: historian whose reconstruction of the compensation records made the scale and destination of the money visible

toll.money: £20 million in 1834, equivalent to roughly 40 per cent of the government's annual expenditure that year. About 46,000 awards were made. The loan raised to pay it was only redeemed in 2015.
toll.note: Modern equivalents for the £20 million range from about £17 billion to over £100 billion depending on the method used, which is why this record gives the contemporary figure and its share of the budget instead.

pedagogy.hook: Britain valued 800,000 people, wrote cheques to the 46,000 who had owned them, and borrowed the money. The loan was still on the books in 2015.

misconception.belief: Slave-owners were a small group of distant Caribbean planters.
misconception.correction: The compensation records name about 46,000 claimants, and most of them lived in Britain. They included clergymen, widows, small investors and MPs, in every county of England, Scotland and Wales. Slave-ownership was a normal middle-class investment, which is why abolition had to be bought rather than simply legislated.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The records exist and are searchable, so this is the one part of the story a student can check for themselves: type a British town into the Legacies of British Slavery database and see who was paid.

evidence.author: Nicholas Draper
evidence.work: The Price of Emancipation: Slave-ownership, Compensation and British Society at the End of Slavery
evidence.supports: The commission, the awards, the claimants and the loan.

evidence.author: Catherine Hall, Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland, Katie Donington and Rachel Lang
evidence.work: Legacies of British Slave-ownership: Colonial Slavery and the Formation of Victorian Britain
evidence.supports: Where the compensation money went in British society.

contested.note: Any modern-money equivalent of the £20 million is contested: retail price, average earnings and share-of-GDP measures give figures an order of magnitude apart, and this record deliberately avoids choosing one.

events.title: The end of apprenticeship, 1 August 1838
events.summary: The four-to-six-year 'apprenticeship' imposed on freed people in 1834 was abandoned two years early, after apprentices' resistance, evidence of continued flogging including of women, and a campaign in Britain led by the Quaker Joseph Sturge. On 1 August 1838 about 700,000 people became fully free.
events.significance: It is the real emancipation date for most of the British Caribbean, and it came early because the system failed on the ground. Emancipation Day, 1 August, is a public holiday across the region and in Canada; almost nowhere marks 1834.

places.name: Spanish Town, Jamaica
places.note: Where the Jamaican assembly voted to end apprenticeship early after mass refusals to work.

people.name: Joseph Sturge
people.role: Birmingham Quaker who travelled to the Caribbean in 1836, published what he found, and led the British campaign to end apprenticeship

people.name: James Williams
people.role: Jamaican apprentice whose 1837 narrative of being repeatedly flogged and treadmilled while legally free was published in Britain and helped destroy the system

people.name: Thomas Fowell Buxton
people.role: kept the pressure on in Parliament

pedagogy.hook: For four years after Britain 'abolished slavery', freed people worked 40 hours a week for their former owners for nothing, and could still be flogged.

misconception.belief: Slavery in the British Empire ended in 1834.
misconception.correction: On 1 August 1834 enslaved people over the age of six became "apprentices" bound to their former owners for four years in the fields, working most of the week unpaid, punishable by flogging and the treadmill. Only Antigua and Bermuda skipped it. It ended two years early because apprentices refused to cooperate.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains why Emancipation Day across the Caribbean is 1 August 1838, not 1834, and why the date a textbook gives for the end of slavery tells you how carefully it has read the Act.

evidence.author: Thomas C. Holt
evidence.work: The Problem of Freedom: Race, Labor, and Politics in Jamaica and Britain, 1832-1938
evidence.supports: Apprenticeship, its failure, and what freedom meant in practice afterwards.

evidence.author: James Williams
evidence.work: A Narrative of Events since the First of August 1834, by James Williams, an Apprenticed Labourer in Jamaica
evidence.supports: First-hand account of punishment under apprenticeship.

events.title: The first indentured Indians reach the Caribbean

endDate.note: The date the Government of India ended recruitment for indenture; existing contracts ran on to 1920.

events.summary: The ships Whitby and Hesperus landed 396 Indian labourers in British Guiana, recruited for John Gladstone's plantations before apprenticeship had even ended. Over the next eighty years about 430,000 Indians were shipped to the British Caribbean under five-year contracts.
events.significance: Indenture replaced slavery on the sugar estates within four years of emancipation. It was not slavery — there was a contract, a wage and an end date — but workers could be jailed for leaving the estate, lived in the same barracks, and most never got the return passage they were promised.

places.name: Plantation Vreed-en-Hoop, Demerara
places.note: One of John Gladstone's estates, where the first indentured Indians were landed in May 1838.

places.name: Nelson Island, Gulf of Paria, Trinidad
places.note: The immigration depot where arriving Indians were quarantined and processed.

people.name: John Gladstone
people.role: Liverpool merchant and slave-owner who petitioned the government in 1836 to import Indian labour, two years before emancipation was complete; father of the future prime minister

people.name: Bechu
people.role: indentured labourer in British Guiana who gave evidence to the 1897 royal commission and wrote to the press about conditions on the estates

people.name: Mohandas Gandhi
people.role: his campaign against indenture, begun in South Africa, was central to the Indian pressure that ended recruitment in 1917

toll.note: About 239,000 Indians went to British Guiana, 143,900 to Trinidad, 36,400 to Jamaica and smaller numbers to the other islands, according to the colonial immigration returns. Roughly a quarter to a third returned to India; most did not.

pedagogy.hook: The first indentured Indians in the Caribbean were shipped in 1838 to plantations owned by John Gladstone — who had just been paid £106,000 in compensation for losing the people he had enslaved on the same estates.

misconception.belief: Emancipation ended forced labour in the British Caribbean.
misconception.correction: Emancipation ended chattel slavery and immediately produced a substitute. Between 1838 and 1917 about 430,000 Indians came to the British Caribbean on criminally enforceable five-year contracts: leaving the estate without a pass was punishable by imprisonment. Historians argue about the word slavery here; nobody disputes what the planters designed it to solve.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is why roughly 40 per cent of Guyanese and 35 per cent of Trinidadians are of Indian descent, why Diwali is a public holiday in both countries, and why Caribbean politics is still shaped by a labour decision taken in the 1830s.

evidence.author: Hugh Tinker
evidence.work: A New System of Slavery: The Export of Indian Labour Overseas, 1830-1920
evidence.supports: The origins, scale and conditions of Indian indenture.

evidence.author: K. O. Laurence
evidence.work: A Question of Labour: Indentured Immigration into Trinidad and British Guiana, 1875-1917
evidence.supports: Recruitment, contracts, estate conditions and the numbers who returned.

contested.note: Hugh Tinker's phrase 'a new system of slavery' is disputed by historians who point to the contract, the wage, the return passage and the fact that indentured workers used the courts; the argument is about how much those differences meant in practice, not about the conditions themselves.

events.title: The Morant Bay rebellion

endDate.note: Martial law in the county of Surrey ran for thirty days from 13 October and ended on 13 November.

events.summary: Paul Bogle led a march from Stony Gut to the Morant Bay courthouse over land, justice and hunger. The militia fired; the crowd killed 18 people. Governor Eyre declared martial law and troops killed 439 people, executed 354 more after courts martial, flogged 600 and burned about 1,000 homes.
events.significance: It ended representative government in Jamaica: the assembly voted itself out of existence rather than share power, and crown colony rule followed for 80 years. In Britain it split the intellectual class, with John Stuart Mill's Jamaica Committee trying to prosecute Eyre for murder and Thomas Carlyle's committee defending him.

places.name: Morant Bay courthouse
places.note: Where the confrontation happened on 11 October 1865.

places.name: Stony Gut, St Thomas
places.note: Paul Bogle's village and chapel; burned by troops during the suppression.

people.name: Paul Bogle
people.role: Native Baptist deacon and small farmer who led the march; hanged on 24 October 1865 and a National Hero of Jamaica

people.name: George William Gordon
people.role: mixed-race member of the assembly and Bogle's political ally; arrested in Kingston, moved into the martial-law district to be tried, and hanged on 23 October; a National Hero of Jamaica

people.name: Edward John Eyre
people.role: Governor of Jamaica who declared martial law, approved the executions and was recalled; twice prosecuted in England and never convicted

people.name: John Stuart Mill
people.role: chaired the Jamaica Committee, which tried to have Eyre prosecuted for murder

people.name: Thomas Carlyle
people.role: led the Eyre Defence Committee, supported by Dickens, Ruskin and Tennyson

toll.note: The royal commission of 1866 counted 439 people killed by troops and militia, 354 of them executed after courts martial, along with 600 floggings and about 1,000 houses burned. Eighteen officials and militiamen died on 11 October. These are the commission's own figures.

pedagogy.hook: Eighteen officials died at Morant Bay. The British response killed 439 people, flogged 600 and burned a thousand homes.

misconception.belief: British colonial rule after emancipation was mild, legalistic government.
misconception.correction: The 1866 royal commission — a British body — found that the punishments were 'excessive', that the floggings were 'reckless' and that the executions were carried out with 'unnecessary rigour'. The dispute in Britain was not about the facts, which were established, but about whether a governor could be tried for them. He could not: two prosecutions failed and Eyre kept his pension.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It cost Jamaica its elected assembly for eighty years, it made Bogle and Gordon national heroes, and it forced Victorian Britain to argue in public about whether colonial subjects had the protection of English law.

evidence.author: Gad Heuman
evidence.work: The Killing Time: The Morant Bay Rebellion in Jamaica
evidence.supports: The rebellion, the suppression, the royal commission and the political consequences.

evidence.author: Catherine Hall
evidence.work: Civilising Subjects: Metropole and Colony in the English Imagination 1830-1867
evidence.supports: The Eyre controversy in Britain and what it revealed about Victorian ideas of race and rule.

events.title: The West Indian labour rebellions, 1934-1939

date.note: The date Antonio Soberanis's Unemployed Brigade began mass meetings in Belize; the wave of strikes, marches and riots ran island by island for five years.

events.summary: Strikes, marches and riots swept the British Caribbean from Belize in 1934 to Trinidad's oilfields in 1937 and Jamaica in 1938. Police and troops killed at least 46 people in Jamaica and 14 in Trinidad. Britain sent a royal commission under Lord Moyne and then suppressed its report until 1945.
events.significance: This is where modern Caribbean politics begins: every major party and trade union in the English-speaking Caribbean traces to these years. The Moyne Commission found conditions so bad that publishing it during the war was thought to be a gift to German propaganda.

places.name: Fyzabad, Trinidad
places.note: Where Uriah Butler's oilfield rising began on 19 June 1937.

places.name: Frome estate, Westmoreland, Jamaica
places.note: Where police killed strikers in May 1938, setting off the Jamaican rebellion.

people.name: Tubal Uriah 'Buzz' Butler
people.role: Grenadian-born oilfield worker whose 1937 strike in Trinidad set off the region's biggest confrontation; jailed for most of the war

people.name: Alexander Bustamante
people.role: Jamaican union leader detained in 1940, later first Prime Minister of Jamaica

people.name: Norman Manley
people.role: Jamaican lawyer who defended strikers and founded the People's National Party in 1938

people.name: Clement Payne
people.role: organiser whose deportation from Barbados in July 1937 set off riots in which police killed fourteen people

people.name: Antonio Soberanis Gómez
people.role: Belizean barber whose Unemployed Brigade began the wave of protest in 1934

people.name: Walter Guinness, Lord Moyne
people.role: chaired the royal commission whose report Britain kept secret until 1945

toll.note: At least 46 people were killed in Jamaica in 1938, 14 in Trinidad in 1937 and 14 in Barbados in 1937, with further deaths in St Kitts, St Vincent and British Guiana. Colonial casualty returns were compiled island by island and no single authoritative total exists.

pedagogy.hook: Britain sent a royal commission to the Caribbean in 1938, read what it found, and refused to publish it for seven years.

misconception.belief: Caribbean independence movements began after the Second World War.
misconception.correction: They began in the sugar fields and oilfields between 1934 and 1939. Every major party and union in the English-speaking Caribbean — Jamaica's JLP and PNP, Trinidad's unions, Barbados's BLP, Antigua's ATLU — grew directly out of those strikes. The Moyne Commission's recommendations, including universal suffrage, were the price Britain paid for order, and it paid it before the war ended.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the moment when the Caribbean's politics stopped being about planters and governors and became about workers and votes — and the moment Britain decided that reform was cheaper than repression.

evidence.author: O. Nigel Bolland
evidence.work: The Politics of Labour in the British Caribbean: The Social Origins of Authoritarianism and Democracy in the Labour Movement
evidence.supports: The 1934-39 rebellions island by island and their political consequences.

evidence.author: Richard Hart
evidence.work: Labour Rebellions of the 1930s in the British Caribbean Region Colonies
evidence.publisher: Socialist History Society and Caribbean Labour Solidarity
evidence.supports: The chronology of the strikes and the casualties, by a participant in Jamaican labour politics.

contested.note: There is no single authoritative death toll for the whole five-year wave: casualties were recorded colony by colony, and the figures in different accounts do not reconcile.

events.title: The West Indies Federation
events.summary: Ten British Caribbean colonies federated, with a parliament at Chaguaramas in Trinidad and Grantley Adams of Barbados as Prime Minister. It had no power to tax, no customs union and no freedom of movement. Jamaica voted to leave in a referendum in September 1961, and the Federation was dissolved in May 1962.
events.significance: Britain wanted one large Caribbean state to become independent rather than a dozen small ones. Instead it got twelve. Every English-speaking Caribbean country's size, and much of its economic difficulty since, follows from the Federation's collapse.

places.name: Chaguaramas, Trinidad
places.note: The federal capital site — on land the United States held as a naval base under a wartime lease Britain had granted without consulting Trinidadians.

people.name: Grantley Adams
people.role: Barbadian labour leader and the Federation's only Prime Minister

people.name: Norman Manley
people.role: Jamaican Premier who campaigned for the Federation and lost the 1961 referendum

people.name: Alexander Bustamante
people.role: Jamaican opposition leader who campaigned to leave and won

people.name: Eric Williams
people.role: Trinidadian Premier who took his country out after Jamaica left, saying that one from ten leaves nought

people.name: Theophilus Albert Marryshow
people.role: Grenadian journalist who campaigned for West Indian federation from 1915 and did not live to see it fail

pedagogy.hook: Jamaicans voted by 54 per cent to 46 to leave the West Indies Federation, and Trinidad's premier answered with the arithmetic that killed it: one from ten leaves nought.

misconception.belief: Colonies became independent as the natural units their people wanted.
misconception.correction: The English-speaking Caribbean nearly became one country of three million people. Britain preferred it, and the federal parliament sat for four years. It failed because it had no power to tax, no customs union and no free movement, and because Jamaica and Trinidad did not want to pay for the small islands.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains why there are twelve independent states and several territories in a region of seven million people, and why they built CARICOM afterwards to recover some of what the Federation was supposed to do.

evidence.author: John Mordecai
evidence.work: The West Indies: The Federal Negotiations
evidence.supports: The negotiations, the structure of the Federation and its collapse, by its former federal secretary.

evidence.author: B. W. Higman
evidence.work: A Concise History of the Caribbean
evidence.supports: The Federation's design, the Jamaican referendum and the regional consequences.

events.title: The Anguilla revolution and Operation Sheepskin
events.summary: Anguillians expelled the St Kitts police from their island rather than be part of a self-governing St Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla, voted 1,813 to 5 to break away, and declared a republic. On 19 March 1969 Britain landed 315 paratroopers and 40 London policemen. Nobody was hurt.
events.significance: It is the only case in the history of decolonisation of a British colony rebelling in order to remain British, and the only British military intervention in the Caribbean aimed at keeping a territory in the empire rather than out of it.

places.name: The Valley, Anguilla
places.note: Where the island's provisional government sat and where the paratroopers landed nearby at dawn.

people.name: Ronald Webster
people.role: leader of the Anguillian revolution and later the island's first Chief Minister

people.name: Atlin Harrigan
people.role: Anguillian who raised the flag and edited the Beacon, the island's paper through the revolution

people.name: Robert Bradshaw
people.role: Premier of St Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla, whose plans for the island Anguillians were rebelling against

people.name: William Whitlock
people.role: British minister whose visit in March 1969 ended with him being driven off the island, which triggered the intervention

toll.note: Nobody was killed in the revolution or the British landing. The main casualties were reputational: the British press called the operation the Bay of Piglets.

pedagogy.hook: In 1969 Britain invaded one of its own colonies to stop it leaving another colony. The islanders had asked to be re-colonised, and greeted the paratroopers with flowers.

misconception.belief: Decolonisation was a single movement in one direction: colonies wanting out, Britain resisting.
misconception.correction: Anguilla wanted in. Anguillians had petitioned to be governed directly from London in 1825, 1872 and 1958, and in 1967 they voted 1,813 to 5 against being part of an independent St Kitts. Britain spent three years trying to send them back before finally separating them in 1980. Small territories often preferred a distant empire to a nearer neighbour.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the cleanest counter-example in the whole atlas, and it explains why fourteen British Overseas Territories still exist: most of them, like Anguilla, chose it.

evidence.author: Donald E. Westlake
evidence.work: Under an English Heaven
evidence.supports: The revolution, the negotiations and Operation Sheepskin, from interviews and contemporary reporting.

evidence.author: B. W. Higman
evidence.work: A Concise History of the Caribbean
evidence.supports: Associated statehood and Anguilla's separation from St Kitts and Nevis.
